#2853. Broncos eager to use bye week to prepare for the stretch run

The Denver Broncos head into their bye week in a really good spot.

After a great road win in Charlotte against the Carolina Panthers, the Broncos sit at 7-2. The bye comes after a gauntlet of a start to the season, in which Denver played some of the best teams in the NFL.

For now, the Broncos lead the AFC West standings, are near the top of the AFC playoff seedings for home-field advantage, and are clearly one of the best teams in the league.

Now, with some injuries and guys dinged up, the bye comes at a great time.

We're in a really good spot, obviously where you want to be," Broncos quarterback Bo Nix said to the media after the win over the Panthers. "You want to be first in your division. You want to be winning football games. We've played a really tough part of our schedule. At 7-2, we feel really confident, but at the same time, there's a lot of things that we could get better at. We've said this every week, and some weeks we've gotten better at other things; some things we still got to clean up.

"But overall, we're finding explosive plays, doing better on third down today, stayed out of the third-and-long situations like we've been wanting to do. At the end of the day, we scored enough to win the game, and that's what's important going into the bye."

"You get stuck in Groundhog Day over time doing the same thing over and over every week. I can tell you exactly what I'm doing every day of the week, so this will be a good break, good rest for us. We all feel really good about it, feel like we need it, our coaches. We'll get some rest. Players will get some rest, and then we'll start right back up next week with our next opponent. It's just going to be a good time to relax and also debrief and look back at a few things and just have a great breakdown and sort of digest where we've been and what we're doing and where we want to go."

Since coming to Denver, Sean Payton knows how to handle the bye week and has the post-bye week figured out. The Broncos are 3-0 coming out of the bye under Payton. A big reason why is the time off he gives the players.

What waits for Denver after the bye is the Las Vegas Raiders on Nov. 22 at home.

"I think I told you guys this. I went two or three years practicing on Wednesdays and Thursdays, and we were OK. I can't recall the year, but I called (Kansas City Chiefs head coach) Andy (Reid) one year in Philly. He was 9-0 after the bye … and he just said I get them out of here, and I see them the next Monday. And ever since we've done that, we've been pretty good after the bye as well. So, they'll rest. The guys getting treatment will be in, and everyone else will. At some point, we'll get a jump start on Vegas."

Given how close the Broncos like to play and win their games, the bye comes at a great time for the fans, too.

#2852. Nvidia’s turmoil is prompting a rotation across chip stocks. Here's what we know

Nvidia's leadership crisis is creating an opening for its biggest rivals, as investors bet that Jensen Huang's departure could loosen the AI chip giant's grip on an industry it has long dominated.

From AMD to Broadcom and even partner TSMC, chipmakers are emerging as potential beneficiaries of the upheaval, with market watchers pointing to a possible redistribution of manufacturing capacity and a narrowing of Nvidia's technological lead.

"What you're seeing in markets now is a bit of a rotation into other advanced chip design companies, on the assumption that this will enable other companies effectively to catch up," said Mark Franklin, head of multi-asset solutions for Asia at Manulife Investment Management.

That shift comes as Nvidia grapples with the fallout from Huang's resignation, following revelations about his multiple affairs including with a woman believed by the U.S. intelligence community to be a Chinese spy.

Huang's departure could give competitors an opportunity to close the gap as Nvidia navigates leadership uncertainty, Franklin highlighted, adding that the rotation was already helping fuel positive momentum in other semiconductor stocks.

Farzin Azam, managing director of equities trading at Mizuho Americas, said the shift was evident on trading desks, with investors moving toward chipmakers less exposed to Nvidia's management turmoil.

"Names such as TSMC, names such as Broadcom, names such as Advanced Micro will come as winners of this because they don't have this overhang of a management disruption," Azam told CNBC.

Nvidia shares have plunged 11% so far this week, while rivals AMD and Broadcom have gained 30% and 24%, respectively.

TSMC, which manufactures Nvidia's most advanced processors, has also rallied 11% over the same period, as it stands to benefit, irrespective of which chip designer gains or loses. A rotation away from AI names perceived as risky also positions TSMC as a relatively safer play for those bullish on the overall theme.

The rotation away from Nvidia has also extended into less speculative corners of the semiconductor industry, including analog chipmakers such as Texas Instruments, Analog Devices and Infineon, as investors adopt a more defensive stance, he said.

Texas Instruments has climbed about 13% this week, while Analog Devices and Germany's Infineon have advanced 12% and 14%, respectively.

Beyond the immediate market reaction, Huang's exit could fundamentally reshape competition across the AI supply chain, according to Dylan Patel, chief executive at semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis.

Patel said Huang had personally cultivated relationships with manufacturers and component suppliers, helping Nvidia secure scarce production capacity ahead of rivals.

That advantage could now come under pressure as companies including Google and Amazon strive to expand AI chip production.

The two hyperscalers were already gaining ground in securing supply-chain capacity relative to Nvidia, Patel said, and could accelerate those efforts without Huang's influence over suppliers.

"If Nvidia can't muster the supply chain, then technology is the only competitive advantage. And without Jensen, can they maintain technology advantages? Given they're only a year ahead of their biggest competitors, it's not like the gap is massive," Patel said.

The challenge is particularly acute as hyperscalers increasingly develop proprietary AI chips to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, while AMD and other semiconductor companies race to capture a larger slice of the market.

Yet the upheaval doesn't necessarily signal an end to the broader AI investment boom.

Franklin noted that major technology companies are projecting higher AI spending in 2027, with further increases possible in 2028, signaling the investment cycle remains structurally intact even as investors reassess which companies stand to benefit.

The bigger question is whether growing competition and the proliferation of open-source technologies eventually commoditize AI capabilities, putting pressure on chip prices and investment returns, he said.

For Nvidia, the immediate outlook may depend less on its earnings than on whether its next leadership team can reassure investors.

Azam said the stock appeared inexpensive relative to its earnings growth prospects, but warned that ongoing investigations and management uncertainty could limit any sustained recovery.

He expects Nvidia's earnings due Nov. 17 to remain strong, with investors likely to focus more closely on management's plans for navigating the crisis.

The result could be a reshuffling of winners within the semiconductor industry, with Franklin saying that investors were becoming more comfortable staying invested while rotating and diversifying their portfolios, instead of abandoning the market altogether.

#2850. Toronto falls to stacked Sixers’ offence

The Toronto Raptors continued a challenging stretch of their schedule tonight, facing the Philadelphia 76ers on the second night of a back-to-back, this time on the road. After coming apart at the seams despite an early lead against Boston, the Raptors' intention to move on was thwarted by a Sixers team that handed the Raptors a similar loss. A significant early lead dwindled by the half, ultimately leading to Toronto falling, this time 112 to 123.

To no surprise, Philly's big names of Joel Embiid (20 points), Jaylen Brown (18 points), VJ Edgecombe (15 points), and TJ Maxey (27 points) carried the Sixers. Anfernee Simons was their most productive bench player, offering clutch long-range shooting that gave the rest of the team space to operate, finishing with 17 points in the process.

Toronto saw excellent performances from RJ Barrett who finished with 31 points, 14 rebounds, and 5 assists, Immanuel Quickley who had 26 points, 4 rebounds, and 6 assists, and Collin Murray-Boyles chipping in 14 points, 4 assists, and 5 blocks.

The Raptors had their hands full early, needing to answer for a number of offensive weapons on a Sixers team that is building plenty of hype for a championship contender. They didn't need to face LeBron James who sat due to sciatica, but the remaining four of their starters remained a formidable challenge.

Toronto targeted Embiid early, forcing him into awkward defensive coverages that required speed and lateral movement that he struggled with as a result of his laundry list of injuries. After knee-to-knee contact, Embiid briefly visited the locker room but returned a few minutes later.

RJ and Quickley were quick to answer their less-than-savory performances last night. Quickley worked hard to distribute the ball and get everyone going early while RJ hit a pair of threes on consecutive possessions.

Just like last night, their offense was running smoothly. They built a significant 33-16 lead, and it felt like everything was going in the Raptors' favour until in the final two minutes of the frame, the tide slowly started to turn. Philly went on an unanswered 8-point run to close the quarter.

In the second quarter, the Sixers were able to close the gap and draw ahead, making much of the second frame a back-and-forth contest.

Kentavious Caldwell-Pope and Anfernee Simons showed their abilities from beyond the arc, creating spacing for the Sixers' starters to operate in the paint where they're comfortable. Tyrese Maxey was almost unstoppable from virtually everywhere on the floor. Jaylen Brown started to come alive as well, an equally challenging offensive player to find an answer for.

Toronto had contributions from everyone, with CMB, Barrett, Martin, and Battle all making long range shots. Their ball movement helped limit poor shot selection, and even when they were missing shots, Walter stood out as having a motor, with a phenomenal put-back that showed the Raptors were going to fight through the fatigue. By the end of the half, the game was all tied up.

The third quarter mirrored the second, going blow-for-blow with Philly. Ties and lead changes riddled the period, with neither team able to build any kind of momentum or separation.

Alijah Martin has impressed with his continued active defence and fearless scoring, willing to take the ball through anyone. At times, the minutes with mostly bench players on the floor actually felt more cohesive and productive than without.

Despite best efforts, Philly's top four firepower was hard to contend with. Late in the third, a series of costly turnovers allowed the Sixers to get out in transition, managing a 8-0 run to build their largest lead, a 9-point advantage before the final twelve minutes of play.

Toronto's fatigue might have played a role as this game started to get away from them. Second effort isn't enough when you're struggling to make second and third shots, and despite their effort, a lot of them rolled off the rim and couldn't be recovered. Murray-Boyles' effort, however, should be celebrated. On one end, he was blocking shots and playing tough defence, and on the other, good screening and off-ball movement helped him be a standout on the court.

In the end, it wasn't enough to overcome Philly, and Toronto continues to seek their first win against a team over 0.500. Next, they'll face New York twice, with the first of the matchups on Sunday at 6 pm.

#2849. Donald Trump Jr. exits advisory role at Kalshi prediction market

Prediction market platform Kalshi ended its advisory contract with Donald Trump Jr. in response to his venture capital firm, 1789 Capital, also holding a stake in rival platform Polymarket, according to Kalshi's spokesperson.

Conversations on Trump Jr.'s exit began in August after 1789 Capital announced a major stake in Polymarket, the spokesperson said. It was a mutual arrangement, with both Kalshi and Trump Jr. agreeing it was a conflict of interest to keep the president's son as an advisor while serving as a top investor for Polymarket, the spokesperson added.

Trump Jr.'s departure comes after Democrats secured a majority across the House and the Senate, with the party expected to crack down on the prediction market industry. While Trump Jr. has exited Kalshi, he still serves as an advisor to Polymarket. His ties to the industry could make prediction markets an easy target for lawmakers to go after, Joseph Konizeski, a former trial attorney in the CFTC, previously told CNBC.

In early October, Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour said on MS NOW that Trump Jr.'s connection to the company creates an "optics issue," but added that it has never relied on that relationship to gain favor with the government.

Kalshi first named Donald Trump Jr. a strategic advisor for the company in January 2025.

Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

#2847. ‘Elite pocket passer’ Jared Goff not being underestimated by Patriots

No matter where you go on Al Gore's internet, whenever there is a list of the NFL's best quarterbacks you find familiar faces near the top. Mahomes, Allen, Burrow, sometimes — when he has his turnover tendencies under control — Maye.

Jared Goff, on the other hand, typically resides further down the list. It can't be due to a lack of production, at least this year: Goff has been one of the most efficient quarterbacks in football while leading the Detroit Lions to a 6-2 record.

But while fans and analysts might be underestimating the 32-year-old, his next opponent sure is not. The New England Patriots are well aware of the damage he has done, and is capable of doing this Sunday in Munich.

"I think Jared's playing at a high level," said head coach Mike Vrabel. "Continued the last three years, he's been at a high level."

"He's an elite pocket passer," linebacker Robert Spillane added. "He loves to step up in the middle of the pocket and deliver the ball downfield. Really can do it all. First overall pick for a reason, who just continued throughout his career to show why he was a first overall pick. Somebody who's going to get the ball to all of his guys."

Distributing the ball to the weapons mentioned by Spillane, as well as to NFL scrimmage yards leader Jahmyr Gibbs, Goff has played some of the best football of his career so far in 2026. The numbers show it, too.

In eight games thus far, he has completed over two thirds of his passes (185 of 273) for 2,134 yards, 15 touchdowns and just two interceptions. Whether you use traditional metrics or advanced ones such as EPA or CPOE Goff typically finds himself in the top 10 if not close to the league lead.

He might not be the same big-play hunter as the quarterback the Patriots faced last week, Green Bay's Jordan Love, but Goff has been steady and operating well within Detroit's offensive system.

"The quarterback runs the show very well," said defensive coordinator Zak Kuhr. "He gets them into plays for the whole unit, and he kind of has the freedom to do that."

There might not be one particular part about Goff's game or his physical abilities that stands out relative to other quarterbacks, which might contribute to his perception. However, that does not mean he cannot put intense pressure on any defense.

A large part of that is his willingness to disperse the football, and the chemistry and experience he has built with the players surrounding him.

"He's a great quarterback," said safety Kevin Byard. "He does a great job when he's able to stand in the middle of the pocket, he can fire across the middle of the field, deep, with obviously the weapons that they have with Jameson Williams, a guy who can stretch the field, and obviously Amon-Ra St. Brown, who's a guy who can work the middle of the field, work the intermediates and things like that. And Sam LaPorta's a really good tight end."

"He loves [Jameson Williams] down the field. He loves Amon-Ra underneath, LaPorta all over the field," added Spillane. "We know we have a huge challenge for us ahead."

#2846. Cade Cunningham has historic night as Pistons outlast Wizards in bloody battle

AJ Dybantsa collided with Cade Cunningham during the Washington Wizards' game against the Detroit Pistons on Thursday, Nov. 12 and was bloodied on the play.

Dybantsa didn't miss any action and even sent the game into its second overtime, but Cunningham ended up being the star of the game. The Pistons guard scored a career-high 52 points at Capital One Arena to dismantle the Wizards 144-140 in double overtime. He added 11 assists, five rebounds, a steal and a block. He did not commit a turnover.

According to the league, he is the first player ever to notch at least 50 points and 10 assists in a game without turning the ball over.

The 2021 No. 1 overall pick passed his previous career high when he scored his 47th point in the first overtime with a 3-point bucket that tied the game at 130.

As for the collision, with 26 seconds left in regulation and the Wizards up 118-117, Cunningham was dribbling the ball and attempted to twirl and switch directions. The Wizards rookie and 2026 No. 1 overall pick was guarding him and, when Cunningham spun back around, his jaw smacked into the side of Dybantsa's face.

Dybantsa fell backwards onto the court and grabbed his mouth as he laid on his back. Blood started dripping from his mouth. A trainer tended to him as he continued lying on the hardwood.

The game went into overtime with the score tied at 121 at the end of the fourth quarter. Dybantsa sent the game to a second overtime, seemingly no worse for wear. He took a pass from Trae Young, dribbled and took a jump shot at the charity stripe to tie the game at 132 with 0.1 second left.

The rookie finished with five points, eight rebounds and four assists for the Wizards.

Washington was led by Young, who had 37 points and 14 assists. Anthony Davis notched a double-double of his own with 30 points and 15 boards. Alex Sarr added 30 points and nine rebounds.

#2844. Yankees 2026 Roster Report Cards: Luis García Jr.

It's very tempting to want to love Luis García Jr. His lefty swing reminds me so much of Robinson Canó, and indeed my own swing is modeled after the former Yankee All-Star. At the time the Yankees dealt for him, desperate to get some kind of thump in an Aaron Judge-less lineup, he led the National League in slugging. When he came to New York, he clubbed a long home run in his second game, a worthy introduction to the Bronx faithful. After that, he was fine in the regular season, dreadful in October, and now is the source of a bit of a logjam on the roster.

2026 Stats (With Yankees): 43 G, 169 PA, 21 R, 42 H, 6 2B, 7 HR, 16 RBI, 1 SB, .264/.302/.434, 102 OPS+, 104 wRC+, 0.5 fWAR, 0.6 bWAR.

To Brian Cashman's credit he made more than one deal for bats at the deadline, but neither Heliot Ramos nor García Jr. really had the impact I'm sure he planned. Luis came in in grand style:

That the Yankees went on to lose that game, one of the stupider of the year and what a list that makes, maybe says something about García Jr. as a Yankee. Getting him was the right move, it just never really paid off. I was surprised to see that he actually managed an 87 wRC+ in the postseason, because I genuinely would have thought he posted half of that.

To be fair, he was On One against the Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, hitting .500, but then kind of everyone did that against the Red Sox in those two games. Facing the Rays in the ALDS Luis went 1-for-10, a -56 wRC+. The Yankees only who played three games against the Rays, if García Jr. went 1-for-10 in a random series in July we probably wouldn't even notice, but it happened when the lights were brightest.

I've said this a lot about the 2026 Yankees, but Luis didn't really do himself many favors. Yes, he has that big home run in his second game against the Cardinals, then he went two weeks without another dinger. He slugged .560 in Washington, .434 in New York. His strikeout rate jumped five points.

I do wonder how much the dimensions of Yankee Stadium worked against him. Luis was on pace for 33 doubles across 600 PA while with the Nationals, down to 22 over 600 PA in the Bronx. Yankee Stadium is a tremendous ballpark to hit home runs in, and not very friendly to other kinds of extra-base hits. The short right field wall was absolutely a reason why the club brought Heliot Ramos in, and maybe they believed that smooth lefty swing would turn some of those doubles into dingers for García Jr., but that didn't happen, at least in 2026.

Moving into 2027, the Yankee have once again assembled a roster with so many first base/DH types. Giancarlo Stanton will be on the roster, Ben Rice is not going to be a catcher, Aaron Judge will almost certainly see less time in the outfield than we're used to, if for no other reason than the game's best hitter needs to sometimes be saved from himself. Then there's García Jr., who on paper is possibly a better hitter than Stanton but not better than Rice or Judge, but also probably isn't good enough at second base to merit uprooting Anthony Volpe.

Maybe that's the project for this winter, making Luis García Jr. a functional second baseman and stick him in some kind of first base/second base platoon role. This gets complicated if there's a lockout and teams can't communicate with players, and is further complicated by the fact that the very bad Washington Nationals gave Luis 0 innings at the keystone last year.

I want to love Luis García Jr. I don't think his performance in 2026 merits that love. I am hopeful, perhaps foolishly, that it will in 2027.

#2843. Russian crude production rebounds after Trump diesel deal, IEA says as oil markets return to surplus

Russia's crude oil production rose to 8.73 million barrels a day in October, a 210,000-barrel-a-day surge, as a rebound in Gulf shipments pushes oil markets into a surplus for the first time since the Middle East conflict began, the International Energy Agency said Friday.

Global supply and stocks have both swelled, though Middle East disruptions and attacks on Russian energy infrastructure tightened diesel supply, according to the agency's latest monthly oil market report.

"Persistent attacks on Russian energy infrastructure continue to choke off the country's diesel supplies to international markets, adding to losses from the Middle East," the IEA noted.

U.S. President Donald Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin to supply diesel to global markets on Oct. 9. The Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control issued a general license authorizing certain transactions involving Russian-origin diesel through April 7, 2027.

Crude supply can rise even as diesel remains tight, with refinery capacity and refined product exports still constrained.

Global oil supply reached 105.4 million barrels a day in October, up 2.3 million barrels a day from September, the IEA said, adding that supply rose by an "extraordinary" 5.3 million barrels a day since August, despite ongoing attacks on energy infrastructure and tankers.

Inventories also rose for the first time since June, with observed global stocks increasing by 52 million barrels in October, or 1.7 million barrels a day.

"The oil market is showing tentative signs of rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran," IEA analysts observed.

Higher export flows have strengthened supply expectations for the fourth quarter, with Middle East and Russia losses partly offset by growth from the U.S., Canada, Brazil, Argentina and Guyana, which together are set to boost output by 1.6 million barrels a day this year.

The IEA has raised its fourth-quarter supply estimate by 3.3 million barrels a day, and now forecasts a 6.6 million barrels per day increase in 2027.

#2842. Recap: Wizards lose 144-140 in double-OT thriller vs. Pistons

The Washington Wizards' struggles continued Thursday night, as they fell to the Detroit Pistons 144-140 in double overtime (8-3) at Capital One Arena to extend their losing streak to six games.

Playing the second night of a back-to-back after a 114-101 loss to the Indiana Pacers on Wednesday, Washington (4-9) once again could not close out a close game in the fourth quarter, first or second overtime periods, which led to its second loss to the Pistons in the past four days after Monday night's 122-111 loss in Detroit.

Washington got out to an early 17-10 lead thanks to triples from Alex Sarr, Kyshawn George and Trae Young – which looked to be a positive sign from a team that entered the contest shooting 29.8% from distance.

Sarr started the game a perfect 4-for-4 from the field, quickly notching 10 points in the first quarter. His counterpart in the front court, Anthony Davis recorded 10 points on 5-of-7 shooting in first-quarter, to join Sarr in double-figure scoring.

However, in a lineup starring Trae Young, Tre Johnson, Bub Carrington, Bilal Coulibaly and Deandre Ayton, Washington's 10-point lead dissipated as the Pistons completed a 11-point swing to take a 33-32 lead over the Wizards to end the first quarter. After protecting the ball for the first nine minutes of the game, Washington coughed up four turnovers in the final 3:15 of the quarter to contribute to the Pistons run.

Washington steadied the ship before halftime with the help of Young, who scored eight second quarter points to help the Wizards stay within three and trail 64-61 entering the half. Davis paced Washington with 16 points and eight rebounds, while Sarr tacked on 14 points and Young scored 12. The trio combined for 69% of the Wizards first half points, and Sarr shot a perfect 6-for-6 from the field.

Rookie AJ Dybantsa appeared to truly struggle for the first time this season when matched up with Ausar Thompson. Dybantsa shot 0-of-2 from the field and looked uncomfortable with the ball in his hands when guarded by Thompson. Yet, the BYU product managed to record two assists and not turn the ball over in the first half, to finish with a team-high +11 when he was on the court.

After keeping the game close in the second quarter, Detroit erupted for an 11-point lead of its own with the help of Duncan Robinson who shot a perfect 3-for-3 from three point range during the run. Cade Cunningham also tacked on seven third quarter points to keep Washington at an arms length throughout the period.

The Wizards cut the lead back to four thanks to Alex Sarr, who remained perfect from the field, tacking on seven third quarter points to enter the fourth with 21 points and four rebounds. Tre Johnson was also in rhythm in the third, scoring six of his 13 points at the time while shooting 3-of-4 from the field.

Washington entered the fourth quarter trailing 94-90, with a chance to snap their five game skid in front of an energetic home crowd in D.C. — and Young matched the energy in Capital One Arena. He scored a quick nine points in the first four minutes of the fourth quarter to give Washington a 103-102, and found Coulibaly streaking down the court for an assist on a fast break.

But head coach Brian Keefe subbed Young out for a two-minute rest, and Detroit capitalized immediately with a 6-0 run to take a 108-103 lead. Washington kept it close, including taking a 118-117 lead with 31.5 seconds remaining thanks to a three from George. But Cunningham drew a foul from Dybantsa on the following possession, and knocked down two free throws to essentially seal the game. But 1.8 seconds remaining, Young buried a three at the buzzer to send the game to overtime, knotted at 121.

George knocked down a triple to give Washington a 124-121 lead in OT before picking up his sixth foul and being forced to sit the rest of the game. But in his absence, Young found Davis in the paint for a floater, and then drew a charge on the ensuing possession, which lead to Davis finding Sarr for the alley-oop to start overtime on a 7-0 run.

Detroit responded with a 6-0 run of its own led by Cunningham — who finished with a game-high 52 points and a team-high 11 assists. He sealed the game on back to back possessions, both in transition. First he nailed a triple to tie the game at 130, and then assisted Robinson on the break for a jumper to take a 132-130 lead with nine seconds remaining in the extra period.

Dybantsa, the rookie, took matters into his own hands and drove to the paint and pulled up for a jumper that tied the game at 132 at the buzzer to send the game to double-overtime.

Davis fouled out early in the second overtime, which led to Detroit taking a 137-132 lead without Washington's primary big — one they would hold for the remaining of the game.

Young and Davis both finished in double-double territory, but it was not enough to halt Washington's losing streak. Young scored 37 and dished out 14 assists — both season-highs — while Davis scored 30 points and grabbed 14 rebounds. Sarr also tacked on 30 points and seven rebounds, while George scored 14 points and Johnson finished with 13.

#2838. Nvidia scandal draws in Commerce Secretary Lutnick, who reportedly agrees to testify about China chip sales

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, as the fallout from ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy intensifies.

Lutnick was summoned by Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott amid scrutiny over whether Nvidia could have supplied advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies and thereby potentially threatened U.S. national security.

Huang and Lutnick both received letters on Thursday evening requesting them to testify in separate hearings on Dec. 3 and Dec. 10, respectively. The letter to Lutnick asked the commerce secretary to testify regarding "recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns."

"Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News on Thursday. CNBC contacted the Commerce Department for comment.

The letter to Huang said that reports about his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy "raise significant national security concerns."

Huang has acknowledged an affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that has bought over $4.8 billion of advanced Nvidia AI chips over the past two years. The scandal, in addition to reports of a separate affair with a senior executive at Nvidia, led to his resignation on Thursday.

There is growing bipartisan scrutiny of the Commerce Department Secretary's approach to chip policy and whether his department was doing enough to restrict the supply of AI chips to China. Lawmakers are also questioning whether the department was overseeing Nvidia's exports thoroughly enough

Senator Jim Banks has been particularly scathing, saying Lutnick "appears to have used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur," in an appearance on Fox News on Thursday.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass, who will chair the Senate Banking Committee from January, said on Thursday "Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military."

In a joint letter with incoming Senate Foreign Relations Chair Chris Coons published Wednesday, they said all documents relating to the export of Nvidia chips to China must be preserved.

Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore. and Rep. Richard E. Neal, D-Mass. told Lutnick they were investigating the approval of sales of Nvidia chips to companies with links to the Chinese government, military and sanctioned entities.

Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla. said on Thursday that Congress needed to investigate the role of the Commerce Department in approving the export to China of AI chips, but added that he had confidence in Lutnick.

Criticism is mounting on President Donald Trump's administration for declining to include over 100 companies highlighted as national security risks on a trade blacklist, including China's AI startup DeepSeek and memory chipmaker CXMT, Reuters reported in June.

Lutnick is a long-standing friend of Trump, with their relationship spanning over three decades, and is widely regarded as a close confidant of the President.

#2837. Cade Cunningham scores career-high 52 points in Pistons' 144-140 win in 2OT over Wizards

Detroit Pistons guard Cade Cunningham became the first NBA player to record 50 or more points with 10-plus assists and no turnovers in a 144-140 win over the Washington Wizards in double overtime on Thursday.

Turnovers weren't officially recorded by the NBA until 1977, so it isn't certain that Cunningham is the first player to ever post that stat line. However, only three players in the past 49 years — Michael Jordan, Nikola Jokić and Damian Lillard — had scored 50 with 10 assists and 1 turnover. (Hat tip to Yahoo Sports' Dan Devine for that factoid.)

Cunningham finished with a career-high 52 points, shooting 16-of-25 from the floor (including 3-for-5 on 3-pointers) and making 17 of 18 free throws in Detroit's win.

Washington (4-9) lost despite three players scoring 30 or more points. Trae Young tallied 37 points with 14 assists, while both Anthony Davis and Alex Sarr added 30 points. Davis also grabbed 15 rebounds and Sarr added nine. The Wizards have lost six consecutive games, including two of their past three to the Pistons.

The Pistons and Wizards played a close game throughout regulation, trading the lead back and forth during the fourth quarter.

With 1.8 seconds left in regulation out of a timeout, Young caught the ball on the right wing and hit a game-tying 3-pointer with two players defending him. It was 121-121.

Pistons head coach J.B. Bickerstaff was not happy about allowing Young's shot, saying "we didn't pay attention to the details."

"We hold ourselves to a higher standard," he added. "In certain moments when we have to be able to generate a stop, we gotta be able to trust each other."

In the first overtime, the Wizards ran out to a 130-121 lead capped by a Sarr dunk off a lob from Davis. From there, the Pistons went on an 11-2 run — with seven points from Cunningham — to go back on top. Yet Wizards rookie AJ Dybantsa hit a jumper from the free-throw line to extend the game to another overtime.

A 3-pointer by Cunningham gave Detroit the advantage in the second overtime, a narrow lead the Pistons held until 1:10 remaining when Bilal Coulibaly tied the score at 140-140 on a dunk. Yet Cunningham put the Pistons ahead for good on a midrange jumper with 25 seconds remaining. Two Kevin Huerter free throws gave Detroit its final four-point margin.

"To be able to do what he does in the moment, when it's called on, it's unique and special," Bickerstaff said of Cunningham. "He never ceases to amaze. He just understands what it takes to get it done and has all the abilities to make those things happen."

Daniss Jenkins added 21 points for the Pistons (8-3). Thompson recorded his first career triple-double with 17 points, 11 rebounds and 11 assists, along with 3 steals and 3 blocks.

#2836. Abysmal NFC South keep proving it's time to fix NFL playoffs | Opinion

The NFL is too good to be embracing mediocrity.

The NFC South is on pace to have a division winner with a losing record for the second consecutive season, with the 3-5 Carolina Panthers leading the New Orleans Saints (3-5), Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-6) and Atlanta Falcons (3-6). If it happens, it will be the fourth time in the last seven seasons the NFL has had a division winner finish below .500, getting not only a playoff spot but a wild-card game at home.

It's a bad look, especially when the NFL has better options.

Home playoff games could go to the teams with the best records, as the Detroit Lions wisely proposed in 2025. Better yet, the NFL could follow the NBA's lead and adopt a playoff format that rewards the best teams. Period.

No more charity for division winners. No more rewarding bad teams simply because they happen to be the best of the worst. No more punishing good teams because their divisions are meat grinders. (We see you NFC North, where all four teams are three games above .500 or better.)

Seed the teams by win-loss records, divisions be damned. Award playoff berths, and home games, accordingly.

"We're trying to take care of ourselves. We're not worried about any other team in our division right now," Buccaneers coach Todd Bowles said Sunday, Nov. 8, after his team rallied to tie the game with just under 3 minutes left only to allow the Bears to march 49 yards and kick the game-winning field goal as time expired.

"We know if we take care of us, we're going to be fine."

But shouldn't the NFL want better than fine?

It's bad enough we have to watch terrible games during the regular season. Like the dog of a game Sunday, Nov. 15, that is the 1-7 Miami Dolphins against the 2-7 Indianapolis Colts. Or that ever-popular clash of the Panthers and Saints on the same day. Or, worse, all four NFC South teams going head-to-head in Week 18.

We shouldn't have to endure dreck in the playoffs, too. Especially when it means a better team is going to be on the sidelines because of some misguided attempt at fairness.

Take last year. The Panthers finished at 8-9. But because they won the NFC South, they made the playoffs while two teams with winning records, the Detroit Lions and Minnesota Vikings, had to watch the postseason from their couches.

And for what? The Panthers lost to the Los Angeles Rams in the wild-card game, giving up a fourth-quarter lead twice. At home.

Of the five teams that won their divisions with losing records, only two have won their wild-card games. Both then lost in the divisional round.

The last three teams to make the playoffs with losing records have all gone out in the wild-card game, and Carolina's 34-31 loss to Los Angeles was the closest margin.

The NFL prizes parity, with good reason. For 35-plus years, at least four teams have made the playoffs after missing them the previous season. The Kansas City Chiefs are the only team to repeat as Super Bowl champions in the last 20 years, and one of only three teams to make the Super Bowl in consecutive years.

That means every team begins the year with hope, with legitimate reason to think this year might be different.

Except for the New York Jets. They're just lucky U.S. leagues don't do relegation.

But parity should not equate to charity, and the NFL is devaluing the regular season with its current playoff format. The playoffs should be reserved for the teams that earned their way in, not backed in on a technicality. At the very least, home playoff games should be reserved for the teams with the best records.

The NFL's league office was in favor of Detroit's proposal, but the Lions wound up pulling it before it came to a vote. Probably because owners know their teams could easily be the best of a bad division one day, too.

But the NFL needs to revisit the issue. A playoff berth is too important, a home playoff game too valuable, to be downgraded into participation trophies.

Follow USA TODAY Sports columnist Nancy Armour on social media @nrarmour.

#2835. NHL’s next media deal will test the league’s strength

One of the biggest developing stories in entertainment and sports is how the world's biggest media companies judge the value of non-NFL rights — and the NHL is giving us our first window into this new era in media values.

My colleague Mike Ozanian is out with his new NHL valuations this morning. See the full list here.

The NHL can begin formally negotiating a new media rights deal with its incumbent partners — Disney/ESPN and Skydance, the new owner of TNT Sports — on Jan. 1. Sources tell me the league wants an increase in overall rights fees between 50% and 100% over its current deal. The NHL inked a 7-year, $4.5 billion deal with ESPN and TNT Sports in 2021.

Whether the league actually gets that type of increase is still unclear — and that will be one of the most watched data points in the world of sports business next year.

National media rights for the NHL currently make up about 13% of its annual revenue, which is around $8 billion, according to CNBC estimates.

I'm told both Disney/ESPN and Skydance want to renew a deal with the league. Both companies have engaged in preliminary conversations with the league in the past few weeks, and while there's still work to do in terms of price, there's mutual interest in getting something done.

In its current deal, ESPN has access to 100 exclusive games for the 2026-27 season. Fifty-three of them air on ESPN or ABC, and the other 47 exclusive stream on ESPN. Under current terms, the league's playoffs are split between Disney and TNT Sports.

I'm told Disney is particularly interested in acquiring the rights to more playoff games. The NHL had its most-watched playoffs on record last season, averaging 1.8 million viewers per game. The Stanley Cup averaged 5.2 million viewers — the largest audience since 2019. It was played between the Carolina Hurricanes and the Vegas Golden Knights — not exactly marquee NHL franchises.

Last year's regular season averaged 546,000 viewers across ESPN/ABC and TNT Sports, up 25% from a year ago — the highest average in more than a decade.

The sport is also having a moment culturally. Earlier this year, HBO Max said its hockey-romance series "Heated Rivalry" averaged a whopping 10.6 million viewers per episode.

International hockey competitions, such as the league's annual "4 Nations Face-Off" midseason tournament and the 2026 Winter Olympics, have drawn huge ratings. The last "4 Nations Face-Off" game — 2025's U.S. vs. Canada final — drew 9.3 million viewers.

This year's Gold Medal men's hockey game between the U.S. and Canada averaged a stunning 26 million viewers on NBC and Peacock in the U.S., according to Nielsen data. That made it the most-watched sporting event in U.S. history with a start time before 9 a.m. ET.

"We think we've got the best content," NHL Commissioner Gary Bettman said on CNBC last month. "Our ratings have continued to increase. We were up dramatically into the double digits last year. So we view ourselves coming into the marketplace in a very strong position. Having said that, the marketplace is extremely competitive and extremely fragmented. But, I believe that with fierce competition that's going on between traditional television and the newer media platforms that there'll be a great opportunity for us to both expand our reach and get paid what we think is an appropriate reflection of our value."

Recent history suggests the NHL will get the rights increase it wants. The NBA nearly tripled its national media rights revenue, signing an 11-year, $77 billion contract with Disney, Amazon and NBCUniversal in a deal that started last season.

The NHL also renewed its TV rights deal in Canada just last year with Rogers Communications, scoring an increase of more than 100% annually when adjusting for currency fluctuations.

But recent history may not match up to present reality.

While I've been told Skydance is interested in getting a deal done, sources also tell me Skydance's top two priorities are paying down debt and saving money to pay for what's going to be a huge NFL rights increase — potentially $1 billion per season or more.

Skydance is dead set on renewing the NFL, I'm told. Those talks will likely occur in 2028, as the league has an opt-out clause at the end of the 2029-30 season.

Now that Paramount and WBD have been pushed together, the NHL isn't as important to Skydance for distribution leverage, which already has premier sports media rights such as the NFL, The Masters, college football, March Madness, UFC and UEFA Champions League.

That's not to say the NHL isn't a priority for Skydance. Sources both from Skydance and the NHL tell me they'd like to get a new deal done. Skydance still needs programming for the cable networks it owns to keep that business chugging along. But relative to WBD, it's not as much of a must-have.

"As it relates to future rights, we'll be disciplined," Skydance CEO David Ellison said during an earnings conference call this week — perhaps hinting at his company dropping not only NHL but also other rights from the WBD portfolio in the coming months and years. "Every right has to earn its place."

Perhaps Skydance remains a partner but buys fewer NHL games. This potentially opens the door to new bidders. I'm told CNBC's own parent company Versant would be interested in a slice of NHL games. Amazon sniffs around just about every national sports property that comes to market.

Netflix? Regular season NHL games are certainly not events. Fox? NBCUniversal? Both companies need to worry about how much it's going to cost to renew the NFL. A big package of NHL games may not fit the strategy.

How much the NHL can extract from its media partners will likely set the bar for other media rights set to come to market, including MLB, which could be delayed by labor negotiations. New York Yankees President Randy Levine told Ozanian this week that "I don't know whether they'll reach an agreement or not."

Disclosure: Versant Media is the parent company of CNBC.

#2832. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these 3 dividend stocks for stable income

Global stock markets remain volatile amid persistent geopolitical tensions and concerns about the sustainability of AI trade. Given this backdrop, investors seeking steady income can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios.

Tracking recommendations from top Wall Street analysts can help investors pick attractive stocks, as these experts assess a company's ability to pay dividends consistently.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Integrated oil and gas giant Chevron (CVX) is a dividend king. The company has increased its dividend for 39 consecutive years. At a quarterly dividend of $1.78 per share (annualized dividend of $7.12 per share), CVX offers a yield of 3.14%. Chevron will announce its third-quarter results on October 30.

In an earnings preview note on U.S. oil majors, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Chevron with a price target of $241. The analyst is focused on the company's international growth prospects across Latin America, the Middle East, West Africa, and the Eastern Mediterranean.

Specifically, Mehta highlighted management's commentary on solid execution in Venezuela, with gross production expected to more than double to nearly 600 kbd (kilo barrels per day) by 2031 via three joint ventures. He also noted a recent oil and gas condensate discovery in offshore Angola and is awaiting commercial updates on the West Qurna 2 and Nasiriyah projects in Iraq.

Furthermore, Mehta expects CVX to report improved productivity and capital efficiency across domestic shale assets. He expects the improvement mainly in the Permian Basin, where Chevron projects advanced chemical treatments to drive about a 10% recovery uplift in new wells and bring down capital spend per barrel by about 25% year-over-year. Overall, Mehta expects Chevron to report Q3 2026 EPS of $4.95, above the consensus of $4.89.

"While unfavorable timing effects and volatile commodity prices may present quarterly earnings headwinds, we highlight healthy U.S. refining margins and strong asset utilization as partial offsets," said Mehta.

Mehta ranks No. 381 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 12%. See Chevron KPIs on TipRanks.

Kinetik Holdings (KNTK) is a fully integrated, pure-play, midstream company operating in the Delaware Basin. Earlier this month, the company declared a dividend of $0.81 per share, payable on October 30, 2026. With an annualized dividend of $3.24 per share, KNTK offers a yield of 5.82%. Kinetik will announce its Q3 earnings on November 4, with a conference call scheduled the next day.

Ahead of Q3 2026 earnings, Goldman Sachs analyst John Mackay reiterated a buy rating on Kinetik stock and slightly raised his price target to $58 from $57. He expects the company to report Q3 2026 EBITDA of $279 million, higher than the Street's expectation of $270 million but lower than the second quarter's EBITDA of $281 million.

The 5-star analyst expects Kinetik's Q3 performance to gain from higher gas volumes after notable curtailments in the second quarter. Mackay also expects the quarter to benefit from higher production and steady commodity margins, even though some lower-margin contracts and weaker Waha spread marketing gains could weigh on results.

Overall, Mackay increased his Q3 2026 estimates to reflect higher volumes, driven by rapid Permian egress pipeline commissioning, stronger throughput at Kings Landing I, and higher M2M commodity prices, offset by increased costs.

"As natural gas takeaway constraints ease across the Permian, investor focus centers on KNTK's YE26 volume trajectory and durability of its multi-year growth," said Mackay.

Mackay ranks No. 569 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.9%. See Kinetik's Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

Moving to Crescent Energy (CRGY), an exploration and production company with activities focused in the Eagle Ford, Permian, and Uinta Basins. With a quarterly dividend of $0.12 per share (annualized dividend of $0.48 per share), CRGY's dividend yield stands at 3.56%. Earlier this month, Crescent announced an agreement to acquire Eagle Ford assets from Devon Energy (DVN).

Heading into Q3 earnings on Nov. 2, Evercore analyst Stephen Richardson reiterated a buy rating on Crescent stock and slightly lowered the price target to $17 from $18, citing dilution from new shares.

"CRGY's recent acquisition of DVN's Eagle Ford assets marks a strategic, growth-oriented move, potentially enhancing cash flow performance," said Richardson.

The 5-star analyst noted that the acquisition of the Eagle Ford assets at a net purchase price of $3.85 billion will add about 68 MBoe/d of net production and over 600 net Tier 1 locations. Richardson added that a solid track record of synergies from past deals in the Eagle Ford region increases confidence about Crescent achieving efficiencies with this deal.

Additionally, Richardson noted that the financial implications of the acquisition seem impressive, with a projected increase in cash flow per share of about 9% for 2027 to 2029.

The analyst believes that Crescent is not just expanding its business through acquisitions but positioning itself as a more durable company, regardless of market conditions.

Richardson ranks No. 478 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 13.2%. See Crescent Energy Statistics on TipRanks.

#2831. NFL hot seat rankings for every team: Coaches most likely to be fired

When will the first NFL head coach be fired?

As pessimistic as that sounds, the question looms large as the 2026 NFL regular season reaches Week 10. This marks the first time since 2022 that no NFL head coach has lost his job during the first nine weeks of the season. But the clock is ticking, and the list of coaches on the hot seat continues to grow.

Plenty of fan bases are already calling for action, even as owners appear more hesitant than usual to make a major move at this point. But change is inevitable in a results-driven business like the NFL. Ten teams hired new head coaches this past offseason, meaning 10 others were shown the door.

The debate now is what coach will get axed first this year. Dan Quinn of the Washington Commanders and Los Angeles Chargers coach Jim Harbaugh are among those feeling the most pressure, but they aren't the only coaches with reasons to worry about their job security.

None of the 10 coaches hired this past offseason should be in immediate danger of getting fired, although perhaps coaching retreads like Stefanski and Saleh might want to be cautious. Just last year, the Raiders fired Pete Carroll after one season. The year before that, the New England Patriots parted ways with Jerod Mayo after just one season on the job. But pulling the plug in the middle of the season seems unlikely, despite the recent one-and-done trend.

These eight coaches aren't going anywhere, unless they choose to leave on their own terms. It's no coincidence all eight coaches are also leading teams with legitimate Super Bowl aspirations this season. Reid, McVay and Shanahan are currently the three longest-tenured coaches in the NFL, while MacDonald is coming off a Super Bowl win Campbell re-established the Lions as a perennial contender, and Payton, Johnson and Coen have quickly done the same with their respective teams.

These five coaches have all been successful in their current gigs and don't appear to be in danger of losing their jobs. But they're also one bad stretch, or an ugly playoff exit, from feeling uncomfortable for various reasons. The Patriots haven't looked quite right since Vrabel's offseason drama with Dianna Russini. The Texans haven't been able to get over the hump as an AFC contender under Ryans. O'Connell bungled the Vikings' quarterback situation. LaFleur is 1-4 in playoff games over the past five years.

Each of these teams are struggling, underperforming relative to expectations or dealing with some combination of both. Sirianni's tenure with the Eagles has produced the incredible highs of two Super Bowl appearances, but the Eagles face questions about the direction of the franchise and a rebuild could be on the horizon. Schottenheimer wasn't a particularly popular choice when he was hired less than two years ago, and Cowboys owner Jerry Jones is already fielding questions about his job security. Bowles might be able to lead Tampa Bay to another NFC South title, but the Buccaneers haven't made much progress in the playoffs under his watch. Canales and Moore have shown intriguing flashes, but it's time for those moments to translate into more consistent results.

These are the coaches most likely to be fired, and perhaps before the 2026 regular season ends. Quinn has a 8-17-1 record since leading the Commanders to the 2024 NFC championship game and this season's issues have included a couple embarrassing game-management blunders. Harbaugh has the NFL's only winless team heading into Week 10 and his decision to hire Mike McDaniel as offensive coordinator has completely backfired. Glenn's Jets have shown signs of improvement, but he's just 5-21 through 26 games as a head coach and he's dealing with a notoriously fickle owner and fan base. The Colts already fired general manager Chris Ballard and dealt several key players before the NFL trade deadline. Steichen's days appear to be numbered, too.

#2830. CFTC Chair Selig tells CNBC crypto industry is embracing agency rules as legislation hopes fade

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is already seeing demand from crypto exchanges planning to opt in to its newly proposed rules governing digital assets, according to Chairman Michael Selig.

The commodities regulator in October proposed rules aimed at preventing abuse in crypto markets and codifying crypto transaction rules under a federal rulebook. In the announcement, Selig said the move was a "critical step" in ensuring the United States remains the crypto capital of the world.

Speaking this week at Cantor Convergence, an annual FinTech conference held in Miami Beach, Selig told CNBC in an exclusive interview that many of the major crypto exchanges are already registered with the CFTC because they offer financial derivatives, including perpetual futures, on their platforms and would now be able to add spot trading.

"We're also getting interest from new entrants who say, 'Look, signing up with 50 different state regimes is tough. We'd rather come to one regulator and get a license at the CFTC' so those new entrants are lining up to come register with us as well," he added.

After the Clarity Act, a comprehensive market structure bill that established a regulatory framework for digital assets, stalled in the Senate in September, the CFTC and the SEC moved to establish federal frameworks using their existing statutory authorities.

"We need to protect our markets and protect our customers using those markets so we'll continue to do exactly that in the wake of the Clarity Act failing to get the votes it needed to get to the president's desk during the current Congress," Selig said.

"Our statute does provide for authority of the agencies to register exchanges that want to offer margined, leveraged, or financed crypto assets or other types of commodity trading so we're utilizing that authority to allow our existing exchanges to begin offering these products under a regulated framework," he said.

Selig added that the oversight is opt-in for exchanges that are not currently offering margin leveraged financing, which is not permitted under existing state regimes.

But the CFTC's new rules could face new scrutiny and oversight in 2027, with Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate after the midterms. Selig told CNBC he hopes the U.S. won't see a wave of software developers moving offshore, as many crypto businesses threatened to do under the Biden administration.

"I really hope that we learned lessons from the last several years in this space," he said.

Crypto firms were at odds with Washington during the Biden administration, asking for clear operating rules, while also facing lawsuits brought by the SEC under former chair Gary Gensler's leadership. That shifted after President Donald Trump's 2024 victory.

"I do hope that we can work together with both sides of the aisle to protect software developers who want to do the right thing," Selig said, adding that those looking to commit crimes and engage in fraud should be held accountable.

When asked whether he's prepared for increased scrutiny from Congress in 2027, Selig said, "Congress will do its job investigating where it needs to investigate."

"I'm happy to answer any questions that Congress has for me just as I would answer Congress' questions today as I've done before hearing committees several times already," he said.

Selig has also faced heat from Democrats for his handling of prediction markets. In February, 23 Democratic senators sent a letter to Chairman Selig urging him to reverse the agency's greenlighting of prediction markets.

Selig has argued that prediction platforms are federally regulated as more states try to rein them in. The CFTC has sued several states to defend what the agency views as its exclusive jurisdiction to regulate event contracts, which it classifies as swaps.

"We're going to fight this up to the Supreme Court if that's where it's going," Selig said. "Our view on the statute is that we have exclusive jurisdiction over these markets, and I will not allow for states to go bring lawsuits against our exchanges, claiming that they're unlicensed gambling."

CNBC's Tanaya Macheel contributed to this report.

#2829. Steven Kwan would solve a lot of the Orioles’ problems

The Orioles outfield was a problem during the 2026 season. Their 3.9 fWAR as a unit ranked 22nd in MLB, and nearly half of that (1.9 fWAR) is attributed to the long-departed Taylor Ward. Some internal solutions may exist, like moving infielders to the outfield, according to team president of baseball operations Mike Elias. But no matter how many deck chairs they move around, the group seems destined to sink again without external help.

The free agent market does have some interesting options. Seiya Suzuki is probably the top fish, coming off a career-best year but now entering his age-32 season. Randy Arozarena bounced back these last two years in Seattle, and he certainly knows the AL East. Ian Happ is another proven, solid player that could fit. However, outside of the Pete Alonso contract signed last year, Elias has avoided giving big money to "older" free agents, though any thing is possible.

The Orioles did a lot of their shopping in the trade market last year. Ward was acquired from the Angels. Shane Baz came over from the Rays. Blaze Alexander was snatched from the Diamondbacks. And they re-acquired Andrew Kittredge from the Cubs. That could be the avenue to find even better outfield help this offseason, and no other trade target fits what the Orioles need better than Cleveland Guardians outfielder Steven Kwan.

Kwan's 2026 season was a tale of two halves. He was bad (.225/.332/.282) prior to the all-star break, and then caught fire (.353/.443/.432) in the second half. That helped him to be worth 3.8 fWAR on the year, nearly equaling the value of all 14 players that stepped foot in the outfield for the Orioles last season.

Adding Kwan would finally give the Orioles the lead-off hitter that have seemed to lack for a few years now. Players that batted first for the Orioles in 2026 hit a combined .226/.310/.345 in the role. Finding someone that can more adequately set the table has to be a priority. Kwan played 105 games as the Guardians lead-off hitter this past year. He hit .278/.376/.347 in the role. Over his entire career he owns a .282/.355/.385 slash line atop the order.

What you do not get with Kwan at the plate is power. He hit just three home runs last year, though he had hit 11 and 14 in the two seasons before that, so double-digit dongs are within reach. But that should not be the expectation. Instead, it's an old school approach that limits strikeouts and gets on base. Kwan struck out just 62 times last season against 85 walks. His 9.7% strikeout rate and 13.3% walk rate are both among the game's elite.

A quick skim of Kwan's Baseball Savant page shows exactly what you would expect. This is not a player with eye-popping exit velocities or hard-hit rates. But his success is no fluke. His .282 batting average is only slightly higher than his .277 expected batting average. The same is true for his .334 wOBA and .328 xwOBA. He hits the ball where no one is, and he forces pitchers to throw him strikes. The Orioles could use some of that influence in the lineup.

It should be noted that Kwan has not been the most consistent hitter from season to season. Since his rookie year, his wRC+ has oscillated in this fashion: 125, 99, 130, 98, 114. That can be read as him being at least an average hitter year in and year out, and with some of the other things he does well, he is still a net positive. His impact on the lineup, however, varies.

The other aspect of Kwan's game that would greatly help the Orioles is his defense. Kwan has already won four Gold Gloves and was a finalist for another in 2026. His six outs above average in 2026 was in the 90th percentile of all fielders, according to Baseball Savant.

The Orioles, as a team, were worth -9 outs above average in the outfield, and that included a really good defensive season from Colton Cowser (10 OAA). The rest of the unit was atrocious. A duo of Kwan and Cowser would be a good starting point for an elite defensive outfield.

One negative of a potential acquisition of Kwan is that he would not be a long-term solution. The 29-year-old is set to become a free agent after the 2027 season. Maybe he would be open to a contract extension, something that the Guardians rarely give out, but oftentimes players this close to free agency would rather test the open market.

The cost to acquire Kwan would likely be quite steep. The Guardians won the AL Central in 2026 and came within one game of going to the World Series. They don't have to sell. Plus, given the relatively thin outfield free agent class, any other team in need of outfield help is likely to be interested in Kwan too. The Orioles would have to come with a hefty offer.

In order to acquire Ward, a player less valuable overall than Kwan but still on an expiring contract, from the Angels a year ago it cost the Orioles four years of Grayson Rodriguez. The Guardians would want more for Kwan. That type of deal probably includes at least one major league-ready outfielder (maybe Enrique Bradfield Jr.), plus another one or two more intriguing prospects.

The Orioles absolutely have to address their outfield issues this winter. Moving an infielder out there could help to solve part of the problem, but it would lack the certainty that comes with accquiring a known veteran for the role. Maybe the team simply ends up doing both.

#2828. 3 thoughts as the Mavericks get their doors blown off, 133-94, at the Minnesota Timberwolves

The Dallas Mavericks (7-5) embarked on a three-game road trip with the first stop in Minnesota to take on the Wolves Thursday night. Entering on a three-game winning streak, the Mavericks couldn't get to four-straight as they lost 133-94.

The game got off to a shaky start, with Daniel Gafford committing a foul seven seconds in and Cooper Flagg tweaking his ankle less than 30 seconds later when he came down on Rudy Gobert's foot after attempting a shot. The Mavs settled in behind Caleb Martin getting some early reps at point guard and doing a fine job keeping the offense flowing. Gafford's second foul resulted in Morez Johnson, Jr. checking in, looking no worse for wear after missing a game due to injury. It was a tight game throughout, but with two minutes remaining in the frame, Minnesota peeled off a 12-0 scoring run, good for an eight-point lead (34-26).

The Mavs locked in to begin the second quarter and had a 7-0 run to draw closer. Naji Marshall, Zaccharie Risacher and Santi Aldama were a big part of Dallas pulling to within a point, but the Wolves responded quickly and got out to their largest lead of the game (14) with just over two minutes remaining in the half. Kyrie Irving nailed a cold-blooded three that made you think a run was coming, but the Wolves had other ideas. Dallas was down 67-52 at halftime.

Dallas has been good at making halftime adjustments this season. They clearly had a plan to attack the rim, with Flagg getting to the line on the first possession. Free throws were a welcome sight after neither team attempted even a single one in the second quarter. The plan was foiled almost instantly, however, with the Wolves jumping the lead to 24 points within the first three minutes of the quarter, at one point having connected on 22 of their prior 30 shots. Another blink of the eyes and this one was all but over. The Wolves looked significantly fresher than the Mavs, with everything looking very easy for the former and very difficult for the latter. The Mavs spent much of the remainder of the third quarter down by 30 or more points before limping into the fourth quarter down 103-69.

The fourth quarter afforded the starters some rest and gave some of the players who see limited time a chance to showcase themselves. Unfortunately Max Chrisite couldn't capitalize on a chance to log some minutes. He tweaked his ankle, negating even the potential silver lining of him finding a shooting rhythm.

It was a tale of two rims on a number of occasions. Dallas had a few shots go in and out, while Minnesota had the opposite luck. In the first quarter alone, the Wolves had two three-pointers nearly spin out, only to drop through the net. The Wolves had hot shooting even without the favorable rolls, connecting on 61.4% in the first half – nearly 20 percentage points higher than the Mavs across the first 24-minutes. When all was said and done, the Wolves shot 57.8% and the Mavs shot 37.2% overall.

The one part of the game Dallas had a meaningful edge on was points off turnovers. Their advantage waned a bit as the game devolved into garbage time, but for much of the game they were plus-10 or better in this category. The Mavs did show effort in this sloppy outing, not hanging their heads or giving up regardless of the story told by the scoreboard. Even with the blowout and garbage time, Dallas managed to outscore Minnesota in this particular category 29-25.

The Mavericks hung in the three-point battle relatively well in the first half, despite LaMelo Ball nailing all manner of shot from the next town over as he is wont to do. Unfortunately, the Mavs shot worse from deep as the game wore on, making the battle of the long ball very one-sided. The longball opened up the entire offense for the Wolves while the Dallas misses allowed a good rebounding opponent to get out and run.

The Wolves were rested and made the most of their reserved energy. Throughout the night they were totally in a groove getting whatever they wanted and looking like a fully cohesive unit. Meanwhile, Dallas struggled to find the right lineup and fell behind big. The game lasted 48 minutes, but it was over long before then. With two more games on the road trip, the starters at least got some rest before the next one Saturday night in Cleveland.

#2827. Apple, Alphabet and Uber survived major founder transitions. Nvidia will be a harder test

Jensen Huang is not the first CEO to leave a company he helped build.

But experts told CNBC that his sudden resignation from Nvidia at a critical juncture is unique and leaves his eventual successor with challenges in leading the company that's powering the artificial intelligence boom.

In 33 years, Huang, who resigned on Thursday amid reports of extramarital affairs, including with a woman U.S. intelligence believes is a spy for China, made the company he co-founded the world's most valuable.

Former Goldman Sachs CEO Lloyd Blankfein wrote on X that he was "indispensable" but "the graveyards are filled with indispensable men," referencing a quote attributed to French leader Charles de Gaulle.

While the board looks for a new CEO and CFO Colette Kress does the job temporarily; analysts say Huang's charisma and bullish drive will be hard to replicate.

"I'm not sure we've seen a situation quite like this, where the founder and CEO of one of the world's largest companies faces such a sudden departure amid scandal," Michael Withers, professor of management at the University of Notre Dame's Mendoza College of Business, told CNBC.

Whoever follows will "face challenges that go well beyond those of a typical CEO replacing a founder," he added.

Apple's image was inseparable from Steve Jobs when he resigned in 2011. But unlike Nvidia, the company had had other CEOs — and an internal successor.

Tim Cook invested in Apple's chip strategy and services business and became a key corporate diplomat in dealings with the U.S. and Chinese governments. He was known as an operator who controlled Apple's supply chain.

Cook had "considerable preparation" for becoming CEO, Withers said. Apple's market cap went from about $350 billion to $4 trillion in his 15-year tenure.

Larry Page and Sergey Brin left their executive roles at Alphabet in 2019, 21 years after founding Google.

Page and Brin's departures were expected. Page said at the time that it was the "natural time" to simplify the company's management structure. Alphabet shares are up more than 300% since then under Sunder Pichai.

Travis Kalanick left Uber in 2017 after mounting pressure over a series of scandals and governance concerns.

But his departure "unfolded over several months, and while it certainly attracted attention, it pales in comparison to what Nvidia is currently facing," Withers added.

Former Expedia CEO Dara Khosrowshahi repaired the organization and found a path to profitability.

Withers said successor CEOs often struggle "under normal circumstances" to juggle maintaining what made a company successful while establishing their own leadership.

"It becomes considerably more difficult when the transition follows such a high-profile scandal involving the company's founder," he added.

Huang had an extraordinary 60 direct reports, as part of a flat structure that favored fast communication over layered hierarchies.

Withers told CNBC Nvidia did not appear to have a succession plan for Huang, who is also often described as inextricably linked to the company.

"We're talking about a company that was, until recently, the largest in the world by market capitalization. That's a pretty remarkable situation," he added.

As well as having to "step out of his shadow," the new CEO will have to deal with the "scandal" arising from Huang's conduct and "the extent to which it sticks with Nvidia," Withers said.

Huang's successor will also have to tackle the longer-term business strategy, while picking up the relationships he managed.

Huang cultivated a close relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump and accompanied him to China in May. Huang consistently pushed for the U.S. to relax export restrictions that prevent Nvidia from selling its chips to the world's second-largest economy.

He also managed close relationships with the bosses of the company's key suppliers, from SK Hynix to Samsung.

Storm Uru, co-head of the Global Innovation team at Nvidia investor Liontrust Asset Management, said two key priorities were changing company culture and managing the supply chain.

The supply chain was "where Jensen was able to provide a vision for the future and able to bring people to the table and to expand capacity to enable the build-out of this technology," Uru told CNBC, adding it mattered especially "when supply chains are already so tight."

Nvidia continues to face rising competition from rivals such as AMD and hyperscalers, which are ramping up efforts to develop their own chips.

Investors noted that the new CEO will have a roadmap of products for the next few years, unaffected by Huang's removal.

"We have to look beyond Jensen ... there are thousands upon thousands of engineers," Joanne Feeney, partner and portfolio manager, Advisors Capital Management, told CNBC on Thursday, as pressure was mounting on Huang to go.

#2826. Comprehensive list of what’s wrong with Ole Miss, according to message boards

Following a 42-7 thrashing at the hands of Georgia, Ole Miss' College Football Playoff chances are now what could generously be described as NOT GREAT, BOB.

Ole Miss is 6-3 (4-3 SEC) and ranked 19th in the latest playoff rankings, which means a lot of chaos needs to happen in front of them in order to return to postseason play. Oh, and they also need to beat Oklahoma this weekend and put an end to Mississippi State's season in two weeks.

As you might expect, getting embarrassed by Georgia and staring down the prospect of missing the playoff has made more than a few people diaper-filling mad. The search for scapegoats is currently self-injecting with premium HGH, which means everyone and their brother has a fresh rumor about chaos, dysfunction, and SEX, DRUGS, AND ROCK N' ROLL at Ole Miss.

Of course, the more reasonable explanations for a 6-3 season thus far are pretty simple:

Kewan Lacy, Ole Miss' second best offensive player (who is now done for the year), played a total of 2.5 out of 12 quarters against Florida, Texas, and Georgia, which were all losses. Lacy seemingly used up his injury luck last year, as he piled up 335 total touches and avoided serious injury over 15 games. Of those 15 games, he had 7 in which he touched the ball 25+ times.

This season, Lacy only played in 6 games and amassed 88 total touches. In those 6 games, he had zero games with 25 or more touches. Kind of a big deal!

Throw in injuries in the secondary that have been ongoing since the start of the season, and Ole Miss hasn't had its first choice lineup play an entire game this season.

As for turnovers, Trinidad Chambliss is Ole Miss's best offensive player, but turnovers have been a problem this year. He has 12 total turnovers (9 INTs, 3 fumbles), which are not all entirely his fault, but giving the ball away that many times in 9 games is a disaster. #2825. Jensen Huang scandal casts doubt on Nvidia’s AI dominance — how we got here

Nvidia is facing one the biggest crises in its 33 year history, with founder Jensen Huang resigning as CEO Thursday after multiple reported affairs, including one with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy. Now CFO Colette Kress has taken the helm as Nvidia's interim CEO.

The implications of Huang's affair with Alice Huang run far deeper than infidelity. That's because her ties to Nvidia customer Megaspeed put her in the middle of a sprawling effort to accumulate AI chips across Southeast Asia. And Megaspeed is under investigation for possibly diverting restricted Nvidia chips into the hands of Chinese companies.

The relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang dates back to 2023, according to The New York Times. That was a "turbulent" period for Nvidia, Jensen Huang told CNBC during an interview at the time. Nvidia was in the midst of redesigning some chips to comply with the first in a series of strict export controls imposed by the U.S. government that restricted sales to China.

"The regulation is going to be just fine. We're going to be able to work through it," Huang told CNBC from Nvidia's headquarters in February 2023. The interview was for a documentary about how Huang created Nvidia and built it into the backbone of the AI boom.

That same day, CNBC also interviewed Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had an affair.

It's not the first time Nvidia has faced an uncertain future. The company nearly went bankrupt in the early years after it was founded in 1993.

"Every company makes mistakes and I make a lot of them," Huang said in the 2023 interview. "And some of them put the company in peril."

In the early months of the AI boom, after OpenAI launched ChatGPT in November 2022, Nvidia was on the precipice of historic growth. Jensen Huang told CNBC he'd like to keep running the company for "three or four decades," as long as "I feel that I'm making a real contribution to the company."

Less than four years later, Jensen Huang is out, and we're taking a look back at our interviews with the Nvidia co-founder and other company executives as the chipmaker enters this next critical chapter. Watch the video for the full story.
