#2824. Sixers Bell Ringer: Six double-digit scorers lead Sixers over Raptors

Bell Ringer Standings:Tyrese Maxey – 3.5Jaylen Brown – 2.5VJ Edgecombe – 2Joel Embiid – 1LeBron James – 1Anfernee Simons – 1Dean Wade – 1

The Philadelphia 76ers started slow but roared back for a 123-112 win over the Toronto Raptors on Thursday night.

LeBron James sat this one out for the Sixers for sciatica management, joining Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain) and Dominick Barlow (back) on the injury report. Joel Embiid was able to play after spending the day questionable for plantar fasciitis management. The Raptors had some notable injuries of their own with Kawhi Leonard and Scotti Barnes both sidelined, as well as Trayce Jackson-Davis and Nate Bittle.

It was a brutally rough start for the Sixers, with Philadelphia letting Toronto — on the second leg of a back-to-back — build a 16-point lead at one point in the first frame. Thankfully, someone finally told them the game had started and they came out of the gate much tighter in the second, quickly battling back to tie things up and entering the halftime break knotted at 60 a piece. The Sixers finally took control of the game in the third, with the Raptors trailing right around the double-digit mark into the final frame.

The Raptors continued to battle just within striking distance of the Sixers, but Philadelphia was able to hold on to take the double-digit victory at home thanks to six Sixers scoring in double-digits Thursday night.

The Sixers get back in the win column and are now 10-3 to start the season. They will now get a few days off before a Sunday afternoon matinee hosting the Indiana Pacers.

Until then, let's get to the Bell Ringer. We have quite a few candidates tonight…

VJ Edgecombe: 15 points, 8 rebounds, 8 assists, 3 steals, 1 block, 0 turnovers

(Photo by Jesse D. Garrabrant/NBAE via Getty Images)

With LeBron James out, VJ Edgecombe was tasked with commanding the Sixers' offense — and the sophomore was up for the challenge. This was another great example of Edgecombe doing what he can do well and not worrying about forcing things that aren't working. Edgecombe was careful and protective with the ball but didn't hesitate to whip quick passes in and out of the paint for assists, while utilizing his own lightning-fast speed and athleticism to get out ahead for easy buckets for himself when the chances arose. He was aggressive grabbing the boards and wasn't afraid to get involved on defense, even if it meant picking up a few more fouls then he probably wants to on a normal basis.

We mentioned the increased responsibility for VJ with LeBron out, and, frankly, this was a great example of Edgecome doing a LeBron impression: doing all the little things (and some of the big things) right on both ends of the floor, making an impact absolutely everywhere. It all resulted in another all-around great performance from the young guard.

Edgecombe finished with 15 points on 7-for-12 field goal shooting with eight rebounds, eight assists, three steals and a block. Yep, that close to a triple-double. All with zero turnovers. Like I said, not a bad LeBron impersonation.

Joel Embiid: 20 points, 4 rebounds, 3 assists, 1 steal, 2 blocks

(Photo by Jesse D. Garrabrant/NBAE via Getty Images)

From spending all day as questionable to play, to finally being ruled available, to knocking knees in the first period and looking like his night was done… to multiple dunks and a solid overall performance. The Joel Embiid experience!

Seriously, I thought Embiid's night was likely over after the amount of pain he seemed to be in after knocking knees setting a screen. After a quick trip to the locker room, however, the big fella returned to the game and somehow looked better than he did before the knee knock. He didn't miss an opportunity to get up for a block or a dunk, kept setting screens for his teammates and simply got a lot more aggressive and efficient offensively — whether that meant knocking down a bucket, earning a trip to the free throw line, or both. There were moments where, as has been the case many times before, it didn't seem to matter what the opposing defense tried to do with Embiid. He was simply too big, too strong, or too smart. Guess the knee was OK.

The only downside to his performance was that the jumper wasn't falling tonight, as evidenced by his 7-for-17 field goal shooting, but even those were just rimming out. That's the sort of thing you just hope is early-season rust and will only get a little better — or even a little luckier — with time.

Embiid finished with 20 points, four rebounds, three assists, a steal and two blocks.

Tyrese Maxey: 27 points (8-for-13 FG), 2 rebounds, 8 assists, 2 steals, 1 block

(Photo by Jesse D. Garrabrant/NBAE via Getty Images)

It's pretty impressive that this sort of performance is considered just a usual night at the office for Tyrese Maxey at this point, but that's how it feels. It's the same way that sometimes Jaylen Brown can put up an excellent, consistent performance throughout an entire game but almost without anyone noticing. A bucket here, a steal there, an assist when the opportunity presents… Maxey is just ol' reliable at times for the Sixers. Tonight, it didn't come in the form of a complete Maxey takeover we see sometimes, but the guard just kept chipping in on both ends of the floor throughout this one with impressive efficiency.

Maxey finished this one with 27 points on 8-for-13 field goal shooting. He also had two rebounds, eight assists (including a LeBron-esque cross-court lob to Jaylen Brown), two steals and a block.

Jaylen Brown: 18 points, 6 rebounds, 2 assists, 2 steals, 1 block

(Photo by Nathaniel S. Butler/NBAE via Getty Images)

The start of this one was not good for Jaylen Brown. It wasn't great for a number of Sixers early, but it really wasn't good for Brown. He couldn't seem to score and struggled with sloppy turnovers in the first. It was looking like it might be another rough night for JB, who had a rough outing last game against his former team.

But, like the Sixers did overall, Brown turned it around. He kept rebounding. He kept up his solid defense. And, as more offensive opportunities presented themselves, Brown started knocking down shots and, other than having a few lay-ups blocked later on, put together a decent overall performance.

A rough start after a tough overall game the other night could have been enough to mess with the mental of any player, but Brown didn't seem to let it stymie him. He turned a bad opening into an excellent 18-point performance on 8-for-15 field goal shooting, filling the stat sheet also with six rebounds, two assists, two steals and a block.

Anfernee Simons: 17 points (6-for-9 FG, 5-for-6 3PT), 3 rebounds, 2 assists

(Photo by Jesse D. Garrabrant/NBAE via Getty Images)

When Anfernee Simons is on, boy is he on. An incredible scorer off the bench, this was one of those nights that any shot coming off of Simons' hand you knew had a good chance of going in. Simons chipped in 17 points off the bench on 6-for-9 field goal shooting and sinking 5-of-6 from long range. For a team that can go completely stagnant at times when the subs come in, having someone like Simons ready and willing to knock down the big buckets is huge for keeping momentum on the Sixers' side in games like tonight.

(Frankly, with how badly this team shoots from beyond the arc at times, shooting this well from three-point range in it of itself will always earn a Bell Ringer nomination from me at least…)

#2823. Bruce Arians says he wants to be a head coach in the NFL next season

Bruce Arians is thinking about coming out of retirement. Again.

Arians told Jordan Schultz that when he announced his retirement from the Buccaneers in March of 2022, it was because of health problems that have since been resolved, and he now wants to coach again.

"I had torn my Achilles early in that season, and I was wearing these prosthetic high heels, and it threw my back out, and I couldn't stand on the sideline for four hours anymore without a lot of pain," Arians said. "I was also monitoring an aneurysm on my heart, so I had some health issues. We did everything we thought we could do in Tampa after winning the Super Bowl, trying to get two, and then it was time to give it to Todd [Bowles]. Now that I'm all healthy again, I got the itch again. So, we'll see."

If Arians does come back next year, he'll be the oldest head coach in NFL history. That distinction currently belongs to Pete Carroll, who was 74 when he coached the Raiders last season. Arians will turn 75 next season.

Arians' first retirement announcement came from the Steelers after they did not renew his contract as their offensive coordinator following the 2011 season, but Arians later said he was forced out and didn't want to retire. He then took a job as offensive coordinator of the Colts in 2012, and was their interim head coach for most of that season while Chuck Pagano battled leukemia. Arians coached so well that he was named the NFL's Coach of the Year.

Once Pagano returned to the Colts, Arians became head coach of the Cardinals, and he won a second Coach of the Year award. He announced his retirement following the 2017 season, after five years as head coach of the Cardinals.

But in 2019 he came out of retirement to become head coach of the Buccaneers. He won a Super Bowl in Tampa Bay, then retired after three seasons. Arians thought that was it, but he said that his son is now coaching high school football, and in talking to his son about the job he realized how much he misses it himself.

"Another fire got lit," Arians said. "I had no desire to go back, and I was still fighting some health issues, but now after the open heart surgery I've got so much more energy, it's amazing."

Arians may find, like Bill Belichick before him, that all the accomplishments in the world don't guarantee an NFL head-coaching job. Or perhaps he'll convince some owner to give the oldest coach ever a chance to do what he's done three times before, and turn a franchise around.

#2822. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

#2821. Huang's downfall may undo cozy ties between business and government: analysis

The resignation of Jensen Huang, together with the results of the recent congressional election, could make this a watershed moment in the relationship of American business to government, one that sees the pendulum swing back toward greater regulation and greater separation of finance from politics.

Corruption topped the list among issues that motivated voters in the overwhelming and nationwide midterm election victory for Democrats, according to the CNBC Voter Poll. It showed 90% identified corruption as a crucial or major issue in their voting decision, a percentage point higher than the cost of living.

When voters were asked which party was best able to deal with the corruption issue, Democrats led Republicans 37% to 30% — though, significantly, 32% said neither party.

It's impossible to know exactly what voters mean when they say corruption, but there are hints it involves the relationship of business to government. The CNBC All-America Economic Survey, taken two weeks before the election, asked respondents if elected officials, including the president and members of Congress, should personally own or trade stocks in companies that have contracts with the federal government. An overwhelming 93% said it should not be allowed. A similarly bipartisan 89% objected to the president's family members receiving government contracts.

The upshot: The very close relationship between business and the government, which has existed under both political parties but has come plainly and brazenly to the fore in President Trump's second administration, is now a major issue for voters.

The Huang affair encompasses all of that. Nvidia, along with several other large corporations, made large donations to the president's ballroom. Meanwhile, there are allegations that the administration did not act when informed of potentially illegal sales of Nvidia chips to China. It may be that the president ignored warnings from inside his own administration that Huang was involved with a woman who was reportedly a potential Chinese spy, instead bringing Huang on a state visit to China and giving him say in U.S. export policies for chips.

The Trump era has seen the virtual creation of the CEO Statesman: Huang and other tech execs draped around the president during foreign trips, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff negotiating with Russia, Elon Musk deciding who the federal government fires.

Could the Huang affair be the end of that phenomenon?

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., wasted no time in signaling the new Congress was ready to get tough on tech execs.

"It's clear that the American people cannot rely on Big Tech billionaire CEOs to put our national security above their bottom line – which is why Congress must pass the AI Overwatch Act and other bipartisan bills to keep advanced American AI technology out of China's hands."

The enormity of Huang's fall cannot be overstated. Imagine J.P. Morgan resigning — or Jack Welch or Steve Jobs or Tim Cook. Few have stood astride the pinnacle of political and corporate power during their era like Huang during the AI boom.

This comes at a time of massive wealth increases for the elite that have helped undermine faith in capitalism. The CNBC Voter Poll showed 56% with a strong or somewhat favorable opinion of capitalism, with 32% reporting an unfavorable opinion and 12% saying they don't know.

But those numbers are overwhelmingly driven by older Americans. Younger Americans, ages 18 to 34, have a deeply negative opinion. Those aged 35 to 49 are favorable toward capitalism by only a 46%-41% margin.

For starters, it could result in a return to more traditional separation of business and politics, where business has less of a direct say in policy. But this could be the start of a more significant change.

In the wake of the Great Financial Crisis, the banking system was put under such strict regulations, many of which exist to this day, that one commentator remarked it was "in receivership in everything but name only." One can go back even further to more extreme measures taken when the public was deeply dissatisfied with business — to the fallout from the robber baron era when the trusts were busted up, or the wake of the Great Depression when the government put stricter regulations on banks and Wall Street and gave unions more power.

Democrats will be limited, even with large gains in both houses, in their ability to overturn presidential decisions with veto-proof majorities. But executives themselves may decide that it's not a good look any longer to be seen being too cozy with the White House. And some Republicans, especially those from swing states, may read the change in the electoral winds and side with Democrats on some of the most populist issues, like the data centers, the environment and even regulation.

The irony is that Trump ran, among other things, on a strong deregulatory agenda, one that business welcomed as unshackling overregulation during the Biden administration. With potential support from the public, and an overwhelmingly Democratic Congress, the pendulum may be about to swing the other way.

#2819. Pistons vs. Wizards final score: Cade makes history in double OT win

Cade Cunningham scored a career-high 52 points, and the Detroit Pistons needed every single one of them in a 144-140 victory in double overtime against the Washington Wizards. It was not just a career-best night for Cunningham, not just one of the top-5 scoring performances in Pistons history, it was the first game in NBA history that saw a player score 50 points, dish 11 assists, and commit zero turnovers.

Cunningham simply did it all. He scored 30 points in the fourth quarter and overtime. That includes a critical 3-pointer after the Wizards had crawled their way back into the lead in the first overtime on an Anthony Davis alley-oop dunk.

The Pistons trailed 130-127 and each team had traded misses. Cunningham calmly took the ball up the left side of the floor, took a pass from Ausar Thompson, and walked into a movement 3-pointer that hit nothing but net to tie the game. On the next possession, Cade swung the ball to Duncan Robinson for what felt like a game-sealing 3 with 9 seconds left, but a video review determined Duncan had approximately 1 milimeter of his foot on the line and changed it to a two.

The scoring barrage also included critical stretch in the fourth quarter where he scored eight points and assisted another to account for 11 of Detroit's final 12 points of the fourth quarter. Cunningham also locked up Trae Young on defense with Detroit up 119-118 in the final 30 seconds of the fourth. He forced Young into the sideline, cut off any passing lane, deflected the ball, and forced shot clock violation.

Sadly, after Cade hit two free throws to make it a 3-point game, Young redeemed himself by hitting an off-balance three from 29 feet away to give us our two overtimes of fun.

Cunningham's performance slightly overshadowed another notable feat — Ausar Thompson tallied his first career triple-double. He was aggressive on offense driving to the rim, and delivered crisp passes in narrow lanes to keep Detroit's offense moving.

On a night where Cade scores 52 and Ausar gets a triple-double, how the heck was it so close to begin with? How does a game like that feature 20 lead changes and 13 ties? It was a weird game.

Alex Sarr was 12-of-14 from the floor and hit his first four threes of the night. He scored 30 points and was one of three Wizards to hit the 30-point threshold. Young scored a team-high 37 points, including a perfect 17-of-17 from the line. Anthony Davis scored 30 points and added 15 rebounds.

Honestly, Detroit's biggest issue was the same issue they've had all season. Their bigs were dominated and DEtroit really misses Jalen Duren. Washington outscored Detroit in the paint and were outrebounded. The biggest issue was John Collins yet again. He was a minus-18 on the night and it felt like it was even worse.

Collins started the overtime period at center in place of Paul Reed, who was a plus-25, and promptly was the primary factor in Detroit giving up a 7-0 run to the Wizards right out of the gate. It was ugly. Come back soon, Jalen Duren.

Yeah, the Pistons might be missing Duren something fierce, but they have Cade Cunningham. And that's enough.

#2818. Browns have a penalty problem: All the stats and details- where does the blame fall?

If the 2026 Cleveland Browns were a 1970s TV sitcom, on Monday's game review they would have been saying, "Marsha! Marsha! Marsha!" But instead, the Browns are a professional football team, and as the game film continued, the coaching staff could be heard saying, "Penalties! Penalties! Penalties!" (or so we would assume).

The fact of the matter is, Cleveland is the most penalized team in the league. And that's no laughing matter.

RELATED: RECENT LOSSES – WHICH IS MORE DISAPPOINTING?

At the halfway point of the schedule, Cleveland is ranked #1 in team penalties. 82, to be exact, for 563 yards. That averages out to 9.1 penalties per game. 97 total flags, which also ranks #1. 13 declined, which is tied for #1. What is this called? The "best at something?"

Part of the problem is that the Browns' offensive line is a collection of five new starters. Has that ever happened before in the league's history? Probably, but wow, it stands out.

This is a critical aspect of this year's roster. Yes, the offensive line is five athletes, but more importantly, it is considered one group instead of a handful of individual players. An offensive line works more on cohesiveness rather than single-man stats.

OT Tytus Howard came from the Houston Texans during free agency. Another free-agent signing was OG Zion Johnson, inked from the Los Angeles Chargers. OT Spencer Fano and OG Austin Barber are rookies. C Elgton Jenkins was signed away from the Green Bay Packers.

This means none of these guys were on the Browns roster last year. And none of them have played together at any point until they showed up for Browns training camp. This means they had to get to know each other and find a way to communicate during a game. Even in camp, there was no certainty about who the starting five would be, so this group didn't get a chance to become cohesive right away.

Two holdovers from last year's group, OT Dawand Jones and OG Teven Jenkins, have barely seen the field. In Jenkins' case, he was penciled in at right guard before he started having back issues. He never started a game this year. On October 24, he was placed on IR.

Jones was expected to become one of the offensive tackles, but came out of camp as the backup and is more considered the "swing tackle," meaning he can come in at any point and play either side. He has played with the offense in just three games, but is on the kick teams, so he has played in every game as a blocker.

What has this group contributed as far as team penalties?

For starters, the Browns are ranked as the most penalized offense in the league. Yeah, there's that. This unit features 17 false starts and 12 holding calls across the roster. Great googly moogly. A whopping 41 pre-snap flags is leaps and bounds greater than any other team.

Is this because these five guys are still trying to figure each other out? Is it because there are two rookies starting? Is it because of the coaching style of OL coach George Warhop or his assistants? Is it because these players just aren't very good?

It has to be something, right? Nobody seems to be able to place a finger on the exact issue, though. It's a major problem and is keeping this Browns' offense from reaching its potential. One thing everyone knows: It just keeps happening.

Illegal block above the waist: 1 – ranked #4 (tie)

Illegal downfield pass: 1 – ranked #3 (tie)

Why do the Browns have so many penalties?

Take the game against the New Orleans Saints. Cleveland had six penalties called in the first quarter alone. But the team settled down and had 10 for the entire game. The week before, against Pittsburgh, seven flags were thrown against the Browns in the first half alone, with nine total. Seven were called on the offensive line, including two holding calls on the rookie tackle, Fano.

The pre-snap penalties are the ones most preventable. Every player knows when the actual snap will occur, so why jump?

LG Zion Johnson was asked about pre-snap penalties after the Saints loss in the post-game press conference. He said:

"It is a focus; it's a big focus for us right now. We're really attacking it in practice. When you're playing on the road, there's definitely an added level of difficulty with the communication and the pre-snap, getting the call in and cadence, all those types of things. But we're just working each week to improve on those things. We're going to have some games at home, which will definitely be better for us. We might be able to go verbal, those sorts of things that can help us. But each day we're just striving to get better, whether we're on the road or at home in those regards, and it just has to continue to be a focus and something we press on."

The offensive line must attack it harder. If the issue is problematic in practices, will running laps cure that? That and/or stiff game fines? HC Todd Monken addressed the penalties recently:

Cleveland jumped out to a 5-2-0 start, beating some of the most mediocre teams in the league (except for Pittsburgh). They lost to the only good teams on their schedule, which means the franchise can only defeat the downtrodden clubs. They also lost to two bad clubs, which is troubling. Now, they are on a two-game losing skid.

This means the Browns are an average team at this point, but perhaps on the rise. But they aren't talented enough to have a bevy of penalties that hurt key offensive drives or give the other team an advantage with some stupid defensive penalty.

Johnson's assertion of a lack of focus on details seems fishy. These guys are paid a king's ransom to pass-block and aid in the rushing attack. They are compensated extremely well to pay attention and already be focused. Nobody should have to remind them to be attentive to the details.

There is only one thing left to consider: It apparently is a lack of discipline. Is that coaching? The players? Both?

And if this problem persists, talk of a post-season berth will just get further and further out of the picture.

What do you think is the cause of the Browns penalty issues this year, specifically on the offensive line?

#2817. Nvidia stock inches higher as investors continue to weigh Jensen Huang’s departure

Nvidia shares were slightly higher in premarket trading on Friday as investors navigate the fallout from Jensen Huang's resignation after reports of at least two affairs.

It follows a wild day for the stock on Thursday, which dropped sharply before recovering to close just over 4% lower.

Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday after The New York Times reported that Huang had a romantic relationship with Kimberly Powell, vice president of health care at Nvidia.

Huang was already under scrutiny following an investigation by the board into his relationship with a businesswoman who intelligence agencies say is a Chinese spy.

Reuters reported on Thursday the existence of another affair with an Nvidia employee, which the news agency did not name. Nvidia did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

Shares of Nvidia were 1.7% higher as of 8:13 a.m. ET.

Before Huang resigned, several Wall Street analysts told CNBC that his departure could cost Nvidia as much as 20% of its market value, given how critical he has been to the company's success. Nvidia's stock is already down more than 20% over the last month.

A lot of the company's success has been built around Huang, said Stephane Houri, head of equity research at ODDO BHF.

It's about more than just Nvidia, but also about the "architecture of the AI industry that really depended on the vision" and expertise of Huang, Houri told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday.

#2816. Michelle Beadle reflects on ‘SportsNation,’ how sports media changed, and why she keeps going

When Michelle Beadle was around 13, her family moved from Dallas to San Antonio, and she fell in love with the San Antonio Spurs. To this day, she wishes her teenage self hadn't impulsively scribbled her face out of a photo with David Robinson. Luckily, a lifetime in sports media — with the Spurs, at ESPN, and various other ventures — created more than enough experiences and memories to make up for it.

More than seven years after her buyout from ESPN, Beadle is having the time of her life because she's having the most fun. Now hosting Run It Back on FanDuel and co-hosting Pregame with Matthew Berry on The Roku Channel, Beadle knows how to find purpose in her work without letting it swallow her identity.  Plus, all the wiser, she also knows never to blemish a photo with Victor Wembanyama.

In the conversation below, Beadle reflects on the past, evaluates the current state of sports media, and forecasts the future.

Note: This interview has been edited and condensed for length and clarity.

Right now, you're on Pregame with Matthew Berry and Run It Back. How do you juggle two daily shows?

Michelle Beadle: It's not so bad because FanDuel basically completely just collapsed at the end of last season. So we knew that something was coming, but we were happy that they were having us back in any capacity because everything else is basically done. The fact that they brought us back, we knew it was gonna be remote, which opened up the ability for me to do other things. And we only really do Run It Back twice a week, and we'll do three times a week once we hit the new calendar year because it lives on YouTube, and YouTube's all about clips. Who knew? I'm learning this stuff as we go. So it's actually quite easy. The hardest part is I had to move back to Connecticut [for Pregame].

You're in your fifth season of Run It Back. At what point did you realize, oh, we might actually have something here?

Beadle: Well, you know, Chandler [Parsons], I always describe him as kind of the a**hole brother that I never had. I mean, I already have an a**hole brother, but now I have another one. I love him to death, and I think he is inappropriate and loud and foul, and sometimes, we could not be more different. And at the same time, we're completely the same, because some would say I'm inappropriate and loud and foul. And so that was such an easy click on the first day.

When we added Lou [Williams], I knew résumé and credibility-wise, that's automatic. Nobody's gonna turn on a TV and be like, "I don't care what Lou Will has to say." They care. And he's not a hot-take artist. He's genuinely thoughtful about what he says and what his face is attached to. I respect that. Sometimes it's hard because you're like, "Just answer the question." And he's like, "No, I'm going to explain why."

And then Boogie is Boogie freaking Cousins, love or hate him. He came in [to the NBA] as one of the biggest, most talented dudes, and he's got an opinion on everything. And so I just felt like it was such an easy blend.

Look, I'm gonna be 100% honest, I miss being in studio with them. Obviously, every show that exists is better if everybody's in studio, and I know that that's not realistic for some, but I just thought this was such an easy group, no butting of heads, different enough, each personality that you're getting something different from each one.

And that's actually great because, if you get a panel and three people say the same sh*t over and over again, you're like, "This isn't a good show at all." But you can't force it, either. That's the thing about shows. The ones that force it, I hate.

Given your current experience with Lou, Chandler, and Boogie on Run It Back, not to mention all your past experiences with athletes-turned-media stars at ESPN, what is your opinion on the stereotypes about former athletes in the media?

Beadle: I mean, I think there are so many levels to it. You've got sort of the buttoned-up, super professional type that blend right in. Those are usually your play-by-play guys. They're not going to get you in any trouble, and they're not going to say anything crazy or upset sponsors. And then we've got that entire new class of podcast-starting, entrepreneur types. They find themselves in great positions simply because, money-wise, they're golden. And they're being left alone, for the most part. There's a freedom in that that is glorious, but also where you get a lot of the crazy takes and sh*t you're not supposed to say out loud.

I'll say this: the one thing that always amazes me, working with some of these guys, their salaries and their career earnings are not secrets. It's all available publicly. We have a pretty good idea that these dudes are rich, right? I'm always amazed that they're doing it at all.

Chandler and those guys getting up at 5 in the morning to be in studio by 6 in the morning on the West Coast? Every time that I would show up and they were there, I was like, "Well, this is a pleasant surprise. Why are you here?" I respect the hell out of that because, you know, us normies, we have to work. We've got bills. We have stuff we have to be responsible for. They could, if they wanted to, just kind of ride off into the sunset. I love watching how many of these guys have committed to a responsibility in the media world, and they're proud of it. There's work ethic here that maybe people don't understand. They don't have to do it — they want to do it — and I will never stop respecting that.

I remember our conversations after you left ESPN and became a pseudo-professional traveler, and you seemed really happy. You mention riding off into the sunset. You temporarily did that and could have done it permanently. What drew you back into sports media?

Beadle: Yeah, I legit didn't work for 800-and-something days. I forget the exact number. It was glorious and beautiful. I felt so lucky to get to do that. You know what's funny about this? When I knew that FanDuel was becoming remote, I actually was going to go to Italy and bring my dog. We have a house there that we haven't sold yet, so it's sort of just sitting there. I was just going to do the show from there and live and do things and travel. Then, it was Matthew Berry who was attached to [Pregame], and I was like, "Oh, I do love Matthew. I'll give it a shot. Why not?" I love change.

But the house in Italy is still there. My joke, but it's not really a joke, I genuinely mean it, is that I'm one canceled show away from, just, I'm out. I believe that I don't want to work forever. I like only doing the things that are fun, which is what these shows are. And if any of it becomes un-fun, as I like to make up words, then I'm more than happy to travel the world. I would love to do that. So, yeah, I'm a canceled show away.

Which NBA or WNBA player represents where you are in your career?

Beadle: Oh, gosh. Sue Bird. She's living her best life, and she does work, but she's only doing the stuff she wants to do, which is awesome. Somebody like that who's retired, but not. It sure as hell isn't any of these young ones.

I feel like it would be irresponsible of me to mention the NBA and not allow you room to talk about Victor Wembanyama.

Beadle:  Oh, you mean the greatest thing that's ever happened?

I saw an Instagram photo he posted of his teammates painting in a field with him in France this summer, and I need someone to give me the backstory on that.

Beadle: He's a renaissance man. There are a lot of athletes, and they're all different types of personalities, but there are quite a few that are too cool for school. I just love that this Spurs group has found each other, and they're like, "Sure, we'll go to a field and paint." There's no other team he could've been with. I really believe that with all my heart, and not just the homer side of me. This team, this organization, the way they have done things and continue to do things, they sort of embrace the weird, and he's perfect for here. I'll be back home in San Antonio for Thanksgiving, and I'm just like, yes, it's a new world, and it's all Victor.

What is the most significant sea change you've observed in sports, whether in culture at large or within our industry?

Beadle: Well, the gambling thing is obviously one, because it happened within my shift, right? I was at ESPN when you couldn't even mention "the line." And P.S., I didn't even know what that meant. If it's not a silly prop or a slot machine, I don't know what's happening. By the way, bad news for me: The FanDuel app in Connecticut. It only is in certain states where you can have the casino aspect of it, and I've already lost so much money. I play slot machines on my couch like an absolute degenerate by myself. That might be my most shameful 2026 admission so far. I have to talk about it because I feel like if I keep saying it out loud, I'll get shamed into not doing it again.

I'll make sure to pause and underscore that part of the interview.

But the biggest change has to be that. It has to be these uber personalities and the amounts of money that have been paid out to just amplify some of the voices that aren't necessarily the most knowledgeable or the most truthful. They're just the loudest. And that's been fascinating to watch—not in a great way, either.

I'm not going to sit here and preach about journalism because I'm not going to pretend like I'm some big-J journalist by any stretch of the imagination. But the lines are definitely blurred now. Everything falls under the umbrella of entertainment, which I think sometimes gives us an excuse to not expect better. Like, oh, it's just entertainment, whatever! And I'm like, no, we can still be better. For me, I'll tell you what, it's diminished the number of sports shows I watch to basically zero. If it ain't a game, I'm not watching it. And that's sort of where I am.

There's a meanness to a lot of things, which I don't like either. But on that same note, I'm also noticing some of the old heads and people that I once worked with, they're kind of getting off of the mean and the snark. I don't know if that's because we're getting older and it's like, what's the point? But that part is interesting as well. I just think we've made some monsters in this business, and it's crazy. Maybe someday it'll balance out.

As television has drastically changed, has your approach to television changed?

I actually found old SportsNation clips, and my gut reaction was that you do TV now as you did TV then, which I hope you'll receive as a compliment.

Beadle: That's literally the biggest compliment. We have this new kid that does [Pregame] with us, Mo Hasan, who played quarterback at USC and Vanderbilt. He's smart, and he's hungry, and in some interview, he was like, "She's the OG, but most importantly, the way she is on camera is exactly the way she is off camera, minus cussing." And I was like, that's the biggest compliment a human can give me. I will take it.

How have you managed to adapt without selling out?

Beadle: I mean, the simple answer is I don't need to sell out, right? I'm pretty comfortable. So that's a good thing. I've also been very weird about my principles, and I've become a little more flexible in certain things than others. Other things, I'll never change on. And I just feel like once you've decided what's important or not important, just stick with it. I have to be the one looking in the mirror and being good with that. It's crazy because it's really not that hard. Are you proud of being attached to something? No? Then don't do it.

Do you think SportsNation was ahead of its time?

Beadle: Oh my God, we were just talking about that the other day. We want to do that more, in the sense that SportsNation just sort of was this bright, colorful, loud, silly program. Same topics as everyone else, but we tried to deliver it in a much more unserious way. And the timing of when that show came out was also great because we really were left alone. I think the ESPN suits at the time thought it was dumb, and being left alone was the best thing that ever could have happened to us because we were allowed to just try the most ridiculous themes, and costumes, and guests.

So it feels like a lot of the really fun shows or shows that exist today probably have taken something from that. I mean, the ones that were old enough to watch it, or the producers that were old enough to watch it. But I'm proud of it. I know that it was silly, but it was really fun.

What annoys you about the state of sports media?

Beadle: God, that's a good one. I think part of it is that the loudest voices, to me, aren't good. They're not doing as well as they could be. They've sort of been enabled to just be loud and have that be the product. I don't get it.

To be honest with you, there's a real bro vibe undercurrent. And this is coming from me, who's been in this forever. People like to tell me I'm a dude. That's always fun. But I get it. I've never ever been like, "Oh my God, these boys!" I've been pretty mellow about it all. Then, lately, I'm just like, "Man, this is some bro-y sh*t, and I don't love it." Who is this for? Who is supposed to watch this?

And it doesn't appeal to everyone. I know that for a fact because I talk to other human beings, and I've yet to hear anyone be like, "That's so awesome. I love the way everything's being done." That bums me out a little bit because there are a lot of us that are not bro-y that consume sports and everything around it, and it just feels like none of this is made for us anymore. Message received. That's why we're not watching.

But it's disappointing because I think we're more intelligent than some of the stuff that we're putting out there. To me, that's the biggest part. We're better than this. And by the way, as a person who fancies herself as somewhat humorous at times, I'll tell you what's also insulting: People who aren't funny but think they're hilarious. Enough is enough.

What encourages you about the state of sports media?

Beadle: Well, because at the end of the day, the constant is the sport itself, right? It's about the games, and it's about the athletes, and it's about the stories. That's not going anywhere, and that makes me happy because ultimately, every single one of us, no matter what we think of each other or the people watching think, we all got into this for the same reason. We love sports, and something drew us to it, and that won't change.

I do feel good about that, and I still get excited about big events and ridiculous moments and whatnot. I'm not jaded in that sense. That would be a shame. If I got to that point, maybe it is time to check out completely, but we ain't there yet. For me, that's what's going to keep everything good. And honestly, it's all cyclical. It'll be interesting to see what this business looks like in the next 10 years or so.

How have you detached your identity and worth from your career?

That has come with age, and that break I took was a huge part of it. I was leaving the industry with a bad taste in my mouth, but I also was not leaving empty-handed. And as much as that's weird or bizarre to talk about, that is a big part of leaving with your head held high. Now, I didn't anticipate COVID, and a whole other year attached onto it. But I genuinely believe that something happened in that two-year period where I knew I would probably work again, but I also knew I wasn't going to just do a job to be on TV. I stopped equating or attaching my worth with my visibility in this industry.

I genuinely think it was just time and being away from it and getting older. You realize it's a job and then you're yourself, and those are two different things. It's healthier. I know that. I know basically what I'm describing is what a workaholic feels like and what a workaholic who's been sort of rehabbed is supposed to feel like because it just doesn't matter. Oh, you don't know any shows I'm on? Cool. That's not going to bother me. I think an old version of me, or any of us that have been in this rat race for a while, you feel competitive. You feel left out. I don't have any of that.

At this point, given everything you've accomplished and experienced, what matters most to you now?

Just to be having fun. Going to work and knowing that I like the people, and knowing that what we talk about is silly and it's fun and it's entertainment. It gives me something to do a few hours a day because, you know, idle hands! I can only play so many slot machine games on my phone before I'm completely broke! I do love that part of it. It's such a generic, cliché thing to say, but it gives me a little bit of purpose every morning that I just, I guess, and I learned this about myself, wasn't quite ready to not have.

#2815. ‘We will sue them’: Canada threatens Stellantis as Trump trade war reshapes Jeep production plans

Canada has threatened to sue auto giant Stellantis over the planned sale of an idled assembly plant in Brampton, Ontario, alleging breaches of a federal funding agreement after the carmaker announced plans to shift production to the U.S. amid President Donald Trump's trade war.

Speaking at a news conference on Thursday, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said the government had served Stellantis with a formal notice of default, giving the company 30 days to address its concerns or face legal action.

"We sent a notice of default and, basically, they have 30 days — or else, of course, we will sue them," Joly told reporters in Toronto.

Joly said Stellantis had violated its contractual commitments to the Canadian government and the workers at Brampton by announcing an agreement to sell the plant to armored vehicle manufacturer Roshel earlier in the week. She added that the company was now "on the hook" for hundreds of millions of dollars over the move.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has described the situation at the Brampton plant as "unacceptable" and a "betrayal" of its workers.

The standoff comes as the U.S. and Canada remain locked in a bitter trade dispute, with Trump repeatedly putting pressure on automakers to move vehicle production south of the border.

Stellantis, which owns auto brands including Dodge, Fiat, Chrysler and Peugeot, had scrapped plans to build its Jeep Compass at the Brampton plant and shifted future production to a factory in Illinois amid U.S. auto tariffs and other market pressures.

Stellantis Canada CEO Trevor Longley said in a statement shared with CNBC that the company would return $24 million it received in government support for the Brampton Assembly's original retooling plan. This amount, however, falls significantly short of the Canadian government's own estimate of what the company owes.

"We recognize the disappointment and uncertainty surrounding the future of the facility. While our decision to sell the plant represents a change from the original plans for Brampton, the agreement we have advanced with a Canadian manufacturer provides a path to return the facility to productive industrial use," Longley said.

"As Canada's largest automotive employer, this decision also allows Stellantis to focus its resources on sustaining competitive manufacturing operations in Canada in the face of challenging market realities," he added.

Stellantis said Monday that it had agreed to sell the Brampton assembly plant to Roshel for an undisclosed amount.

It also acknowledged its obligations to employees at the facility and said it remains prepared to work with Unifor, Canada's largest private sector union, to negotiate a settlement to assist union-represented employees.

Stellantis stock has fallen sharply since the start of the year, with its Milan-listed shares down more than 60% for 2026 so far.

— CNBC's Michael Wayland contributed to this report.

#2814. Cunningham’s 52 points help the Pistons outlast the Wizards 144-140 in double overtime

Cade Cunningham scored a career-high 52 points and had 11 assists, and the Detroit Pistons outlasted Washington 144-140 in double overtime Thursday night after the Wizards twice extended the game with last-second shots.

Trae Young's 3-pointer at the buzzer forced the first overtime, and then rookie AJ Dybantsa's midrange effort with less than a second left sent the teams to another OT. But Cunningham quickly made a 3-pointer, and then Anthony Davis fouled out to give Detroit the upper hand.

It was still a two-point game in the final minute, but Cunningham scored from the baseline to make it 142-138 with 25.3 seconds left. Washington has lost six straight.

Detroit's Ausar Thompson had 17 points, 11 rebounds and 11 assists for his first career triple-double.

Young had 37 points for the Wizards but shot just 8 of 23. Davis and Alex Sarr scored 30 each as the franchise had its first trio of 30-point scorers since Mike Davis, Earl Monroe and Gus Johnson for the Baltimore Bullets on Nov. 18, 1969.

Young had 14 assists, two more than Washington's whole team managed in a loss at Indiana the previous night.

Cunningham's previous career high was 46 points, just over a year ago — and also against Washington. He became the first NBA player with 50 points, 10 assists and no turnovers since the league began tracking turnovers in 1977-78, according to OptaSTATS.

Detroit beat the Wizards for the second time in four games. The Pistons overcame Davis' 44 points to win Monday, and Washington looked ready to end its skid when it scored the first seven points of the first overtime Thursday to lead 128-121. Then Cunningham rallied Detroit.

He finished 16 of 25 from the field and 17 of 18 on free throws. Daniss Jenkins scored 21 points for the Pistons before fouling out. Kyshawn George fouled out for the Wizards after scoring 14.

Sarr was 10 of 10 from the field in regulation and finished 12 of 14.

Pistons: At Miami on Saturday night.Wizards: Host Houston on Sunday night.

#2810. CNBC's Official NHL Team Valuations 2026: How the 32 franchises stack up

For the first time, hockey team valuations have crossed the $4 billion threshold, with CNBC's NHL valuations led by the Toronto Maple Leafs, at $5.4 billion, the New York Rangers, at $4.7 billion, and the Montreal Canadiens, at $4.1 billion. The average NHL team is now worth $2.71 billion, 23% more than a year ago.

Don't be fooled by the lone NHL control sale to close over the past 12 months: the $1.8 billion sale of the Pittsburgh Penguins to the Hoffmann family. Although the transaction was approved by the league in June, the price was negotiated about 18 months ago.

Look instead at the latest minority stake transactions. In March the NHL approved the sale of a 12.5% stake in the Carolina Hurricanes by Tom Dundon in a transaction that valued the team at $2.66 billion. Scott Malkin and other shareholders are close to selling a 15% stake in the New York Islanders at a $3 billion valuation. Sports bankers tell CNBC these deals are representative of what control stakes in the two teams would sell for given the hot market for sports teams.

"Like the other major sports leagues there is a strong demand to own hockey teams because their media content values are high and there is a scarcity of teams," said Sal Galatioto, whose firm, Galatioto Sports Partners, advises clients on both the buy and sell sides of sports team transactions. "Capitalism and technology are creating more wealth and the NHL, like the NFL, NBA and MLB, is an industry with a very long product life cycle, a hedge against risk in AI."

The NHL's current national media rights deals with Walt Disney and Warner Bros. Discovery are worth a combined annual average of close to $650 million through the 2027-28 season, but given the league's strong television ratings last season, a big increase could be in the offing.

"The 2025-26 NHL regular season averaged 546,000 viewers across ESPN/ABC and TNT Sports, up 25% from last year and the highest average in more than a decade," Sports Media Watch wrote. "The 25% increase is on the high end of a general rise in sports viewership that includes gains of 35% for the NBA, 19% for men's college basketball and 10% for the NFL."

Sports Media Watch also wrote that the 2026 NHL Stanley Cup Playoffs averaged 1.8 million viewers in the U.S. across ESPN/ABC and TNT Sports. That's up 68% from 2025, and it's the highest average on record for the playoffs on American television, going back to 1994, it said.

The NHL is pondering adding teams in cities such as Houston and Atlanta, and another factor fueling NHL valuations is the belief that the expansion fees paid by the new teams would surpass $2 billion. The Seattle Kraken, the NHL's most recent expansion team, paid a $650 million fee to join the league for the 2021-22 season.

According to CNBC's figures, revenue for the league's 32 teams averaged $257 million for the 2025-26 season, 6% more than the previous year, while EBITDA — earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization — averaged $48 million per team, a decline of 11% due to arena expenses. The league's profitability should rebound as money spent on hospitality, concessions and merchandise stores boosts revenue.

In April 2025 the NHL and Rogers Communications agreed to a 12-year national Canadian media rights deal worth $7.79 billion, based on exchange rates as of Nov. 24, that will begin with the 2026-27 season. That's more than twice the amount the league is getting from its existing 12-year deal with Rogers. This will help push up the league's hockey-related revenue — which includes media rights, sponsorships, premium seating, tickets, concessions and parking — to around $7.25 billion for the 2026-27 season, 7% more than last season.

CNBC's Official NHL Team Valuations are current enterprise values — equity plus net debt — calculated using revenue multiples, and include the economics of the team's arena, including non-NHL revenue that accrues to the team's owner. The valuations are meant to represent what a control stake valuation would go for in an arm's-length transaction and do not include the value of the arena or the real estate it sits on.

Revenue figures are net of revenue sharing and the 35% of home playoff non-premium gate revenue that goes toward the league's revenue-sharing pool. Revenue multiples are based on historical transaction prices, as well as what investors, league executives and bankers say about the current market.

CNBC values exclude other businesses related to the teams with separate financial statements, such as the Edmonton Oilers' mixed-use real estate project. For teams that sell their own merchandise, such as the Oilers, CNBC deducts the cost of goods sold from merchandise sales. Likewise, CNBC excludes the market value of affiliates/equity method investments to ensure consistent enterprise value-to-revenue and enterprise value-to-EBITDA multiples. Debt figures are the latest available and include both team debt and stadium debt.

CNBC incorporates the value of a pending new arena in our valuations if construction has begun and financing has been secured. For example, the $2.25 billion valuation for the Calgary Flames incorporates their new arena, which is scheduled to open in time for the 2027-28 season. Likewise, CNBC valuations anticipate a substantial increase in the NHL's next U.S. national broadcasting deal, which would begin with the 2028-29 season.

Revenue and EBITDA figures are for the 2025-26 season and net of revenue sharing and player escrow. CNBC presents revenue and operating income figures on a cash basis, rather than an accrual basis. CNBC figures are different from the league's official hockey-related revenue because we include non-NHL arena revenue that goes to the teams. When the owner of the arena also owns both the NHL team and NBA team that play in the same building — as is the case for several teams, including Toronto's Maple Leafs and Raptors, who are both owned by Rogers Communications and play in Scotiabank Arena — we divide revenue from non-sports events held at the arena evenly between the two teams.

All valuation figures are in U.S. dollars. The exchange rate for revenue and EBITDA is based on a one-year average, from June 2025 to June 2026, of CA$1 = US$0.72, and the exchange rate for team values and debt, as of Sept. 21, is CA$1 = US$0.71.

Sources for CNBC's Official NHL Team Valuations include team owners, investors and executives, as well as sports bankers and league consultants; public documents such as stadium lease agreements, stadium authority budget audits and credit rating reports; and sponsorship and broadcasting industry executives. Certain figures were provided by league executives who spoke to CNBC on the condition of anonymity because agreements are private and they do not have permission to speak about them publicly. Figures that could not be confirmed with sources are CNBC estimates.

— CNBC's Jungwoo Ethan Kim contributed to this report.

#2808. Stats Rundown: 3 numbers to know from the Mavericks’ 133-94 embarrassment at Minnesota

The Dallas Mavericks (7-5) had no stomach for the fight on Thursday, dropping an embarrassing 133-94 loss to the Minnesota Timberwolves (9-3) at Target Center. Bones Hyland led all scorers with 24 points off the Minnesota bench, while LaMelo Ball dropped 22 for the Wolves in just 25 minutes in the win.

Zaccharie Risacher led the Mavericks with 22 points off the bench in the loss.

Let's not belabor the point. This was a straightforward ass-whipping. Here are some stats from the Mavericks' no good, very bad day at the office.

If you blinked late in the first quarter, you may have missed the moment the Mavericks went from firmly in control to flailing. PJ Washington drove for a contested layup, and Naji Marshall followed that, the next time down, with a pair of free throws to extend the Mavs' early lead to 24-19 as Flagg took his normal rest stretch on the bench.

From there, Bones Hyland and Ayo Dosunmu keyed a 15-2 run over the last 2:48 of the first. Dosunmu hit his first bucket of the game, a 3-pointer from the right wing with 1:38 left in the opening frame, to swing the Wolves back in front, 26-24. Then, after Marshall stopped the bleeding with another 2-for-2 trip to the line, Jaylen Clark banged in a last-second 3-ball of his own to extend Minnesota's lead to 34-26.

The Mavs did not connect on a field goal in the final 3:34 of the quarter after Flagg went to the bench a minute before that. Dallas finished the first 9-0f-25 (36%) from the floor, while the Timberwolves shot a much healthier 12-of-22 (54.5%) to open the game.

The Mavericks scored 22 of their first 42 points off Minnesota turnovers on Thursday. That's a full 52.8% of the points the Mavs scored over the first 19 minutes of the game that came off the Timberwolves' nine turnovers.

Dallas got out and ran early in the second to battle back from what eventually bloomed into a 10-point hole. Flagg got into a passing lane for his first steal of the contest with seven minutes left in the half, which led to a ferocious dunk from Zaccharie Risacher that cut the Timberwolves' lead to 43-42.

But Minnesota embarked on another 12-3 run from that point, and guess what they didn't do during that run? If you guessed "turn the ball over," you would be correct. The Mavs weren't able to manufacture a whole lot of offense in the halfcourt throughout the first half. Dallas' defense was the only thing fueling the team's offense. Meanwhile, on the other end, The Wolves were pouring it on.

Minny shot 27-of-44 (61.4%) from the field in the first half, while the Mavs shot just 20-of-48 (41.7%). That disparity led to the Timberwolves' swolen 67-52 lead at the break.

A vibrant, colorful and above all, ridiculous rapid-fire discussion erupted in the MavsMoneyball Slack channel in the third quarter on Thursday, partially debating whether it was the Mavericks' offense that failed the defense or the defense that called it a night early and left the offense on an island. Whichever way you lean, neither of these things can happen when you're facing a bona fide early-season juggernaut like the Anthony Edwards-less Timberwolves. The Wolves came into the game with the NBA's best defensive rating (105.1).

Flagg did nothing on the defensive end. Marshall one-upped him by beating his head against a wall on both ends of the floor. Someone tried to make the argument that Martin was the best player on the floor for Dallas for long stretches of the first half. Risacher's stat line ended up looking good in the loss, but that was influenced loudly by the fact that garbage time against the Wolves stretched into most of the second half. For the record, Risacher led the Mavs with 22 points on 9-of-14 shooting (4-of-8 from 3-point range), to go along with six rebounds, two steals and a blocked shot in the loss.

After coming into the second half leading by 15, the Timberwolves outscored the Mavs 36-17 in the third to put Dallas to bed early. Just a piss poor effort on all fronts against a foe that will embarrass you if effort and execution elude you for 48 minutes. Which it did. So they did.

#2807. U.S. seizes $1.2 billion in cryptocurrency stolen from Binance

U.S. authorities have seized around $1.2 billion in virtual assets stolen from cryptocurrency exchange Binance last month, the Department of Justice said Thursday, as it vowed action to tackle cyberscams originating from North Korea.

Over $6 billion was stolen from industry giant Binance on Oct. 29, which the DOJ attributed to actors linked to the North Korean military.

Collective efforts between the U.S. government and private sector have resulted in more than $2.7 billion of that amount being frozen.

The FBI blames the attack, which shook confidence in crypto market security, on members of the North Korean military it refers to as "TraderTraitor."

The DOJ said it was taking coordinated action against what it called the North Korean government's "schemes to fund its regime through the massive theft of cryptocurrency."

That includes "the court-authorized seizure and restraint of more than $1.2 billion worth of cryptocurrency recently stolen from Binance," it said.

DOJ units, law enforcement partners and virtual asset service providers have been working to intercept the stolen assets.

But efforts to track and freeze the assets are ongoing, as TraderTraitor actors continue to launder them through various cryptocurrency channels.

Authorities have also seized cloud-based infrastructure used in a massive identity impersonation scam known as "FaceStealer," which has seen more than $400 million worth of cryptocurrency stolen over 18 months, the DOJ said.

The scheme sees hackers set up fake video meetings using stolen accounts and recordings of people known to the target by using AI-generated deepfakes. The hackers then say a technical problem requires a fix, install malware on a computer and take over the victim's communications, steal their cryptocurrency and target their contacts — sometimes months or more than a year after the initial compromise.

Individuals working in the cryptocurrency and web3 industries are prime targets.

Assistant Director in Charge Patrick Grandy, of the FBI's Los Angeles Field Office, called FaceStealer "a highly effective social engineering scheme capable of deceiving even the most experienced technical and security conscious computer user."

"It exploits our trust in ubiquitous video conference platforms and valued personal relationships. If you can't imagine a scenario where you might fall prey to it, you are not thinking creatively enough," Grandy added.

"North Korea's government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft," Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor said in a statement.

"America will fight back against that corrupt regime's effort to profit through cybercrime. The National Security Division will use every tool at its disposal to seize and return North Korea's ill-gotten gains."

#2806. Pirates Should Strengthen Their Bullpen with Taiwanese Right-Hander

The Pittsburgh Pirates must add to their bullpen this offseason. The free-agent market will offer plenty of options for the Pirates to reinforce their bullpen. However, one especially interesting option recently became available. Taiwanese right-hander Jyun Yue Tseng was recently posted by his Chinese Professional Baseball League team, the Fubon Guardians. He is now looking for an opportunity in MLB, and the Pirates should consider kicking the tires on Tseng.

Mason Montgomery is entrenched as the Pirates' closer, with trade deadline acquisition Luke Weaver and breakout right-hander Yohan Ramirez, who went from a depth reliever to a high-leverage arm, as his setup men. The rest of the 'pen, however, is largely unproven. Relievers including Carmen Mlodzinski, Evan Sisk, Lake Bachar, Noah Murdock, Brandon Eisert, and former top prospects Wilber Dotel and Antowne Kelly will all be vying for major league roster spots on the Pirates' pitching staff to open 2027. Enter Tseng?

Apr 22, 2026; Pittsburgh, PA, USA; A general overall view of Honus Wagner statue at PNC Park. The stadium is the home of the Pittsburgh Pirates. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images

Tseng finished up his sixth season in the CPBL. Although Baseball-Reference does not list how many innings the right-hander pitched, he allowed only nine earned runs and three home runs in 48 total appearances. He struck out 65 of the 199 batters he faced, while allowing just 13 free passes and 36 total hits. Tseng has served as the Guardians' closer since his debut in 2021, recording 91 saves over the last six seasons. 2026 was his best campaign yet.

What we do know is that Tseng pitched extremely well in the five seasons prior to 2026. From 2021 through 2025, the Taiwanese righty posted a 2.02 ERA, struck out 26% of opponents, and handed out a walk to 8.2% of opponents he faced. Tseng allowed just seven home runs as well.

Don't let Tseng's 5'8″, 149-pound frame fool you; he has some power on the mound. The right-hander works in the mid-to-upper-90s, having topped out at 99 MPH in the past. He appeared in two games for Team Chinese Taipei during the World Baseball Classic and averaged around 95 MPH with his fastball. His four-seamer showed above-average induced vertical break at 17.4 inches.

Aside from his four-seam fastball, FanGraphs states he throws a slurve. He also used an upper-80s cutter during this year's WBC. Tseng has flashed solid command over his entire arsenal. He posted his lowest single-season walk rate in 2026, and his career BB% in the CPBL is only 7.9%. Tseng has stuff that would translate to Major League Baseball.

The question is what sort of contract could Tseng land in MLB? Tseng just turned 25 this month. Previously, Yuki Matsui, who was a dominant closer in his respective Asian league, in his case, Japan's Nippon Professional Baseball League, signed a three-year contract worth $28 million guaranteed with the San Diego Padres.

Of course, there are some differences. 2024, Matsui's rookie year in MLB, he was 28 years old, with ten years of experience in NPB prior to signing with the Padres. He is also left-handed, compared to Tseng, who is a righty reliever. NPB is also considered the highest level of professional baseball in Asia, while CPBL is considered below both Japan's NPB and South Korea's Korean Baseball Organization (KBO).

Regardless, given his age, the Pirates could sign Tseng for multiple seasons. That is important, as Weaver is a free agent after the 2027 season, and Yohan Ramirez is a free agent after the 2028 campaign. Tseng may not immediately start his MLB career in a high-leverage role; however, he could certainly work his way into one after accumulating some experience in US baseball and acclimating himself to his new environment.

Tseng would certainly be a step up from Evan Sisk, Brandon Eisert, and Noah Murdock, and would allow the Pirates to use Wilber Dotel and Antwone Kelly as starters or long relievers. Depending on how the offseason goes, Mlodzinski may not be an option for the Pirates if they trade him. Even as a middle reliever, the Pirates could find plenty of use for Jyun Yue Tseng, and could slowly work him into higher leverage situations as the season goes on.

#2805. Trump says he wants to ‘get Cuba done’ before leaving office, would consider military force

U.S. President Donald Trump has said he wants to "get Cuba done" before leaving office in 2029, adding that he would "certainly consider" military intervention against the communist-run Caribbean island.

In an interview with conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt on Thursday, Trump said his administration was monitoring the situation in Havana "very closely" and described Cuba as a "failed" state.

"I want to get Cuba done before I leave," Trump said. His comments marked the first time he has put a timeline on possible military intervention to topple Cuban authorities, according to Politico.

Trump said Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose parents are from Cuba, "would love to do it" and said he would "certainly consider" a short military operation.

It comes as the U.S. continues to enforce a comprehensive economic embargo against Cuba, a campaign which has contributed to a deepening energy and economic crisis on the island. Cuba has suffered repeated nationwide blackouts in recent months, as well as fuel and food shortages.

The Cuban Embassy in Washington, D.C., estimated on Thursday that the cost of the U.S. blockade to Cuba between March 2025 and February 2026 amounted to $8 billion.

Earlier this month, the Treasury Department imposed further sanctions on Cuban oil tankers and shipping companies and threatened to target any international entity or person doing business within its marine or maritime industries as part of a push "to end the Cuban regime's malign activities, both in Cuba and across our hemisphere."

In response, Cuba's Embassy in Washington, D.C., said these steps "deepen an energy siege that already leaves hospitals without reliable power and families facing blackouts. The blockade is not targeted at a government. It is collective punishment that hits ordinary people every day."

Trump has previously talked up the prospect of a "friendly takeover" of Havana and said the White House could turn its sights on Cuba after the Iran war. The U.S. president has also said he could do anything he wanted with the country, adding that he thinks he will have the "honor" of "taking Cuba."

In May, Cuban Energy Minister Vicente de la O Levy said the country of roughly 10 million had run out of fuel oil and diesel, describing the country's predicament as "extremely tense."

Analysts have typically been skeptical about the prospect of a U.S. military campaign against Cuba, suggesting that further economic pressure against the island's authorities appears more likely.

#2804. Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 dividend stocks for consistent income

Democrats' midterm election win has put the artificial intelligence trade in question, as voters clearly expressed opposition to the rapid buildout of data centers. The stock market could remain volatile amid AI trade concerns, macro uncertainties, and geopolitical tensions.

In this scenario, investors can add dividend-paying stocks to their portfolios to earn steady income. However, the extensive universe of dividend stocks can make selection challenging. Top Wall Street analysts' recommendations can help investors shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as these experts assign ratings after in-depth financial analysis.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Viper Energy (VNOM) is a subsidiary of Diamondback and owns and acquires mineral and royalty interests, primarily in the Permian Basin. The company reported upbeat third-quarter earnings, supported by recent acquisitions and continued development activity from Diamondback and third-party operators. Viper announced a base cash dividend of 50 cents per share for Q3 2026, payable on Nov. 19. Based on the base and variable dividends announced over the past 12 months, VNOM's dividend yield stands at 5.7%.

Following the Q3 results, TD Cowen analyst Aaron Bilkoski reiterated a buy rating on Viper Energy stock with a price target of $61. The analyst noted that the company delivered solid Q3 results, with production, including oil and natural gas liquids, exceeding both TD Cowen and consensus estimates.

The 5-star analyst highlighted that the key update was the announcement of two royalty acquisitions for $809 million in cash, including deferred consideration, and $82 million of newly issued shares.

Given the recently announced base dividend hike, Bilkoski expects Viper to direct incremental free cash flow toward buybacks. While the acquisitions increase leverage, the analyst believes that Viper has enough capacity for opportunistic buybacks.

Bilkoski noted that Viper has historically delivered one of the highest production per share growth profiles in his royalty coverage, but still trades at a notable discount to the royalty peer average and the company's historical FCF yield range. "In our view, its above-average growth warrants a higher valuation," said the analyst.

Bilkoski ranks No. 525 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 12.80%. See Viper Energy Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Exxon Mobil (XOM) reported robust Q3 2026 profits, as its U.S. refineries boosted production to capitalize on the high diesel fuel prices sparked by the conflict in the Middle East. The oil and gas giant announced a quarterly dividend of $1.07 per share, payable on Dec. 10, reflecting a 3.9% increase. This marks Exxon's 44th consecutive year of dividend increases. At an annualized dividend of $4.28 per share, XOM offers a yield of 2.53%.

Impressed by the Q3 print, TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman reiterated a buy rating on Exxon stock and raised his price target to $193 from $180 to reflect higher downstream earnings, with the expectation of increased mid-cycle margins.

Gabelman noted that the strength in Exxon's refining business continues to offset Middle East-related headwinds. He added that the company increased its ownership in LNG projects, which should reduce its Middle East concentration over time from 75% to 50% and lower the likelihood of diversification-focused mergers and acquisitions. Beyond LNG, Gabelman expects Exxon's growth in the 2030s to come from Guyana, Kashagan, Permian, and possibly Venezuela.

Gabelman noted that Exxon announced a dividend hike of nearly 4% and plans to maintain buybacks at $20 billion for 2027. "The decision to maintain reduces the pro-cyclicality nature of the buyback," said the analyst.
