#2803. Lions vs. Patriots preview, prediction: On Paper

The Detroit Lions and New England Patriots are in Germany for a big international matchup. The Patriots are a bit desperate for a win, sitting at 5-4 and clinging to the final playoff spot in the AFC. The Lions are a little more comfortable in the fifth spot of the NFC playoff race, but if they want to contend in a competitive NFC North, they need this game, too.

So which team has that statistical advantage and will come out on top Sunday morning? Let's dive into the numbers with our Week 10 Lions vs. Patriots On Paper preview and prediction.

Note: Stats may be a little lighter this week because one of my bigger resources—NFL Pro—is not available in Germany.

The Detroit Lions had their worst passing offense performance last week against a bad—but improving—Dolphins defense. Offensive line struggles were the lowlight of the performance, headlined by the "suspension" of left guard Christian Mahogany and inconsistent play of rookie right tackle Blake Miller. Mahogany is back in the lineup, and that should help the Lions' passing offense which has remained near a top-five unit for most of the season. They rank:

And despite the poor offensive performance, the Lions offensive line is still grading out well as a unit. Though they rank 17th in sack percentage (6.5), they're fifth in pressure percentage allowed (19.4%), second in PFF pass blocking grade (75.1), and seventh in pass block win rate (54%).

The Patriots pass defense started off strong, but has struggled as of late, even against some of the most medicore-to-bad passing offenses. For the season, they rank:

For comparison's sake, all of these rankings except for dropback EPA are below the Lions' pass defense. So whatever you think of Detroit's ability to defend the pass, the Patriots have been worse.

But much like Detroit's pass defense, the one place they thrive is pressuring the opposing quarterback. Thought they're just 19th in pressure percentage (22.4), they're sixth in sack rate (8.0%), 11th in pass rush win rate (52%), and second in PFF pass rush grade (82.8).

While EDGE Elijah Ponder leads the team with 7.5 sacks, it's really New England's interior pressure that causes havoc. Look out for Christian Barmore (78.1 PFF pass rush grade) and Milton Williams (20 pressures) to give Detroit's interior offensive line some issues.

But New England's second is very beatable. Christian Gonzalez is having a down year (50.4 PFF grade) and the Patriots will be down Carlton Davis.

Player to watch: Amon-Ra St. Brown. This isn't just a Germany thing, St. Brown should thrive against the Patriots' zone-heavy defense. Brown is the Lions' best weapon when it comes to recognizing the soft spot in zones, just like last week's eight-catch, 86-yard performance.

Advantage: Lions +2.5. The Patriots' pass rush does have a chance to disrupt Jared Goff like the Dolphins did last week, but for most of the day, the Lions quarterback should be picking apart this poor secondary.

The inconsistency of this rushing attack is still very frustrating to watch, but putting things into perspective, it's still a very decent run game in Detroit. For the season, they rank:

Negative plays remain a huge problem, with Detroit's 20% stuffed rate ranking 25th in the NFL. They are improving in short-yardage situations, though, climbing to 18th in power success rate.

Still, the offensive line—though still plagued by some mental mistakes—appear to be moving people. Detroit ranks fourth in adjusted line yards, eighth in run block win rate, and, as a whole, the Lions entire team is fourth in PFF's run blocking grade.

Detroit will face a formidable test this week against a run defense that has allowed 100 rushing yards just three times this entire season, and each of their last five opponents have been held at or below 4.0 yards per carry. Though last week's performance against the Packers' worst rushing attack in the league should provide at least some hope.

Interestingly, the Patriots run defense appears more efficient than the sum of their parts. They rank just 16th in adjusted line yards allowed, 16th in run stop win rate, and 21st in PFF run defense grade.

One thing they do thrive in, however, is limiting explosives. They've only allowed six rushing plays of 15+ yards (third fewest) and just a single run of 20+ yards (t-fewest). But they're just okay in short-yardage situations. They're 10th in power success rate allowed (59%), but sport just a 16% stuffed rate (23rd).

Player to watch: LB Christian Ellis. While the Patriots are not particularly strong up the middle in run defense, Ellis sports the eighth-best PFF grade against the run (82.3), providing a strong second level of defense. The Patriots' secondary is also active and strong against the run.

Advantage: Lions +0.5. Detroit hasn't been as explosive as expected running the football this year, but they have found some consistency running for gains of 5-10 yards, and that could be exactly what we see on Sunday.

Despite a horrible start to the year, Drake Maye has seemingly righted the ship—outside of last week's performance against a very solid Packers pass defense. For the entire year, the Patriots pass offense ranks:

Essentially, if the Patriots could stop turning the ball over, they'd be a top-five passing attack. But turnovers have been a serious problem. Maye's 11 interceptions leads the league and his 4.0% interception percentage is third-highest in the NFL. To sport that dishonor and still produce the 10th-highest dropback EPA is pretty crazy.

So what's causing the high interception rate? It's a little bit of everything. An injured offensive line that ranks 21st in pressure rate (23.6%) and 18th in sack rate (6.6%), a quarterback who is still young and figuring things out, and a receiving corps that lost Romeo Doubs for the season and hasn't had a lot of A.J. Brown available.

But, again, the Patriots passing attack remains pretty dang efficient despite those problems.

I'm still hesitant to believe in Detroit's defensive improvement through the air. Much of that appears based on simply playing a bunch of poor passing attacks, but the one aspect they have seriously improved on is explosive plays allowed. In the first four games, the Lions allowed 20 passing plays of 20 yards (most in NFL). In the last four games, the Lions have allowed 14 (still t-10th most). For the season, Detroit still only ranks:

The pass rush (eighth in sack rate, seventh in pressure rate) remains solid, despite an ever-decreasing blitz rate (26.3%, 18th).

Detroit will be without top cornerback D.J. Reed for at least another week, but Brian Branch's return has allowed them to have a little more flexibility in their coverages, and it has calmed some things down (a little).

Player to watch: Hunter Henry. While Henry is far from 100% as he deals with a foot injury, he remains the biggest threat to Detroit's defense. Henry is first on the team in receptions (32) and second in yards (361). Meanwhile, the Lions is 31st in DVOA vs. tight ends.

Advantage: Patriots +3. This is the matchup that could change the game. New England, in my opinion, have one of the best passing attacks as long as they can avoid turnovers. The Lions aren't particularly great at forcing turnovers, creating just eight on the season—only three teams have fewer. So I would expect a pretty strong day from Maye.

New England hasn't run the ball very consistently, although injuries have played a large part in that, particularly as of late. They have a fullback, a running back, and three offensive linemen on IR. Running back TreVeyon Henderson has already been ruled out this week and top running back Rhamondre Stevenson could miss this one, too. Guard Ben Brown has been declared out already, and his backup Walter Rouse is working his way through concussion protocol. Put it all together, and the Patriots' running game ranks:

That said, running back Corey Kiner has stepped in and provided a bit of a spark in the last two weeks, rushing for 93 yards on just 15 carries, bolstered by a couple of 20-yard runs. Additionally, they are great in short-yardage situations, converting 75% of power situations, ranking fifth in the NFL.

The Lions' run defense is really starting to come on in recent weeks, with one of their best performances coming last week against a sneaky-good Dolphins run game. Overall, though, the numbers remain pretty pedestrian. The Lions rank:

They're still being victimized by some early-season explosives given up, but that has settled down considerably as of late.

What has been true pretty much all season is that Detroit has clogged the middle of the field. Led by the strong play of defensive tackles Tyleik Williams and Alim McNeill, anything between the b-gaps has been out of business. Yet, oddly, the Lions rank dead last in power success rate allowed, ceding an 84% conversion rate. So don't expect many third-and-1 stops from Detroit on Sunday.

Player to watch: Malcolm Rodriguez. Rodriguez is quietly having a very strong season, and with Jack Campbell out for the foreseeable future, his role will continue to increase. Currently, he sports an 83.9 PFF run defense grade (seventh in NFL among LBs) and the third-highest run stop percentage (11.7).

Advantage: Lions +1. With all of the injuries, I just can't trust the Patriots' rushing attack. And given that the Lions finally seem to have some answers on defense, this should favor the Lions. The one aspect that could tilt things in New England's favor, though, is Maye. While he still prefers to throw when he has escaped the pocket, he still does have 219 rushing yards this season, fourth most among quarterbacks.

While On Paper got wins both straight up and against the spread (6-2 overall, 4-4 ATS), it may have been my least accurate column of the year. I overestimated the Lions' advantage on offense and underestimated their advantages on defense. I expected a shootout and got a 19-9 win, instead. Sure, I had no idea Mahogany was going to be out, but that doesn't justify how bad I missed on that one.

To be fair, no one really expected a defensive battle. And the closest prediction in the comment section wasn't all that close: a 24-16 prediction from The Proudest:

I don't have photoshop on the road with me in Germany, so as your prize, enjoy this picture of me with a humongous beer in Munich:

The Lions come out with a slight +1 advantage, but the edge in three of the four matchups. As is the case with a lot of games this year, the outcome could come down to that one disadvantage: the Lions' pass defense. Maye is an electric player with a ton of explosive play potential. Detroit has done better at limiting that as of late, but the only recent quarterback they've played who can consistently do that was Jordan Love. If Detroit can repeat their performance from that game, they'll be in good shape. If not, it could be a long flight home.

#2802. Game Preview: Knicks at Pacers, November 13, 2026

There are sports movies, there are even some good sports movies. And then there is Hoosiers.

As a basketball romantic you are definitely not flipping the channel when old ball coach Norman Dale a.k.a. Gene Hackman drives his 1951 Chevy Styleline Deluxe through the backwoods of Indiana all the way to the little town of Hickory, where he hopes to find a new life, new love and redemption. You let yourself be mesmerized by Angelo Pizzo's and David Anspaugh's timeless fairytale, by the very essence of "Hoosier Hysteria," the beautiful yet tragic tribulations of high school sports, the rough, simple charm of small town America. And you enjoy every second of it, despite a rather predictable underdog story unfolding in front of your eyes that Hollywood has repeated many times over.

The current Indiana Pacers would kill for some of that predictability, the kind they expected going into this season. After a surprising Finals berth in 2025, their following year was doomed by Tyrese Haliburton's ruptured Achilles. They punted on the next campaign and thought, with their point guard's return, everything would return normal; that the half-court offense would run smooth as a "picket fence;" and that the jumpers would automatically fall like the ones by Jimmy Chitwood. But Haliburton (unfortunately) isn't as quiet nor as down to earth as Mr. Chitwood, nor is an NBA season comparable to a Hollywood movie. It's a lot more complicated than that.

The Pacers are finding that out the hard way. It only took testy Tyrese a handful of games until he got injured again (it's a hamstring now) and his team sorely misses the All Star as their 4-8 record puts them in the lower region of the Eastern Conference. On Friday against the New York Knicks, Haliburton will also be reduced to trolling from the sidelines, and he won't be able to right the wrongs that have plagued his squad so far this season. It's a huge advantage for Mike Brown's men as Haliburton is the straw that stirs the Apple Cider for Indiana. Most of their strategy revolves around his talent, his scoring and his distribution.

But it's not like the Pacers are just struggling out of the gate because Hali has only played four games. Even with him they lost to Milwaukee, barely got by New Orleans and were annihilated by Dallas. Indiana can't shoot threes (just over 33 percent), despite a traditionally fast pace their offense isn't even close to functioning well (20th in offensive rating), and their D is nothing to write home about either (15th in the league). The Pacers are an atrocious rebounding team (29th in rebounding percentage) and they struggle mightily to hit their free throws.

Do they do anything well? They do, in fact, take good care of the ball and have a one of the best assist-to-turnover-ratios in the entire Association. Individually Pascal Siakam is enjoying a strong start to the season (22.7 points) and Andrew Nembhard has come firing out of the gates as well (17.1 points, 42.9 percent from downtown). A lot of guys are still left from that Finals team two years ago, so in theory they should know what it takes. And Rick Carlisle is still a tremendously respected coach, at least when he isn't whining like a five year old who didn't get his wish at Toys-R-Us.

The skipper really has his work cut out for him early in the year. New center Ivica Zubac, a classic, plodding back-to-basket big man with considerable post skills, hasn't really found his place in an adjusted Pacers system that once was predicated on playing five-out at all costs. Continuity has also been a big issue as Carlisle has already started 11 different players, at times making it seem like the Pacers are still on their tanking ways from last year. They obviously aren't and it should be noted that slow starts are nothing new for Indiana under Carlisle. Consider yourself warned.

With Friday's game being another Cup contest you can bet that the Pacers will be highly motivated and our beloved Knicks better be ready for a hostile environment. Keep calm if Haliburton tries some stupid sideline voodoo as he certainly will when he senses a camera being on him. Feed Karl-Anthony Towns in a favorable matchup for him, let Brunson do his thing against Indiana's supposed Brunson stoppers who always seem to just limit him to 35. Make use of your more talented depth, outshoot the struggling shooting team and control the tempo. Just show that you are the better team – which the Knicks, even with their current ups and downs, are at this point in the season.

And please leave the Indiana underdog stories where they belong and where they are actually fun. Leave them to Hoosiers.

Who: New York Knicks (6-5) at Indiana Pacers (4-8)Date: Friday, November 13, 2026Time: 7:00 PM ETPlace: Gainbridge Fieldhouse, Indianapolis, INTV: Prime VideoFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky

#2801. Outlook outage continues as Microsoft flags 'encouraging recovery signals'

Microsoft suffered a widespread outage on Thursday and Friday, causing disruption to millions of its customers as engineers scrambled to fix one of its biggest-ever server issues.

Connectivity problems began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday and continued into Friday, with Outlook and Teams, along with multiple Microsoft 365 services such as Sharepoint and Copilot, affected. Numerous external services that connect with Microsoft products such as Outlook Calendar were also hit.

In an update shortly before 8 a.m. ET, Microsoft continued to warn that users may be unable to connect to multiple Microsoft 365 products, including Outlook on either web or desktop and many services that interact with email.

However, it said it was making "continued recovery progress" overall, with "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" in much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in Asia Pacific.

Intermittent issues are expected as recovery efforts continue.

Email and related tools were unavailable for Microsoft users on Thursday afternoon and evening, throughout the Asian business day on Friday and across the European and early U.S. morning.

Engineering teams have been taking affected systems offline for fixes and bringing them back online in stages. They are prioritizing efforts to preserve emails delayed during the recovery process and reduce email queues and backlogs, extending the timeout window, whereby delayed emails continue to attempt delivery, to 48 hours to help protect messages.

Microsoft says it has not detected any malicious activity causing the outage, which it initially blamed on a traffic surge in part of its infrastructure and issues with a component responsible for processing server health.

The company said in its initial updates on Thursday that the connectivity problems related to infrastructure "elevated load across multiple regions," caused by a "number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure." Some servers were failing automated health checks, it said.

Microsoft shares were around 2% lower in premarket trade.

Governments and businesses in Asia-Pacific and Europe said they were monitoring the situation, which was causing widespread disruption.

The U.K.'s National Health Service said the outage was affecting some of its services but that patients should attend appointments as normal. Calls "may be subject to long waits" as a result of disruption to the organization, a hospital group serving South West London and the English county of Surrey said on X.

Earnings for Swiss luxury goods giant Richemont were slightly delayed on Friday due to the outage. Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on Nov. 12, rescheduled the release to Nov. 16, citing business disruptions caused by the global Microsoft outage.

Air India said it had "temporarily rerouted" emails so it could continue to receive customer messages, adding that its flight operations were not affected.

Australian Home Affairs and Cyber Security Minister Tony Burke said in a press conference that Microsoft "believe they are dealing in some ways similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Reuters reported.

A fault with an update issued by cybersecurity company CrowdStrike caused one of the world's biggest IT system outages in 2024, hitting airlines, banks and more.

Microsoft reported in 2025 that Copilot, its collection of AI assistants and tools, had more than 100 million monthly active users.

The incident highlights a business "resilience and dependency issue that has been decades in the making," James Owen, managing partner of Digital Risks at consultancy Control Risks, said by phone.

"We have become, organizationally in the private sector and more broadly, increasingly dependent on a smaller segment of technology and infrastructure as critical to daily life and business activities."

"Organizations are becoming more aware through a geopolitical lens about what technologies they adopt, whether their services are provided by firms in the U.S., or China, or elsewhere, but this shows the importance of proper recovery planning in the case of an IT outage. That could be manual backups, protocols that do not require internet connection, investing in diverse suppliers and crisis management planning rehearsals," he said.

Amazon Web Services and Google users also reported outages on the site on Thursday.

Amazon wrote on X that services were "operating normally" and an "unrelated disruption elsewhere on the internet is prompting some inaccurate news reports." The company referred users to its health dashboard for "accurate data."

At 4 p.m. ET Thursday, Microsoft said it had "validated an alternative service health check method" that brought some affected servers back online.

"We're now applying this change more broadly," Microsoft wrote. "We're also preparing automated recovery systems to continually detect and restart unresponsive servers, to maintain service stability while this change progresses."

#2800. Friday Flakes: Matt Rhule Has Never Lost a Game at Nebraska When His Team Scores How Many Points?

Going through the Game Notes sent out by the Athletic Department earlier this week I noticed an interesting stat on the right side of the Games Notes publication.

Matt Rhule is 14-0 when scoring 30 or more points while at Nebraska.

Throughout his entire career as a college coach, Matt Rhule is 41-5 when scoring 30+ points in a game. That would obviously includes his games at Temple and Baylor.

A couple weeks ago Dana Holgorsen said that to win games in the Big Ten, it feels like it might be a race to 21 points. Well last week alone, seven Big Ten teams scored 28 points or more. Every one of those teams won except Purdue and Ohio State.

I understand the Big Ten makes it difficult to get enough possessions to routinely score 30 points, but there is another side of the coin to the importance of scoring points for Matt Rhule.

He is 0-12 in games in which he was trailing at halftime while at Nebraska.

That means his winning percentage while trailing at halftime or trailing at the end of the game is the same: .000.

If I was Matt Rhule and somebody told me that I'm undefeated when I score 30 points or more but I'm also winless when trailing at halftime that I better do everything I can to get this next offensive coordinator position at Nebraska right.

When it comes to Glenn Thomas and the next three games, I do believe there should be no world in which Matt Rhule decides to give Thomas the full time offensive coordinator role going forward at Nebraska.

I do not care if the Huskers go 3-0 against Rutgers, Ohio State and Iowa.

I do not care if the offense scores 30 points or more in those three wins.

It is too small a sample size for Nebraska to commit Glenn Thomas to a full season and more of being the year round offensive coordinator.

Case in point, watch the press conferences of Rob Aurich and the most recent one of Glenn Thomas. Who exudes confidence? It is definitely Aurich. I would not say the same about Glenn Thomas. That doesn't mean he cannot be a great offensive coordinator in the future but there is a clear difference between the two.

The main difference, I would guess, stems from Rob Aurich running his system at various levels of football and seeing success. He probably has seen "it all" and that is where his confidence comes from and why he received the extension.

#2799. Bessent: Treasury has wanted Megaspeed restrictions for months, but Commerce is in charge

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday said his department and others in the Trump administration have long supported slapping restrictions on Megaspeed, the company at the center of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's spy-sex scandal.

But the Commerce Department is in charge, "and you will have to ask them about their internal processes," Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box."

The Cabinet secretary's comments hinting at disunity within the administration followed an Axios report that Bessent, in the White House Situation Room last week, had asked Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick why he has resisted implementing export controls, especially on Megaspeed.

Lutnick has "repeatedly stood in the way" of cracking down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China, Axios reported.

Commerce Department spokeswoman Kristen Eichamer on Wednesday told CNBC that Bessent and Lutnick had "no such conversation" in the Situation Room.

Asked on CNBC about the reported incident, Bessent said, "We don't repeat conversations in the Situation Room."

But he said that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months."

Asked if he was frustrated with the potential export control delays, Bessent said, "I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above H100s."

"And so any leakage is very frustrating" because it "hurts our great companies in the AI race [and] gives the Chinese an advantage," he said.

Huang, seen as one of Trump's closest corporate ally before resigning as Nvidia CEO under a cloud of scandal Thursday morning, had pushed the U.S. government to ease restrictions on the export of advanced AI chips to China. In December, Trump said Nvidia could sell its powerful H200 chips to approved Chinese customers, provided the U.S. gets a percentage of the sales.

#2798. Devin Booker’s 30 points lift Suns past Hornets, 101-96

The Phoenix Suns led 48-31 halfway through the second quarter, and it looked like they were on their way to another stress-free win against a depleted Charlotte Hornets team. Without the franchise cornerstone players Kon Knueppel and Brandon Miller, and with a superb stretch from the Suns bench, the Hornets looked dead in the water, but ultimately fought back and made this game a slog for the final two and a half quarters for the Suns, who won 101-96.

Two things were apparent in this game: the Phoenix Suns could not rebound, and the Charlotte Hornets could not stop turning the basketball over. The Hornets outrebounded the Suns 64-to-43 and outscored the Suns 16-7 in second-chance points. The Suns forced 27 Hornets turnovers (each Hornets starter had at least four turnovers) while the Suns committed eight turnovers. So the rebounding numbers are skewed in favor of the Hornets because they had 13 fewer shots on goal than the Suns did. However, 22 Suns defensive rebounds compared to 15 Hornets offensive rebounds is not getting the job done at all for a Suns team that can be much better than they have been this season at rebounding.

Because the Suns could not rebound the ball and play as fast as they needed to get the offense going, the game became a half-court slog in the second half. The Suns shot 13-for-42 from the 3-point line, and a lot of the looks that went in on Tuesday did not fall for the Suns against the Hornets. Overall, the Suns were 41% from the field, and only one player had a field goal percentage higher than 50%. Devin Armani Booker scored 30 points on 12-of-20 shooting, 4-for-8 from the 3-point line, and had seven assists with just two turnovers. He made every big shot for Phoenix in clutch time, including a deep dagger 3 with 23 seconds left to give the Suns a decisive six-point lead.

All eyes were on Miles Bridges, Grayson Allen, and Royce O'Neale in this game because of the Bridges trade that happened this offseason. Bridges scored 11 points, grabbed six rebounds, and had three assists, and was effective playing with the bench units, but continued to struggle to make an impact with the starting group. Allen scored 14 points, while O'Neale scored 7 points, all coming in the fourth quarter. The Hornets were led by Coby White, who scored 21 points but did not play in the fourth quarter due to what appeared to be a minutes restriction. That certainly helped the Suns win this game, because White was getting wherever he wanted against the Suns' defense.

A win is a win, but the Suns' starting unit continued to not find any type of consistency in this game. The best stretches of basketball continue to come from this team at the beginning of the second and fourth quarters when there are at least four bench players in. The Suns closed the game with a Booker-Luke Kennard-Jordan Goodwin-Dillon Brooks-Oso Ighodaro lineup, while Jalen Green played just 21 minutes and none in the final quarter.

Green's continuing to show growth in the areas the Suns need him to grow in, but the fit with everyone else on the roster continues to be a problem, and the trust in him is obviously dwindling as he continues to not see minutes in fourth quarters. The Suns' record is now 5-6, and sometime in the near future they are going to have to change the starting lineup if it continues to look this disconnected.

All eyes were on Miles Bridges, Grayson Allen, and Royce O'Neale to start this game, and it was Grayson Allen who got things going for the Hornets early, connecting on a pair of triples. The Suns' defense lacked focus and gave up multiple wide-open layups and threes early, with Coby White hitting a wide-open 3 in semi-transition to go up 15-10. Jordan Ott called a timeout and subbed out Bridges for Ryan Dunn. The Suns' energy immediately changed on that end of the floor, as they quickly jumped on the Hornets defensively, leading to a 7-0 run engineered by Jalen Green knocking down two free throws and a corner 3 off of Suns stops.

There were two big takeaways from the Suns' first quarter: defense forced 10 turnovers and Devin Booker's pull-up 3-point shooting. Booker was dialed in, scoring 13 points on 3-of-4 shooting from 3. His comfort level shooting from long range continues to grow, and it is opening up everything for the rest of his game. The Suns led by six to end the first quarter because the Hornets did just enough on the offensive glass to stay in it, down 28-22 after one.

The Suns bench took over in the second quarter because of their hustle and tenacity on both ends of the floor. Jordan Goodwin forced multiple turnovers, leading to a wide-open dunk for Bridges and free throws off of an excellent out-of-bounds play. Collin Gillespie got free for multiple long-range bombs that went in as the Suns pushed their six-point lead out to 15 four minutes into the second quarter, 46-31.

The Suns led by as much as 17 before putting the starters back in, but there was some slippage. The Hornets went on a 14-2 run to cut the Suns' lead to 50-43. A couple of defensive breakdowns and Bridges fouling Grant Williams on a 3-point shot, leading to a 4-point play, were the catalysts for the Hornets getting back into the game. Williams scored 9 points in the second period, and another Allen 3 got the Hornets' deficit down to five at halftime, 55-50.

Even though the Suns were out-rebounded 28-to-15, the Suns still won the possession battle because the Hornets had 15 turnovers compared to the Suns' three total turnovers in the first half. The two worst stretches of the game came when the majority of the Suns' starters were on the floor, as they continued to get in their own way of being a good team.

The Suns' sloppiness from the starters continued to start the second half. As the Hornets jumped out to a 12-to-4 run to start the third quarter, the Suns' poor offensive flow led to easy shots and even more offensive rebounds for the Hornets, who led 62-59 with 8:22 left to play in the third. Since the Suns' 17-point second-quarter lead, the Suns were outscored 31-to-11 across both halves, and Coby Whites 19 points up to that point were a big reason why.

For the rest of the quarter, the Suns started to play better once Dunn, Gillespie and Maluach checked in for Ighodaro, Bridges and Green. But the Hornets responded immediately after two tough Booker midrange buckets. Both teams finished the quarter cold from the field, but Christian Anderson's solid play off the bench for the Hornets put the Hornets up 76-72 after three quarters. The Suns continued to look allergic to rebounding and playing consistent, mistake-free defense, and now a game that was once in cruise control completely slipped away from them. At no point should Jalen Green ever lead the Suns in rebounding with four total rebounds after three quarters.

It wasn't the prettiest 11-3 run ever to start the fourth quarter, but the Suns bench just never relents on their pressure. It started with the Suns grabbing a defensive rebound and a Bridges dunk in transition. The Suns attacked the rim and glass early in the quarter, capped off by a Gillespie midrange pull-up after a travel from Reid. Next play, the Suns force a turnover, Gillespie misses another midrange shot, but Goodwin chases down the rebound and lobs it up to Ighodaro to give the Suns an 83-79 lead.

The Suns continued to string together good possessions for the most part but could not create much separation. Luke Kennard scored multiple midrange shots, and a Gillespie drive-and-dump off to Maluach should have ended in a dunk, but he mishandled it, and O'Neale sprayed in a triple on the other end.

Booker, Brooks, and Ighodaro checked and left Goodwin and Kennard in. After Williams got open for a layup, Booker found Goodwin for an open 3 that just rimmed out. Booker connected on a midrange jump shot to give the Suns a three-point lead. The Suns continued to get multiple stops, and finally a Brooks 3-point shot gave the Suns a 92-86 lead.

The Suns and Hornets traded multiple empty possessions until Reid broke the seal with a 3 of his own, but Booker responded with a tough floater in the lane to get the Suns back up five with one minute to play. A cutting Diabate layup on the other end got it right back to a one-possession game with the Suns up 94-91. Then it was Devin Booker time as he hit a deep, deep 3-point pull with 23 seconds left to give Phoenix a decisive six-point lead. That is, until Brooks fouled O'Neale on a 3-point shot, which, of course, went in for the four-point play.

The Suns inbounded the basketball to Booker. He quickly passed it back to Bridges, who was fouled by Allen, and he made both free throws. Then Booker poetically stole an Allen pass for the Hornets' 27th turnover of the night, and sank both free throws as the Suns went on to win 101-96.

The Phoenix Suns finish up their homestand with the Los Angeles Lakers on Sunday afternoon.

#2796. Ohio State’s special teams swung 2 games, and now Robby Discher is gone

Ohio State's offense has a freshman quarterback who's been struggling, and their defense has given up 71 points in two weeks. But if you're looking for the moments where the Buckeyes' last two games turned, I keep landing on special teams.

On Monday, Ryan Day made a change. Ohio State fired special teams coordinator Robby Discher after just nine games, the first in-season firing of an assistant during Day's tenure.

Look back at both losses, and special teams shows up right where things started to fall apart.

At USC, the Trojans were already up 7-3 in the first quarter when Trent Mosley returned a punt 44 yards. Two plays later, Waymond Jordan cut through the Ohio State defense for a 9-yard touchdown and a 14-3 lead. Ohio State spent the rest of the night chasing.

The Buckeyes also committed three penalties on punt coverage and returns in that game, giving the Trojans free yards and extra chances in a game they won by 12.

Against Oregon, it was even more obvious.

Ohio State led 14-0 and had Oregon stuck on fourth-and-9 near midfield in the second quarter. The Ducks lined up to punt, and instead, Teitum Tuioti took the snap and threw to Matayo Uiagalelei for a 30-yard gain.

Six plays later, Oregon scored its first touchdown, and then went on to score 38 straight points.

Dan Lanning said afterward that the fake punt "created some momentum," and that's the best way to describe it. Neither play lost a game by itself; the defense and offense had plenty of chances to recover.

Both came at the exact moment Ohio State had control or desperately needed it back, and both completely flipped the game in the opponent's favor.

Entering the Oregon game, Ohio State had committed at least one special teams penalty in every single game this season, including three against both Iowa and USC.

The Buckeyes rank 102nd nationally in special teams efficiency, which is hard to believe for a program with this much talent.

That's what made Discher's firing feel inevitable.

Ohio State hired him from Illinois in January specifically to fix special teams after two seasons without a full-time coordinator. He signed a two-year deal worth $400,000 this year, and the Dispatch reported he could be owed more than $500,000 in severance.

It was supposed to be a fix. Instead, the problems got worse.

Day didn't hold back when explaining the decision, saying, "There's just been too many detrimental plays."

After the Oregon loss, he'd made it clear that accountability starts with the staff.

"The penalties are a killer. At the end of the day, as a coach, you've got to look yourself in the mirror and find out why that's happening."

I think letting Discher go was the right call. Firing a coach midseason is rare, especially for Day, but Ohio State couldn't keep losing the hidden yardage battle at the most important moments.

With their playoff hopes hanging on by a thread, if at all, there's no time left to wait.

For the rest of the season, Ohio State is going back to the collaborative approach they used in 2024 and 2025.

Senior analyst Rob Keys will oversee special teams as a whole. Keys has been in Columbus since 2022, has worked primarily with Ohio State's special teams during that time, and previously coached special teams at Findlay. He knows these players and these units better than anyone else on staff.

Safeties coach and pass game coordinator Matt Guerrieri will lead the punt team, which is the unit that needs the most attention after the last two weeks. Linebackers coach James Laurinaitis will lead the kickoff team, and multiple coaches will share responsibility for the kickoff return unit.

There's some irony in this. Ohio State hired Discher because the collaborative model had its own issues, and now they're going back to that model for the stretch run.

In the short term, it makes sense. Keys and the full-time assistants already know the system, and three games isn't enough time to bring in someone new. The real test will be simple — can Ohio State get through a game without a backbreaking special teams mistake?

That's a low bar, but it hasn't happened much lately.

The stakes are clear. Northwestern is first, then a road trip to Nebraska, then Michigan. Ohio State's Big Ten title hopes are a long shot, but the Michigan game alone is reason enough to fix this. Rivalry games are often decided by one or two plays, and Ohio State can't afford to give away another one on special teams.

Firing Discher won't fix everything. But if Keys, Guerrieri, and Laurinaitis can clean up the penalties and stop giving opponents free momentum, it might give the Buckeyes one less thing to worry about as they desperately try to salvage this season.

#2795. Wholesale prices rose 0.3% in October, putting annual rate at 6.5%, the highest in nearly four years

Wholesale prices increased less than expected in October, but inflation pressures persisted and the Federal Reserve is likely still on target for an interest rate increase soon.

The producer price index, which measures the prices domestic producers get for their products before they reach the consumer, rose a seasonally adjusted 0.3% for the month, against the Dow Jones consensus for a 0.4% increase, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday.

Stripping out food and energy, core PPI posted a 0.3% gain, meeting expectations.

On an annual basis, headline PPI accelerated 6.5%, up 0.2 percentage point for the highest annual rate since November 2022.

The report comes just a few weeks ahead of the Federal Reserve's next policy meeting Dec. 8-9. Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point increase in the central bank's key overnight borrowing rate, with slight odds that the Federal Open Market Committee might opt for a half-point hike.

Stock market futures added to gains following the release while Treasury yields were mixed.

Earlier this week, the BLS reported that inflation at the cash register was hotter than expected.

The headline consumer price index saw a 0.4% increase in October while core was up 0.3%, both 0.1 percentage point higher than expected. Because of the government shutdown in October 2025, the BLS couldn't collect some data and refrained from putting out a 12-month inflation figure for CPI.

However, the figures showed that the Fed remains a good distance from its 2% inflation goal.

"Today's PPI data – which shows some signs of improving, albeit still too-high – is unlikely to change the Fed's approach in December because the CPI data was already outside their comfort zone," said Chris Zaccarelli, chief investment officer for Northlight Asset Management.

Moreover, policymakers are beginning to worry that inflation generated by the Iran war and higher fuel prices, along with President Donald Trump's tariffs, are beginning to spread through the economy. The Fed generally would look through such price pressures as temporary, but the breadth of inflation could indicate that inflation is becoming more entrenched.

"We've had some signs of trouble now for several months in a row," Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said in a CNBC interview Friday. "If you look at how broad-based the inflation is, it's not just that we're above the target and have been for some time. It's that in categories that are not driven by oil prices and not driven by tariffs, you're still seeing stalled progress and in some cases going the wrong way."

Stripping out food, energy and trade services, PPI saw an increase of 0.5% in October.

Goods prices increased 0.5% in October, with more than 60% of that move driven by goods excluding food and energy, which actually saw a 0.1% decrease. On an annual basis, the goods index jumped 10.2%, the biggest 12-month surge since October 2022.

Final demand services prices increased 0.2%, most of which was linked to transportation and warehousing services, and within that category a 3.9% gain in truck transportation of freight.

"We've been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we're not making any progress, and if anything, it's going the wrong way," Goolsbee said. "Inflation is rising; it's it's proved far more persistent than we predicted at the beginning from the supply shocks."

Other items in the PPI report also showed multi-year gains. Prices for intermediate processed goods soared 14.6% from October 2025, the biggest annual gain since July 2022. Intermediate prices for services posted a 6.9% increase, the most since November 2022.

#2793. #PostPulpit mailbag: What’s going on with Christian Gonzalez?

The New England Patriots have landed in Germany where they hold a pair of practices before taking on the Detroit Lions at 9:30 a.m. ET on Sunday.

So, let's get into this week's edition of the #PostPulpit Mailbag.

Like a lot of people, I was mightily disappointed (to say the least) in the recent performance of our resident highest-paid cornerback in the league. But I find myself wondering if he's the only one deserving blame. When he repeatedly lines up in such soft coverage, not pressing at the line of scrimmage — indeed, giving the receiver an obscenely huge cushion to release — that's not entirely HIS decision, right? Isn't that pre-snap alignment dictated by the coaches and their game plan, at least much of the time? How much of the problem do you think lies with coaching schemes that play away from Gonzalez's strengths? – BriGuy301

What happened to Gonzalez last game and why? Was it a one-off, or did the Packers figure something out that other teams might be able to emulate? – fdsafdsa

Gonzalez is certainly not blameless and needs to play better. However, he is also being asked to do a lot within a Patriots secondary that leans heavily on disguising coverages. While the All-Pro cornerback is at his best pressing receivers at the line of scrimmage and playing man coverage, he has been asked to handle a variety of responsibilities, including off-man coverage, inverted Cover 2 (where he is responsible for the half-field safety), playing the deep third in Cover 3 and more.

The question here is whether the Patriots have leaned too heavily into those disguises and reached a point where simplifying things would benefit the defense. New England has a talented secondary that is playing well below its capabilities as they rank dead last in the league in zone coverage EPA per dropback. Opposing offenses like the Bears and Packers have also appeared to be one step ahead with coverage beaters and using tools like quick snaps to catch the defense out of position and generate explosive plays.

At some point, the Patriots may need to prioritize letting their defensive backs play more straight up and to their strengths.

With all the pressure that Maye faces each game, and especially against teams like the Packers who blitz a lot (46.5% of his drop backs against Green Bay), why do we not see more hot reads or short patterns? It looks like the Patriots rely predominantly on mid- to long-range routes, which take more time and require the Offensive Line to hold up longer. I would think that Pop or Chism – who both have short-area quickness – would be great at those routes, especially given that they seem to run a lot of them during the preseason. So I'm curious if A) they're doing it but I just don't see it? And/or B) is there a good reason to not run quick slants and crossers and hot reads? – PatsFanFromNH

The Patriots' offense does feature sight adjustments and hot routes. Earlier this season, players credited opposing defenses for dropping defenders off the line of scrimmage to take away those routes. New England will need to find ways to counter those adjustments or develop other answers against the pressure packages that have repeatedly given the offense trouble.

In recent weeks, both the Bears and Packers have found success attacking the Patriots' offensive line with overload pressures, sending two defenders off the same side of the formation and dropping defenders off the line of scrimmage on the other side. In both games, New England struggled to pick up those pressures early before settling down and finding answers as the game progressed.

Moving forward, the Patriots need to determine how they want to handle those situations out of the gate, whether that means identifying the right protection calls before the snap or trusting Maye and his receivers to make plays after. Finding those answers earlier in games will be critical to avoid early deficits.

Brian, if the Patriots lose to the Lions to fall to 5-5 with 4 very difficult games left, is it time to switch gears and root for draft position? It's been a tough year full of injuries. That happens in football, and the draft is supposed to be a good one. On the other hand, if they pull off the upset in Germany, it's full speed ahead going for the playoffs, with a bye week plus the Chargers game to get healthy. – New England Guy

Sunday's game against the Lions feels like an inflection point on the season, so it will be interesting to see which Patriots team shows up in Germany.

As for the playoffs, 10 wins has historically been a good benchmark for securing a postseason spot. If the Patriots take care of business against the winless Chargers, Jets and Dolphins, they would need just two more wins from their remaining matchups against the Lions, Vikings, Chiefs, Bills and Broncos to reach that mark.

And looking at the current AFC landscape, the threshold could be closer to nine wins. There appears to be a relatively clear-cut top seven in the conference unless the Houston Texans catch fire during the second half of the season.

Why didn't the pats trade for a nose tackle, 3rd safety, or/and a 3rd outside cornerback? Any one, two or all 3 of these positions were a must have to right the ship! – sjamesbossports

After investing significant draft capital in A.J. Brown and looking to avoid taking on a major financial commitment, the Patriots were never likely to make a significant addition at the trade deadline. You could certainly make the argument for adding defensive depth in exchange for late-round draft capital, but the lack of movement at those positions around the league suggests there wasn't much of a market at those spots.

A question more long term :what are your thoughts about next year patriots cap big moves renegotiation with major players (or potential cut or trade) to absorb anticipated Maye super contract ? – 7i165

Who do you think will be the cap casualties next year? Onwenu, Barmore, Davis, Hunter, Byard, DeVitto, Moses, Landry? I know they are a veteran core, but almost all of them don't produce to what they are being paid at, so we might need to cut bait. How much would we gain from trading or letting them walk? – Maxxwell

The Patriots did not sell at the deadline as they still can be a competitve team especially as they get healthier on offense. It will be a different conversation this offseason as there is definitely an argument for the team getting younger and adding draft capital.

Among the names mentioned, I would imagine the team moves on from Christian Barmore, Harold Landry, and potentially Carlton Davis as the veterans have no guaranteed money remaining. Byard's play has not been worthy of a second contract while the guess would be Moses retires. Henry was extended this offseason while there's no rush to move off DeVito. All the moves would free up a substantial amount of salary cap space.

That's all for this week's #PostPulpit mailbag. If you have questions you'd liked to be answered next week, submit them online in our weekly submission post on the Feed. Make sure to follow @iambrianhines and @PatsPulpit as well.

#2792. OSU's Legree leads nation in receiving as WSU clash looms

CORVALLIS — There may be no more appropriate way to describe Oregon State's outrageously successful passing game this season than explosive.

The Beavers lead the country in passing yards thanks in large part to 10 passes of 40-plus yards. Jesse Legree is responsible for eight of those catches, including all five of OSU's 50-yard pass plays this season, making it no surprise that he leads the country in receiving yards and touchdowns entering this week's matchup with Washington State.

"You see him with ball in space, obviously taking the top off a number of times," Washington State coach Kirby Moore said. "I think it's about playing team defense. Obviously communication is going to be really important, where he's at."

The Cougars (1-5, 0-2 Pac-12) have the No. 2 defense in the Pac-12 thus far and are having that success by keeping the top on their pass coverage.

WSU has allowed 11 passes of 30-plus yards, which is tied for 129th nationally and nearly 10% of the passes it has allowed. However, opponents are not breaking through that mark often, with just four passes over 40 yards and none for more than 50, one of 30 teams yet to allow such a play this season.

"We don't want to let the verticals up," Washington State safety Jaylen Smith said. "We take pride in (not) letting deep balls go. We always look to play top down and take away the deep routes first."

WSU defensive coordinator Trent Bray will be tasked with doing what nobody has been able to do yet this season: contain Legree.

OSU offensive coordinator Mitch Dahlen has been creative in moving Legree around to prevent defenses from taking him away. Last week against San Diego State that included moving Legree into the backfield for a variety of plays.

"People are going to try and hit him at the line of scrimmage," Dahlen said. "They're going to try and two-hand jam. If they're going to try and two-hand jam, it's like OK, how can I move this guy enough where you can't do that? You put him in the backfield, unless you want to jump offsides and do it, you can't do it that way.

"That's what we do a good job of as a staff, is moving him around where you can't just put a safety over the top of him because if he's in the backfield, what are you going to do there?"

Even if the Cougars manage to limit Legree, the Beavers have shown they are more than capable of going elsewhere, with an outrageous 14 players catching passes last week.

Aeryn Hampton (20 receptions for 245 yards) and tight ends Eric Olsen and DeCorion Temple each have at least 20 catches and Aaron Butler has four grabs for at least 20 yards. They're confident they can challenge any defense vertically.

"The underneath throws are going to be there," Hampton said. "We got the best OC in the country; we're going to be able to go deep if we want to."

#2790. Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

Miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters."

Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The company posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

Also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

"We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth."

#2789. Patrick Mahomes on Josh Downs: You can tell the intellect, how he can pick things up

The Chiefs brought in a receiver at the trading deadline, acquiring Josh Downs from the Colts.

Quarterback Patrick Mahomes told reporters in his Wednesday press conference that he’s excited to get going with the wideout.

“I think you can tell just the intellect and how he’s able to pick stuff up and that he’s a professional, that he knows what he’s doing and he wants to come in and just compete and to have success, and he wants to win. And so, I’m excited for that,” Mahomes said, via transcript from the team. “And then you can just see him interacting with the other receivers in the room. You can tell that there’s going to be a great cohesion there, and that’s the type of guys you want on the team, that want to compete and that want to win.”

Mahomes noted he’s impressed with the way Downs can win his one-on-one matchups.

“He runs routes really well,” Mahomes said. “He sets them up really well where he will run a route early in the game that he sets up for another one later in the game. And then he has really good feel, you can tell, obviously, playing in the system that he has, he has a lot of read-type routes, and you can tell he knows how to get himself open, settle in the right zones, and win versus man [coverage] when he can.

“And so, I think it will be an easy transition for him to kind of do that stuff in our offense. Then, with how we do things, he can play a lot of different positions as we move receivers and tight ends around.”

The quarterback also sees it as realistic for Downs to play and contribute early on in his tenure with Kansas City. While that begins with plenty of reps at practice, Mahomes and the rest of the offense can direct Downs to where he needs to be during games if necessary.

“[W]e do a great job of kind of moving guys in and out of every single position, and so guys know the entire concepts of the plays,” Mahomes said. “We’re very detailed with how we call the plays in the huddle, which will help him out a ton.

“Then when he doesn’t know, being able to talk to me in the huddle or talk to the guys as they’re breaking the huddle, and that usually helps when the guys like each other. And so, it’s good to have a guy that you can tell everybody’s going to like, and that he has his head on the right way, and he’s going to make sure that he’s going to do whatever it takes to win.”

In nine games with the Colts this year, Downs caught 33 passes for 354 yards with one touchdown.

#2788. Wolves 133, Mavericks 94: You Like That?

Do you remember the last time the Minnesota Timberwolves played basketball?

Since the Wolves last played, the Minnesota football team got flat-out embarrassed on national television, then went through all five stages of grief before building a time machine that sent them back to the days of Kirk Cousins, and now, in one fell swoop, has gone from pumpkins to the NFL's new belle of the ball.

And somewhere in the midst of all of this, Joan Beringer is officially no longer a teenager and is starting to go gray.

I'm not saying having no Wolves games is responsible for any of this, or that if we had played sooner, maybe Beringer wouldn't have had to have a birthday (is that how that works?). I'm not saying that! But man, does it feel good to finally have this team back on the court and on our screens again.

In their first game back in eons, the Wolves laced up and faced off against a team in the Dallas Mavericks that seems to be fast-tracking a soft rebuild. On paper, both teams are pretty evenly matched in several categories, namely FG% (DAL #4, MIN #5), turnovers (DAL #10, MIN #11), and steals (DAL #14, MIN #15), so the Wolves needed to win the possession battle.

Certainly, the Mavericks would be up for the challenge, so it would stand to reason that this would be a challenging game for the Wolves. Right?

To start the game, Jonathan Kuminga was on a torrid pace, muscling to the basket for a lay-up and cutting to the rim for a dunk off a beautiful find by LaMelo Ball, who proceeded to find Jaden McDaniels on a similar play a few possessions later.

The Mavericks settled in and muddied the game as the quarter went on. At the 5:16 mark, TJ Shannon subbed in, and PJ Washington proceeded to bully him to the rim for an and-one. This was a great quarter for Washington, as he finished with 10 points in the quarter.

Perhaps an accurate distillation of the rest of the game, though, is that those 10 points would be it for Washington, and the Mavs 24-19 lead would soon be relinquished and gone for good.

Ayo Dosunmu and the bench mob of Bones Hyland, Jaylen Clark, Trey Lyles, and Joan Beringer burst the Wolves out of the mud like the Snoats brothers in "Raising Arizona", spurring an 11-0 run that got the crowd dancing on their feet. After a couple of free throws by Naji Marshall to stop the run, a Gobert offensive rebound off a missed Dosunmu corner three allowed the Wolves to close out the quarter with this Clark nuke.

The second quarter saw more of the same for the Wolves. After a sloppy turnover by Dosunmu led to a corner three by Zaccharie Risacher, the Wolves had given up 15 points off of six turnovers. Those numbers would balloon to 25 and 11 by the end of the first half, and it wouldn't matter.

Dosunmu continues to truck along as Mr. Consistency, a perfect cog in the absence of Anthony Edwards. He finished the half with 12 points by doing what he does best: being an absolute bully out on the break.

As for Ball, he was unconscious from deep, and finding cutters left and right. Much has been said about his fit with Gobert, and there were still a couple of miscues on the Ball-Gobert feed tonight. Near the end of the half, though, Ball slipped into the paint as the ball guided him around. He faked once, and then floated the ball up for a Gobert slam.

It was a thing of beauty, and exactly why sticking to the process matters.

Going into this game, Ball's assist-to-turnover ratio (1.62) wasn't pretty to look at, but for the most part, I don't mind it.

The way I see it is that they are mostly a statistical fallout of process-driven stuff that should temper with time. Some of the results might be an eyesore for box score perusers, but I love the process. I love that Ball is not afraid to continue to funnel the ball into Rudy, even if his individual numbers risk taking a hit. The box score won't tell the whole story. It seldom does. But Ball's commitment to the process should pay dividends as the season bears itself out.

The Wolves would go into halftime leading 67-52. And then…

Ball continued his unconscious streak from long-range, followed by a Dosunmu transition trey. Dusty May would call a timeout not even two minutes into the second half to try to stop the bleeding. That worked just as well as trying to stop a Beringer nosebleed.

The Wolves were playing loose and fast. McDaniels was gliding down the court for barely contested lay-ins. Kuminga was hitting threes, and the lead would soar to 32 points midway through the third after McDaniels was blocked, got the ball back, and then threw down a vicious slam.

Right before the McDaniels sequence, Beringer re-entered the game with a clear mask (!). Before the mask change, Beringer had zero points and zero blocks. After the mask change: 13 points and three blocks. Need I say more? That new mask is magic.

Although there were times through the third where it looked more like a horse race at Canterbury, with players running around with their manes on fire, any and all sloppy play was a moot point, and the Mavericks would end up waving the white flag before the third quarter had even concluded.

The fourth quarter was mostly a non-event because of the score (Wolves 103 – Mavericks 69 at the end of the third), outside of a Gobert and-one off a Kuminga miss (where he converted on the free throw!) and a smooth jump hook by the magic-masked-man Beringer, but I wanted to shout out Isaiah Evans on his first official points in the NBA.

I know it was on a goal-tend, but still, a milestone is a milestone.

And a shout-out to Jon "Boog" Sciambi on the call tonight, his first Wolves game of the season. I know he is beloved in Wrigleyville as the play-by-play announcer for the Chicago Cubs. As a Twins fan, I hold no ill will towards the Cubs. It's that other team on the South Side that I have problems with.

In the end, the Wolves were able to completely stifle Cooper Flagg for 12 points on just 5-12 shooting. Seeing the Wolves, he was probably having nightmares about his last game against them, when he went 5-19 for 12 points. I guess this game was an improvement? Baby steps, teenager. Baby steps.

The Wolves were also able to silence Kyrie Irving, who up until now had looked rejuvenated and was outperforming his career shooting splits across the board.

Caleb Martin just about doubled his scoring average (seven points tonight). He should be proud of that.

But this was perhaps the Wolves' best all-around effort in this season's infancy. Off a long break against a good team, Target Center was rocking, and from start to finish, it was just a rollicking good time.

Right now, the Mavericks have 13 guys logging double-digit minutes. It's clear that Dusty May and his coaching staff have spent the early part of this season seeing what works and what doesn't. I'd expect the rotations to get tighter as the season wears on, as players fill out their roles and the overall numbers flesh out into something a bit more comprehensive. So far, though, May has struck a good balance of thinking big picture while still keeping his team competitive on a nightly basis.

In a fairly perforated coaching pipeline, May's seamless transition from college to the NBA has been nothing short of impressive. I was late to the magic of May, only first hearing about him last year as the coach of the eventual national champion Michigan Wolverines. Chalk it up to object permanence on my part, but I know who he is now, and it's almost as if he was built in a lab to know ball and coach ball.

Yesterday also marked the one-year anniversary of the Mavericks dumping disgraced GM and possible secret Los Angeles Lakers operative Nico Harrison. Going from Harrison to Masai Ujiri seems to have stabilized this organization. Finally, adults have returned to the table.

Enmities from the 2024 WCF aside, I'm happy for Mavericks fans.

The Timberwolves continue their eight-game homestand on Saturday, as Chicago O'Hare International Airport's Bulls fly into Target Center. O'Hare ranks first as the busiest airfield in the world. Meanwhile, their team ranks first in a bunch of categories you'd rather not rank first in. Liftoff is at 7:00 PM CT on DAZN-MN and NBA League Pass.

#2787. Stampede Blue Reacts results (Week 10): Colts fan confidence falls again, down to 17%

The latest SB Nation Reacts survey delivered another troubling update on the state of fan sentiment in Indianapolis, with just 17 percent of Colts fans saying they are confident the team is headed in the right direction. It is another slight drop from last week's 19 percent mark, and it reinforces just how little confidence remains in the current state of the franchise.

At this point, the result should not come as much of a surprise. The Colts have lost five straight games, fallen to 2-7 on the season and spent the last several weeks making major roster changes ahead of the NFL trade deadline. Quenton Nelson, DeForest Buckner, Keenan Allen and Josh Downs have all been moved, while other notable players such as Jonathan Taylor, Grover Stewart and Daniel Jones remained with the team despite speculation surrounding their futures. Taken together, it has been a clear sign that Indianapolis is no longer focused on salvaging this season, but instead trying to position itself for a longer-term reset.

That does not necessarily mean every fan opposes the direction the organization is taking. In fact, some of this low confidence may simply reflect how painful the current stage of the process looks rather than outright disagreement with the moves themselves. The Colts have finally started making the kind of difficult decisions that a struggling team often has to make, but that does not make the short-term product any easier to watch. Losing games, trading recognizable veterans and entering the second half of the season with significant uncertainty at quarterback, wide receiver and along both lines is not exactly a recipe for immediate optimism.

What this number really shows is that Colts fans are still waiting for a reason to believe. The franchise may have started its rebuilding process in earnest, but rebuilding alone does not inspire confidence unless there is a clear sense that the team knows where it is going. Right now, that part still feels uncertain. Chris Ballard is gone, the roster has been reshaped, and the next general manager will inherit a team with more draft capital, but also plenty of holes and no obvious path back to contention in the near future.

For now, the fan base remains deeply skeptical. Until the Colts start showing signs of a coherent long-term plan, or at the very least begin putting a more competitive product on the field, it is hard to imagine that confidence number rising in any meaningful way.

#2783. Dame Time is back in Portland — and the Blazers look dangerous

A new head coach will roam the sidelines. A franchise icon will make his long-awaited return. An All-Star will begin his redemption tour.

And a new ownership group will watch its first season opener from Paul Allen's former seats along the Moda Center baseline.

The Blazers open the 2026-27 NBA season Wednesday night against the Phoenix Suns — a team they upset in April in the play-in tournament — and if you're just now tuning in for the start of the regular season, well, there's a lot you missed.

RELATED: Suns vs. Blazers predictions, odds and best bets: Dame is home, and the model likes Portland on opening night

The Blazers are expected to unveil a new starting lineup that features a pair of notable All-Star additions: Damian Lillard and Ja Morant. The backcourt duo is joining a fivesome that includes returning starters Deni Avdija, Toumani Camara and Donovan Clingan. It's a versatile, star-studded lineup that features three All-Stars, a former All-Defensive Second Team selection, one of the best young centers in the NBA and loads of scoring potential.

Micah Nori, the Blazers' first-year head coach, said he plans on using a 10-man rotation to start the season, which will allow the Blazers to capitalize on their depth and versatility. In addition to the starters, Jrue Holiday, Scoot Henderson, Sidy Cissoko, Robert Williams III and Vit Krejci are expected to open the season in the rotation. The group could change depending on matchups and Williams' availability — he did not play in back-to-backs last season — and it's likely that Micah Potter, Branden Carlson and Yang Hansen will occasionally see spot duty, as well.

The Blazers stabilized their turbulent coaching situation in June, hiring longtime NBA assistant Nori to replace interim coach Tiago Splitter. Nori, who interviewed for head coaching jobs seven times before finally landing his first chance, is entering his 29th season in the league and is universally revered in NBA circles for his positive approach, ability to connect with players and sharp basketball mind. Early indications have been encouraging, as the Blazers players seem to love him and the front office works well with him. The Blazers' coaching position had been embroiled in controversy, of course, as former coach Chauncey Billups — who was placed on indefinite leave by the NBA — is facing federal felony charges related to money laundering and wire fraud conspiracy for his alleged involvement in a rigged underground poker game.

In a stark contrast to recent seasons, the Blazers are constructed around their offense rather than their defense. The roster is unbalanced, featuring five dynamic ball-handlers and playmakers (Lillard, Morant, Avdija, Holiday and Henderson), a solid center combination (Clingan and Williams) and little wing depth. As a result, the team is expected to play fast and free under Nori, bringing lots of speed, passing, cutting and flow. Nori said he hopes to rotate his players liberally in shorter shifts during games — perhaps as short as three minutes — which will enable them to play with maximum effort before giving way to teammates. The interior defense is strong with Clingan and Williams patrolling the middle, Camara remains one of the NBA's best and most versatile defenders and Cissoko will be asked to guard one-through-five. Holiday is still capable of locking down opposing guards and Avdija has pledged to be more of a two-way threat now that he doesn't have to serve as the team's primary ball-handler. But the backcourt combination of Morant and Lillard, while lethal on offense, is not imposing on defense and relatively small (both stand 6-foot-2).

Portland defied pundits last season, winning 10 of its last 14 regular season games to secure a spot in the play-in tournament, where it beat the Suns in Phoenix to earn the seventh seed in the Western Conference. The San Antonio Spurs dismissed the Blazers with a gentleman's sweep in the playoffs, but the strong run — combined with the additions of Lillard and Morant — has raised expectations in Portland. How much? Camara said in training camp that the Blazers' goal is to win 50 or more games and secure home-court advantage in the postseason. It won't be easy. The league is as deep and talented as ever, and new rules surrounding the lottery should discourage teams from tanking, meaning most of the league will be chasing wins instead of lottery ping-pong balls late into the season. It seemed like a third of the league had given up last year by the All-Star break.

Hopes for a Blazers, Moda Center deal by December deadline appear all but dashed

Joe Freeman's 3 takeaways from the Trail Blazers' back-to-back sweep vs. Thunder

Trail Blazers lose rotation player for 2 months

Joe Freeman's 3 takeaways from Trail Blazers' rout over the Thunder

Thunder vs. Blazers predictions: Portland looks to snap two-game skid in the first of back-to-back meetings

As the Blazers' new-look lineup works to build chemistry and a first-year coach settles into a new role, the schedule will be challenging. Six of the first eight games — and 12 of the first 17 — will come on the road and include a slew of playoff contenders, including the Spurs, Oklahoma City Thunder (twice), Minnesota Timberwolves (twice), New York Knicks, Philadelphia 76ers, Denver Nuggets and Los Angeles Lakers (twice).

The most uplifting part of opening night figures to be the return of Lillard, the franchise icon who is back after spending two seasons in Milwaukee and one season on the injured list. The nine-time All-Star and franchise leader has not played in an NBA regular-season or playoff game since April 27, 2025, when he suffered a torn left Achilles tendon. And he has not played with Portland since March 22, 2023, six months before it traded him to the Bucks. Lillard showed no ill effects from his injury during the exhibition season, when he played in three of the Blazers' four games and averaged 17.3 points, 2.7 assists and 22.7 minutes. If anything, he looked like the same old Dame, swishing three-pointers, creating off the dribble, initiating offense and drawing defensive attention. Lillard joked earlier this week that he's "not an old man," but also acknowledged that he isn't likely to play upward of 38 minutes a game like he used to and may even take a night off here and there for rest, most likely on a random back-to-back. His addition not only should help cover up two of the Blazers' biggest weaknesses last season — three-point shooting and shooting in the clutch — but also inspire a thirsty fan base, which has rarely loved a player more. All the while, Lillard says he intends to play with more "joy" than ever.
