#2741. ‘Things I think’: Giants have themselves to blame for squandered opportunity

EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — You wanted them to, of course. Did you really think, though, that the New York Giants were just going to waltz to the NFC East title without things getting interesting?

The Giants made things interesting, and much more convoluted, by losing to the Washington Commanders on Thursday and missing an opportunity to take firm control of the division.

The 5-3-1 Giants are still in first place, and will remain there through the weekend no matter how the second-place Dallas Cowboys fare on Sunday when they host the 7-1 San Francisco 49ers.

Their path to a first division title since the 2011 Super Bowl season is now much more difficult, and uncertain. If the Cowboys can upset the San Francisco 49ers on Sunday, they will be 5-5, just 1.5 games behind the Giants with eight weeks left in the season. The Commanders are now 3-5-1, and with a tiebreaker advantage over the Giants should also feel like their season is very much alive.

Giants head coach John Harbaugh called the loss "disappointing", a word he used multiple times in his post-game press conference. His tone, though, was meant to remind that the Giants had not suddenly turned into the Titanic.

"It's a missed opportunity, but like I told the guys, it would have been great to win the game, but it doesn't change our goals or our opportunity going forward," head coach John Harbaugh said after the game. "So, it's a tough loss. It's the National Football League. You're going to lose some games. And everybody in this league is good. The Commanders are good. Everybody's good. So, I mean, we have a really good team coming in herenext Sunday [the Jacksonville Jaguars]. A team that we can beat, so, we've just got to get back to work.

"It's disappointing, yeah. I mean, I think that's the best word. It's just disappointing, We worked hard for this, and we put a hard week in. And we were prepared. The guys came out with, I thought, tremendous energy. We played very hard. Plays were made. Plays were missed. But it wasn't good enough to win the game. And that's the disappointment of it. So it's disappointing, but you can't let it bring you down. That's why I said what I said about our spirit. Our spirit's going to be fine. We're going to be good. We're not going to curl up. We're going to come out fighting."

In his 19th season as a head coach, it was clear that Harbaugh wanted to project an image of calm amidst the storm.

"It would have been nice to open up a lead in the division. We didn't open it up as much as we could have if we had got the win. We've got a lot of tough games. What do we have, seven games left? [It's actually eight] So it's going to be seven dogfights. That's what it's going to be," Harbaugh said. "It's [the] National Football League. I'd like to say we're going to win all seven of them. But it's probably not very likely. You're probably not going to be putting any money down on that.

"So we've got to win enough. And this was one that got away. We've got to find a way to get the next one. And the next one after that. And the next one after that. And get as many as we need to win the division. That's what we've got to find a way to do. So just try to keep it in perspective is very important."

"This game would have obviously put us in a great lead in the division, but we're not dead," fullback Patrick Ricard said. "This division can still be won."

"This would have obviously helped us to get the division sooner, but that's still well in our grasp," said center Bryan Hudson.

That is kind of what this game felt like. From the beginning things did not go according to plan.

The Giants, somehow, managed to possess the ball in Washington territory six times without coming up with a point. Let's go through the litany of miscues and missed chances.

They surprisingly chose to take the ball after winning the pre-game coin toss. They drove to the Commanders' 37-yard line, but an Isaiah Likely drop ended the drive. Rather than go for it or try a 55-yard field goal, the Giants punted.

The Giants second drive stalled at the Washington 15-yard line, and Dominic Zvada [more on him later] missed a 33-yard field goal.

In the third quarter, the Giants reached the Washington 19-yard line only to have Malik Nabers fumble the ball away after catching a short pass.

On their first possession of the fourth quarter, the Giants punted on fourth-and-3 from the Washington 46-yard line. That came after a third-down drop by Theo Johnson, and analytics disagreed with Harbaugh's decision:

Honestly, so did I. I would rather have seen the Giants go for it there, especially trailing. My preference? Run the ball on third down and then go for it on fourth if you don't make the first down. It seemed clear from the play call, though, that Harbaugh did not see that spot as two-down, fo-for-it territory.

The Giants had two chances to ice the game in the final 5:27 after interceptions by safeties Jevon Holland at the Giants' 2-yard line and Ar'Darius Washington at the Commanders' 46-yard line. They could not generate a single first down on either occasion.

Washington coach Dan Quinn successfully challenged a Jameis Winston tush push that was initially ruled a first down on the first possession, forcing a Giants punt. The Giants caught a bad break to open that drive when Holland was ruled down at the 2-yard line after his interception, rather than in the end zone. A touchback would have given the Giants the ball at the 20-yard line.

On the second one, J.J. McCarthy was dropped for a loss on a designed quarterback run on third-and-3 from the Commanders' 39-yard line.

Instead of pretty much being able to run out the clock, the Giants punted. Jordan Stout exacerbated the failure with a terrible 12-yard punt, his first bad punt as a Giant.

On their final desperation drive, the Giants got to Washington's 48-yard line before a McCarthy deep pass intended for Nabers was intercepted.

After the Giants took a 10-7 lead with 2:35 left in the half, the Giants allowed Washington to run out the rest of the half with a nine-play, 67-yard drive that ended with a 1-yard touchdown pass to Ben Sinnott, giving the Commanders a 14-7 halftime lead.

The Giants' pass rush was virtually non-existent. They got one sacks and two hits on Jayden Daniels.

On their final drive, Washington went 71 yards for the game-winning score in just three plays and :49 seconds.

Zvada is now just 17 of 23 (73.9%) after Thursday night's miss, which was from extra-point distance. Misses by Zvada in both Washington games (three in Week 5) have proven costly.

After the game, Harbaugh tried to remain supportive of his rookie kicker.

"We're confident. You can't, as soon as a guy doesn't make a play, start firing people left and right. Especially your kicker who's a rookie," Harbaugh said. "So, I'm confident he's going to become a good kicker. I mean, at some point in time, if it doesn't happen, it doesn't happen. But I'm not going to panic halfway through the season when a guy's made a bunch of kicks, if that's what you're inferring we should be doing.

"So, I mean, we're just not going to knee jerk it like that. He's going to make kicks. He's going to make a lot of kicks. I believe in him. I think he's really good and really talented. We're going to give him an opportunity to do it, and it's up to him to do it.

At some point, though, it's not a knee-jerk reaction. Harbaugh lost his job in Baltimore last season in part because rookie placekicker Tyler Loop missed a field goal that would have put the Ravens into the playoffs.

As much as the Giants believe in Zvada's talent, you can argue that he has now cost them chances to win two games. How long can the Giants be patient?

#2737. Observations after Sixers shake off slow start, Embiid injury scare to win

Observations after Sixers shake off slow start, Embiid injury scare to win originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers brushed off their blowout loss to the Celtics and got back in the win column Thursday night.

They overcame a first-quarter deficit as high as 17 points and earned a 123-112 home win over the Raptors. The Sixers moved to 10-3 and Toronto fell to 5-7.

Tyrese Maxey had 27 points and eight assists. Joel Embiid added 20 points.

Jaylen Brown tallied 18 points and six rebounds. VJ Edgecombe posted 15 points, eight rebounds and a season-high eight assists. Anfernee Simons scored 17 points and shot 5 for 6 from three-point range.

RJ Barrett recorded 31 points and 14 rebounds. Immanuel Quickley had 26 points and six assists.

The Sixers were without LeBron James (low back/sciatica management), Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain), Dominick Barlow (lower back stress reaction) and Ariel Hukporti (right Achilles tendon tear).

The team told reporters Thursday morning that Bona will be re-evaluated in approximately one week and that Barlow participated in shootaround. The 23-year-old forward also went through a pregame workout on the Xfinity Mobile Arena floor. There's no formal timetable for his return.

Toronto's sidelined players included Kawhi Leonard and Scottie Barnes.

The Sixers will face the Pacers on Sunday afternoon in Philadelphia. Here are observations on their victory over the Raptors:

Dean Wade began the game in James' normal spot. The Sixers started slowly, missing their first foul field goals and opening 1 for 8 from three-point range.

He stayed down after setting a ball screen and having an apparent knee-to-knee collision with Ja'Kobe Walter. The Sixers called timeout with 8:30 left in the first quarter and Embiid grabbed at his right knee. He eventually rose with assistance from teammates and Sixers head athletic trainer Kevin Johnson, then limped back to the locker room. Jabari Walker entered.

At the 5:26 mark of the first quarter, Embiid checked back in to cheers from the home fans.

"I knew that he didn't twist it or anything," Maxey said. "I knew it was a knee-to-knee, so I wasn't too worried. He kept saying, 'I just got kneed.' That still hurts, though."

Embiid ended up logging 28 minutes, though he certainly wanted to play more.

"He was very, very motivated to play," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. "It was hard to get him out for his scheduled rests tonight, which is a good problem sometimes."

While Embiid's return was a major positive development, the Sixers fell further behind. The Raptors' lead swelled to 32-16 with a Jamison Battle three-pointer and Nurse burned a timeout.

Simons sunk a buzzer-beating three to conclude the first quarter, cutting the Sixers' deficit to nine points.

"Those are big momentum plays that usually have some weight to them and carry you into the next moment," Nurse said.

The Sixers kept rolling against a shorthanded Toronto team playing on the second night of a back-to-back. Simons nailed a triple to kick off the scoring in the second quarter. Brown buried a mid-range jumper and Edgecombe jammed in a crowd-pleasing dunk to give the Sixers a 35-34 edge.

Brown and Edgecombe shined in the second quarter both as individuals and as a duo. The Sixers need Edgecombe to attack a bit more offensively when he shares the floor with Brown and bench players. It doesn't hurt for the second-year guard to have that clarity about his role in those units.

"He's one of our better playmakers," Maxey said of Edgecombe. "He's really good at getting downhill and creating for himself and others."

The Sixers' only three bench rotation players were Walker, Simons and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope (11 points, five assists). In addition to Walker, Wade got center minutes behind Embiid.

Embiid picked up his third foul with 2:23 left in the second quarter and had to take a seat. The teams were tied at 60 apiece through two periods.

The game remained even for much of the third, but Maxey fueled an 11-0 Sixers run late in the quarter.

His speed and the Sixers' collective focus on pushing the pace whenever possible allowed the team to get regular points before Toronto could set its defense. Maxey zoomed in for a layup, then tossed the ball ahead to Brown for an easy bucket. Brown assisted a Simons three. Walker converted a fast-break lay-in and canned a three on the first possession of the fourth quarter. All of a sudden, the Sixers held a 101-87 lead.

Brown, Edgecombe and the bench gave the Sixers more good minutes early in the fourth quarter. They sealed the deal without any late drama. And the fans chanting for a Tacko Fall appearance got their wish with a final-minute entrance by the 7-foot-6 center.

#2733. Buccaneers have more rushing yards than passing yards, a rare feat in today's NFL

With the 2026 NFL season at the midway point, one of the bigger statistical oddities belongs to the Buccaneers, who are the only team in the league with more rushing yards than passing yards.

Through nine games, the Buccaneers have 1,475 rushing yards and 1,277 passing yards. Every other team has gained more yardage passing than running, and no other team is even close to having more rushing than passing yards.

The last time an NFL team finished a season with more rushing yards than passing yards was 2022, when the Bears finished with an NFL-high 3,014 rushing yards and an NFL-low 2,219 passing yards. That Bears team was led by Justin Fields, who rushed for 1,143 yards himself, but netted just 1,883 passing yards. With running back David Montgomery chipping in 801 rushing yards and Khalil Herbert gaining 731, the Bears were a team that could run effectively but couldn't pass for anything.

The Buccaneers' yardage totals come from some fairly unique circumstances. Baker Mayfield has played some of the worst football of his career when healthy, and he was also injured and missed three games, replaced by undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels. That has led the Bucs to rely more on their running game. And the weather contributed a huge portion of the Buccaneers' run-pass yardage differential in Week 8, when the Bucs gained 322 yards rushing and minus-2 yards passing in a downpour against the Falcons.

Despite their one-dimensional offense, the Buccaneers are still playoff contenders, thanks to the NFC South's status as the worst division in football. It won't be surprising if there's a playoff game in Tampa in January. If that happens, Bucs fans may be praying for another downpour.

#2730. ‘Hard to win': Simons, Walker carry Portland lessons into Sixers roles

'Hard to win': Simons, Walker carry Portland lessons into Sixers roles originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Anfernee Simons and Jabari Walker shared the floor for 128 games in Portland. The Trail Blazers won 43 of them.

They sat beside one another in the Sixers' interview room Thursday night after a victory and discussed what the other 85 taught them.

"Whether you've got a big role or a small role, it's hard to win in the NBA," Simons said. "We've seen it firsthand."

Their roles were considerably different then.

Simons was an established starter entrusted with creating and scoring. Walker, a 2022 second-round pick, was trying to establish himself in a rotation. During their three overlapping seasons, Portland went 33-49, 21-61 and 36-46. The Blazers missed the playoffs each year.

Both are now reserves on a Sixers team constructed to contend. In nine games they've both appeared in this season, Philadelphia is 7-2.

They provided 26 points, 11 rebounds and six three-pointers in the Sixers' 123-112 win over the Raptors at Xfinity Mobile Arena. Simons scored 17 points and shot 5 for 6 from three-point range. Walker recorded nine points and eight rebounds, including four on the offensive glass.

The Sixers outscored Toronto by 24 points during Simons' 23 minutes. Neither former Blazer committed a turnover.

Their production helped Philadelphia overcome a 17-point first-quarter deficit and improve to 10-3 without LeBron James.

"You learn once you come off the bench to kind of read the game before you get in there," Simons said. "Obviously, we started off kind of slow. You just want to go in, bring some energy, get some stops, get out and run. I think everybody who got off the bench brought energy."

Simons supplied an immediate lift with a deep three-pointer at the first-quarter buzzer. His shot ended an 8-0 Sixers run and trimmed Toronto's lead to nine.

He remained involved during an 11-0 burst late in the third quarter, knocking down a three and setting up Walker for a basket. Walker then made a three early in the fourth before Simons scored on the Sixers' next possession.

When Toronto pulled within six with less than five minutes remaining, Simons answered with his fifth three-pointer.

Making those shots is the most obvious way Simons can help a roster already featuring James, Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and Jaylen Brown. He said the Sixers have not made him feel as though every opportunity must go in.

"They encourage us to keep shooting the ball," Simons said. "Knowing that a team has that much confidence in us to keep shooting makes the game that much easier. Whether you miss or make, as long as we get the right shots in the right moments, I think everybody can live with the misses and makes."

Simons spent seven seasons in Portland before playing last year with Boston and Chicago. His move to Philadelphia reunited him with Walker and Rayan Rupert, another former Blazer who joined the Sixers on a two-way contract during the offseason.

Knowing familiar faces awaited him helped Simons enter another new locker room.

"It made the transition seamless," he said. "Just being able to have some comfortability with guys that I played with for multiple years. It's been fun, kind of feeling like a little bit of old times. Me, Bari and Rups have been through a lot."

Walker's path to Philadelphia began a year earlier and required an additional step.

After playing 188 games over three seasons with Portland, Walker signed a two-way contract with the Sixers in July 2025. He earned a standard contract in February and has since pushed his way into the backup-center conversation despite standing 6-foot-7.

Walker believes some of the work he did on losing teams was easily missed.

"When I first got to the league, I was part of a rebuilding process," he said. "I just felt like some of the little things I did didn't always get noticed when you're losing. I told myself, if I ever got to be part of a winning organization, then I'd go out and expand my abilities."

Rebounding has made Walker difficult for Nick Nurse to overlook.

Walker credited his timing and strong hands to lessons passed down by his father, former NBA center Samaki Walker. Those instincts have become especially useful while the Sixers piece together their frontcourt behind Embiid.

"Rebounding is a skill I kind of honed in on," Walker said. "My dad was a good rebounder. He was known for his rebounding and his timing. I think it's just a gift that he transferred to me."

Walker has made it clear that he expected to earn a role this season.

"I don't know if I was delusional, but I always felt like I was going to play and I was going to be a part," he said. "I read something where they said it's a surprise, but if you were around me this summer, it wouldn't be a surprise. This is expected, and I just want to continue to get better."

The freedom Simons once had in Portland is no longer necessary. Walker does not need a high volume of touches, either. Both understand that playing beside the Sixers' stars requires shooting when open, moving the ball and handling the less glamorous work.

"You've got to find ways to impact the game multiple ways, even if you're not scoring," Simons said. "Whether it's cutting, making the right read and pass to Joel, being the right swing pass to VJ, boxing out on defense or just being in the right position."

Their opportunities will fluctuate. Simons may take nine shots one night and only a few the next. Walker's minutes will depend on matchups and the health of Philadelphia's frontcourt.

Winning has changed what they are being asked to do. Their three years together in Portland taught them why the adjustment is worthwhile.

"You feel appreciative of the times where you go into a situation where your role might be a little bit less, but you're winning," Simons said. "That's something you can't take for granted."

#2727. How Much Women’s College Flag Football Coaches Make

As girls flag football explodes at the youth and high school levels, NCAA institutions are adding varsity women's flag programs on a near-weekly basis.

Activity is still largely limited to Division II and III. But the NCAA's January 2027 vote to establish women's flag as a championship sport is expected to spur a new wave of adoption by major D-I schools. (Nebraska is the only traditional powerhouse with a varsity flag team so far.)

To gauge the sport's emerging labor market, Front Office Sports reviewed women's flag football coaching salaries at 10 schools across all three NCAA divisions, drawing on public records requests, active job postings, and conversations with coaches and athletic administrators.

Head coaching salaries varied by more than $100,000 across our sample, from $18,540 at D-III SUNY Geneseo to $155,000 at D-I Cal Poly. The average salary is $72,545. Position terms generally span one to five years.

Of the employment contracts obtained by FOS, Nebraska is the only school with a full-time assistant head coach. It's also the only school offering performance-based bonuses to its coaches, and it allows them to make money on outside activities, such as endorsements, with the athletic director's approval.

California Polytechnic State University–San Luis Obispo

$5,000 bonus if program wins a conference championship

$5,000 bonus if program qualifies for an NCAA Championship or equivalent national championship tournament

$10,000 bonus if program wins an NCAA Championship or equivalent national championship tournament

5% of base salary bonus if program wins a conference championship

5% of base salary bonus if program qualifies for an NCAA Championship or equivalent national championship tournament

In October, Nebraska athletic director Troy Dannen told Sports Business Journal that its 21-player women's flag program cost less than $1 million to launch, providing an early benchmark for other major schools looking to stand up their own teams.

"I've had a handful of Power Four schools reach out to me and ask questions," Jami Hagedorn, Nebraska's associate athletic director of financial reporting, tells FOS. She oversees the women's flag budget and hired its two inaugural coaches—twin-sister duo Liz and Katie Sowers—earlier this year. "They want to know what our startup costs were, what the big expenses were … we kind of are the market right now."

The Sowers sisters came to Lincoln from the NAIA's Ottawa University in Kansas, where they founded the women's flag program and led it to five consecutive national championships. Liz served as head coach and Katie as associate head coach, the same roles they now hold at Nebraska.

Hagedorn says their compensation was primarily determined by "looking internally at [Nebraska's] existing coaching salaries for similar women's sports." She adds that finding coaches with prior flag experience was a priority—a sentiment echoed in most of the 10 active head flag coaching job positions currently listed on the NCAA's job board.

"I didn't target many tackle football coaches when hiring, just because there are lots of nuances between the two sports," Hagedorn says. "I don't know that [tackle experience] 100% translates"."

With a professional flag league backed by the NFL and TMRW Sports set to launch in summer 2027 and flag making its Olympics debut in 2028, coaching jobs will grow, prompting a more competitive ecosystem—and, likely, higher salaries.

The post How Much Women's College Flag Football Coaches Make appeared first on Front Office Sports.

After the Commanders punted, the Giants went 55 yards in five plays.

Skattebo has 10 carries for 55 yards and two catches for 37 yards.

Giants safety Jason Pinnock is questionable to return with a back injury.

#2724. In 49-second drive, Daniels & Diggs rescue the Commanders’ season - Daily Slop

Editor's note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy!

This season, Daniels and the Commanders failed to convert a 2-point conversion in the opener against the Philadelphia Eagles, and Daniels failed to throw the ball away in overtime, preventing a chance for a game-winning field goal. In their previous two losses, the Commanders' final drive ended in enemy territory.

Last week the Commanders failed to throw a pass into the end zone despite reaching the 32-yard line with 8 seconds remaining in a 20-13 loss to the Los Angeles Rams.

The losses led to Daniels being scrutinized and criticized. He told ESPN last week that he was "for sure" one of the most scrutinized quarterbacks in the NFL.

Daniels, though, said Thursday night that he had only one thought as he jogged onto the field for the final drive: "One play at a time."

Then he did what he hadn't done since his rookie season: lead a game-winning drive. He did so five times in 2024 en route to being named NFL offensive rookie of the year.

Follow the action and share every cheer, question and instant reaction with fellow fans on the SB Nation app.

Download the SB Nation app on iOS or Android.

Here we go again. The Commanders had a habit of making close and winnable games self-inflicted disasters this season, and this one — a must-win Thursday night matchup with the NFC East-leading Giants — was on the verge of becoming the latest. Owner Josh Harris, who typically comes down to the Commanders' sideline to watch the final few minutes of games, again took his place for what could've been a slow, painful ending to his team's season.

When the clock hit two minutes, Washington came alive, much like it did a couple years ago when it took the NFL world by storm with its late-game heroics. In three drives — a defensive stand, a quick go-ahead touchdown and a game-sealing interception — the Commanders saved their season, and possibly their coach's job, to collect its biggest victory of the year, a 24-21 win over the Giants.

Daniels hit Stefon Diggs on a slant and the veteran wideout sprinted upfield, stopping inches before the goal line before turning and falling backward into the end zone, a la DeSean Jackson.

"Well, he probably could have waited some more," Quinn joked afterward.

It appeared that Daniels changed a signal on the play before the snap.

"Maybe, maybe not. You never know," Diggs said facetiously.

"Baby Kobe," Diggs said of Daniels. "He ain't flinch. He's going to be the same kind of player he is at the beginning of the game as he is at the end of the game."

Cornerback Rasul Douglas intercepted McCarthy on a deep, last-gasp attempt on third-and-10 with 34 seconds remaining.

Maybe it was wishful thinking, the last, mournful hope of a condemned team that hasn't been able to stay out of its own way much of this season. But they put together eight great minutes when they needed it most. The defense made three consecutive stops.

Daniels is, obviously, Washington's North Star. But Styles, the seventh pick overall, is rapidly growing into everything the Commanders hoped he'd be. The speed and force is obvious; the reads are coming, rapidly. On that third and two, Styles' film work, with a verbal assist from defensive tackle Charles Omenihu, indicated to him that the Giants were running a crack back run, with the tight end coming down the line to clear Washington's edge defender, and give McCarthy enough room to get the first down. Styles brushed off Giants center Bryan Hudson, shot the gap, tackled McCarthy for the loss, and gave the offense the ball back.

"I think, if you're just the player you are, the moment can never be too big," Styles said. "I think everyone understood in that moment, 'We've got to get a stop right here.' So guys just bowed up."

Guard Sam Cosmi looked at his teammates as Washington huddled up.

"I have moments where I look, and everybody's just locked in," Cosmi said. "You have that, like, glare, where you know it's game time, this is game time. We're going to make big plays."

Washington is still two games behind New York, with eight to play. But the Commanders, now, have the tiebreaker with the Giants, if it comes down to that. If it comes down to that, though, this already wild ride of a season will have taken an even crazier turn than what happened here Thursday, when the Commanders merely saved their season. For a couple of weeks, at least.

"Back-to-back interceptions, that's hard. It would've been really easy to lose the faith in that moment," Quinn said. "So, to see us battle and stay in the fight, that's what I was looking for. … There's plenty to do, guys. There's a lot to clean up, a lot to get better, but I'm definitely proud of the group.

"Man, that ain't goin' do nothing for me — still dwelling on that," Daniels said. "Everybody was on the sideline saying, 'The defense is giving you an opportunity to go out and win this game.' When I had the opportunity to go out there and win the game, take a deep breath, go out there and just capitalize on the moment."

Daniels completed 23 of 33 passes for 249 yards, three touchdowns and the two picks. On the other side of the ball, the defense ended the game with three consecutive stops.

"We needed that," Coach Dan Quinn said. "We needed every bit of it."

When the Commanders' offense had success, it tended to be when it went to a more up-tempo offense. Offensive coordinator David Blough put an emphasis on huddling more often and slowing down the pace this season, but it hasn't resulted in better results. He showed a willingness to adjust in the first half against the Giants.

On offense, errors like false starts and a delay of game were present but significantly reduced, as the Commanders committed just four penalties for 17 yards. The offensive line, which allowed four sacks against the Los Angeles Rams last week, allowed just one sack against a defense that had the third-highest blitz rate heading into Thursday's game.

That extra time allowed Daniels to work comfortably from the pocket, and he was efficient in the first half, completing 11 of 15 passes for 112 yards and a score. He completed four passes on the Commanders' second drive, hitting Chig Okonkwo with an 11-yard pass to get them into field goal range. The Giants responded with a 16-play, 72-yard touchdown drive, but Daniels responded by driving the offense 62 yards downfield in the closing minutes of the first half and connecting with Ben Sinnott for a one-yard touchdown on third-and-goal.

The Commanders have 11 days to prepare for their next matchup — a home game against the Cincinnati Bengals on Monday Night Football. Many of the Commanders' players labeled the Giants matchup as a must-win moment, and to their credit, they rose to the occasion.

Now, as the NFC East remains up for grabs, they are still in the hunt.

Next Gen Stats Insight for Commanders-Giants (via NFL Pro): Giants QB J.J. McCarthy was blitzed on 50% of his dropbacks in the second half against the Commanders, up from 28.6% in the first half. McCarthy completed 8 of 14 attempts against the blitz for 155 yards, a touchdown and an interception, recording career highs in completions and passing yards against the blitz in a game. After completing the 66-yard touchdown to Isaiah Likely, McCarthy went 0-for-3 with an interception against the Commanders' blitzes. Washington safety Nick Cross blitzed eight times, generating five pressures — a career best.

NFL Research: Jayden Daniels improved to 4-0-1 in his career versus the Giants. The win came thanks to his 32-yard touchdown pass to Stefon Diggs with 57 seconds left. It's the second game-winning TD Diggs has caught in his career with less than a minute remaining. The first was for the Vikings in the 2017 Divisional Round, famously known as the "Minneapolis Miracle."

What to make of Daniels' performance: Jayden Daniels overcame his first two interceptions of the season and delivered when Washington needed him most. His strength has been shaking off bad plays, and after consecutive series ended with picks in the fourth quarter, he led the go-ahead touchdown drive — with a 32-yard touchdown pass to Stefon Diggs. Daniels had been highly efficient prior to that pass. He has gotten better at keeping his eyes downfield, which resulted in one play for 30 yards.

Trend to watch: Washington's defense has forced six turnovers in its past three games combined. The Commanders now have 14 takeaways this season, but none was bigger than corner Rasul Douglas' interception to end the Giants' final possession. Washington forced a fumble in the red zone, preventing a potential field goal if nothing else.

Most surprising performance: Tight end Ben Sinnott. He entered with one reception on the season, a disappointing total for the 2024 second-round pick. He was supposed to get more action in Washington's new scheme this season, but it took until Week 10 for him to play a bigger role. He caught four passes for 42 yards and a touchdown against the Giants. — Keim

The Commanders kicker started the season 3-for-5 but is since 13-for-14. He opened the game's scoring with a 46-yard field goal in the second quarter, Stevens' lone attempt of the game.

The hurdle over a defender's outstretched arms is reason enough for the Commanders' third-year tight end to appear in the winners' column. But the career night is the real motivation. Sinnott came into the game with one catch for 6 yards this season but finished with four for 42 yards. He caught Daniels' touchdown pass with five seconds remaining in the first half as the quarterback fell to the ground.

The more severe issue for the Commanders has been the optics. In three games, there have been questionable – at best – game- and clock-management issues. As a head coach that does not call plays on either side of the ball, Quinn has to be more on top of it. He's dealing with a pair of first-time coordinators, to be fair … but he also hired them.

"Who Let The Dogs Out?" Indeed, Jameis. The backup QB also barked in an effort to get the Commanders to jump offside during a faux fourth-down cadence.

Thirty-seven of Nabers' 44 yards came on one play. His fumble in the third quarter killed a potential scoring drive and he could not come down with a jump ball in the red zone that would have set up a game-tying field goal that was instead intercepted by Rasul Douglas.

Rather than giving the ball to Skattebo, who had 78 yards on 18 carries, offensive coordinator Matt Nagy made the odd decision to call a McCarthy keeper from an empty backfield. The Commanders weren't fooled, as linebacker Sonny Styles burst through the line to drop McCarthy for a 2-yard loss while Skattebo watched from the sideline.

"It sucks, and I think part of it is I put myself in a situation last time we played these guys that kind of killed the trust in coach maybe a little bit, me giving up the ball last time," Skattebo said of his overtime fumble in Week 5. "And maybe he didn't want to give me the ball again. I don't know. I'm not going to say that was something he was thinking. But I would think that as well."

Punter Jordan Stout has been one of the Giants' most reliable players, but he picked an inopportune time for a shank. His 12-yard punt after McCarthy got stuffed gave the Commanders the ball at their own 29-yard line with 1:46 remaining.

Daniels wasted no time attacking cornerback Deonte Banks, who has improved greatly but still doesn't locate the ball consistently on deep passes. Banks got tangled up with Commanders wide receiver Treylon Burks to produce a 33-yard pass interference penalty. Washington was facing third-and-4 from the Giants' 32-yard line three plays later. Giants defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson sent a blitz and Daniels responded by firing the ball to wide receiver Stefon Diggs on a quick slant. Diggs beat cornerback Dru Phillips, who took out Banks on his tackle attempt to clear the path for a walk-in touchdown with 57 seconds left.

[A] jump ball to wide receiver Malik Nabers was wrestled away by Douglas for a game-ending interception with 25 seconds remaining.

It was discouraging that Nabers couldn't come down with the 50-50 ball, especially after all of his demands to get the ball. But it was puzzling that the Giants were throwing jump balls in that spot since they had two timeouts and only needed to gain about 10 yards to get into range.

It would have been hard to have confidence in Dominic Zvada to make the long field goal after he missed a 33-yarder in the first quarter. That came after the Giants elected to punt from Washington's 37-yard line on their opening drive rather than attempting a 55-yard field goal.

You can't totally ignore those interceptions, largely because both came at inopportune times. Yet Daniels was dynamic. He ran the ball effectively, his accuracy continues to impress, and he's finding a way to move the ball without Terry McLaurin, his top receiver, who's out for the season.

Outside of Daniels' heroics, what else stood out for the Commanders?

Didn't see this one coming but … Ben Sinnott? The 2024 second-round pick entered this game with only one catch for 6 yards this season and hadn't totaled more than 36 receiving yards in a game in his career (he got that off one catch against the Giants last December). For the past few seasons, the production from the Commanders' tight ends has come courtesy of two players: Zach Ertz in 2024 and '25, and Chig Okonkwo this season.

But Sinnott finally showed more of what he's capable of in the pass game, catching four passes for 42 yards, including a 1-yard touchdown at the end of the first half. He also hurdled a defender on a 12-yard catch and caught a 24-yarder that helped set up Antonio Williams' 31-yard score in the third quarter.

[T]he comeback victory Thursday lifted Washington back into the edge of the NFC East race. The Commanders are just two games back of the division-leading Giants, and they own the edge over New York, whom they beat and tied.

At this point in Quinn's career, optics matter. The sense at team headquarters in Ashburn, Va., is that Commanders leadership would rather not make a coaching change midseason. But Quinn and his team can't make any more game-management gaffes.

The Washington Commanders have begun warming up at MetLife Stadium for their Week 10 matchup against the New York Giants

Harbaugh wants to be the coach of a dominating running team. The Giants as currently constituted are not that, yet he (and Matt Nagy) play it conservatively until they can't, and then they still do anyway.

The Giants get the ball back at the Washington 46 with 2:15 left, and Harbaugh tries to run out the clock as much as he can and make the Commanders use their timeouts while doing so. The problem is that he doesn't have Derrick Henry, Ronnie Stanley, and Tyler Linderbaum on this team. He has one of the worst run blocking offensive lines in the NFL and a good but not great running back. Skattebo gains 7 of the 10 yards he needs to effectively close out the game on first and second down, and then with third-and-3, rather than have J.J. McCarthy pass to get the first down and seal the win, the Giants dial up another of those J.J. RPOs that I think have not yet worked even once. McCarthy loses yards, the Giants punt from the Washington 39 (that's two punts from inside the opponent's 40), and predictably, Jayden Daniels drives the Commanders downfield for the winning score.

The 49ers have owned the Cowboys in the 21st century. Is Sunday's matchup shaping up to be yet another San Francisco victory or can Dallas rewrite the narrative on a classic NFC rivalry?

Blogging the Boys' RJ Ochoa (in what appears to be a reverse jinx?) and Bleeding Green Nation's Brandon Lee Gowton discuss Cowboys vs. 49ers ahead of Week 10 in a new "Mixtape Mini" clip, an NFC East Mixtape production.

#2722. Sixers, Brown have a ‘humbling' night in loss to Celtics

Sixers, Brown have a 'humbling' night in loss to Celtics originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Whatever Jaylen Brown and the Sixers dreamed up for their first matchup against the Celtics soon flew out the window on Tuesday night.

Brown was whistled for two early fouls, the Sixers fell behind and their early-season flaws were on full display in a 123-101 loss at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

"We've just got to get better," Brown said. "Tonight was humbling. We got outplayed, out-executed. So we go back to the drawing board and get ready for the next one."

Over 26 minutes, Brown had 13 points on 4-for-9 shooting and five rebounds against the team that traded him away this summer.

As for the endless dissection of his relationship with former co-star Jayson Tatum, Brown didn't have much to add Tuesday. There was no public reconciliation, no obvious on-court animosity and generally nothing to satisfy fans hoping for some kind of fireworks on that front.

"I'm just focused on doing what's best for my team," Brown said. "Everything else … to be honest, I wasn't paying attention. But credit to Jayson; he played well tonight. Credit to the Celtics. They executed, they shot the hell out of the ball and they were the better team tonight."

Tatum scored 21 points, two of which came on a third-quarter slam over LeBron James. Paul George continued his fantastic start as a Celtic by dropping 36 points and draining six three-pointers.

The Celtics dominated from beyond the arc, shooting 22 for 49 (44.9 percent). The Sixers went just 11 for 37 (29.7 percent) on another night of underwhelming offense. The team sits 22nd in the NBA in offensive rating, 24th in three-point makes per game and 21st in three-point percentage.

"I think that we've got some guys that are obviously shooting much lower percentages than their last season or their career average — almost a handful of guys," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said. "And I don't think it's because they're shooting fallaway, totally contested ones. I think they're shots we want them to take. So I think they'll continue to take 'em and I'm pretty sure those will even out into their career averages."

Joel Embiid is at 37 percent from the floor and 4 for 33 from three-point range (12.1 percent).

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center got through an injury scare when he rolled his ankle late in the second quarter and hit a three early in the third. It was his first long-range make since the Sixers' home opener back on Oct. 22.

"It's a work in progress," Embiid said. "I think the biggest thing is just not thinking. I'm probably overthinking it. The rhythm of the game is different. I'm so used to having to create for myself, so it's a little bit different.

"But I think I'm slowly getting better. You could see as soon as I made a three, the next shot in the short corner … I didn't even think about it. I just shot it and let it fly, and I made it. … I think it's just about taking what's in front of you. Make or miss, keep working on your game. It's going to get there at some point."

Even with the Sixers second in the Eastern Conference standings at 9-3, Embiid believes the team's defense has "slacked off a little bit" in recent games.

"I don't really look at the record," he said. "I just look at the process of, 'Are we getting better every day?' We can always do a better job at all phases of the game."

"They're one of the top teams in the league and they've been together for a while," Brown said. "We've got a lot to work on over here, so we've got to get to work."

The Sixers will face the Raptors on Thursday night in Philadelphia.

They'll have to wait until Jan. 21 in Boston to see the Celtics again.

"I was looking forward to this," Brown said. "I was looking forward to playing well, but s— happens. Just get ready for the next one."

#2718. Justin Jefferson: It's a joy to see Kirk Cousins take over as a leader

Kirk Cousins is back in Minnesota, and perhaps no one is more excited about that than Justin Jefferson.

The wide receiver had career highs in catches (128) and yards (1,809) and earned the NFL’s Offensive Player of the Year award in Cousins’ last full season with the Vikings in 2022.

Jefferson, though, said he has “no expectations.”

“It’s really just going out there and just executing our plays,” Jefferson said, via Kevin Seifert of ESPN. “It’s not really getting too juiced up about him being here or anybody being back there. It’s just all about understanding the plays that are being called, understanding the jobs that we have and executing our responsibilities. And just the plays that are there, and the plays that could be made, we just need to continue to just make those type of plays. And I’m pretty sure that the results would be a lot better.

“He just understands the game. He’s a guy that studies the game a lot. He understands how the defenses play, especially covering me. And he understands, the plays that we have called that are kind of my plays and he understands the timing and the windows to throw those type of plays, but he also doesn’t force those type of plays to me and he just lets the game come to me.”

Jefferson said it was “a joy to hear [Cousins] just take over and be a leader in the meeting room, on the field.”

“He’s being vocal,” Jefferson said. “Just making sure that everybody hears the plays that he’s talking about and the notes that he has for certain routes, certain plays. And he’s just making sure that everybody’s on the same page. So it’s definitely cool to hear that type of leadership and command. If you know Kirk, that’s pretty normal from him. So it’s definitely kind of cool him being back in that room and him taking that control.”

#2716. Observations after Sixers suffer blowout loss to Cavs, fall in NBA Cup

Observations after Sixers suffer blowout loss to Cavs, fall in NBA Cup originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers couldn't rekindle the magic of their comeback home-opening win over the Cavaliers.

They fell Friday night in NBA Cup action, suffering a 119-95 defeat in Cleveland. The Sixers dipped to 8-2 and the Cavs improved to 5-4.

The Sixers' top scorers were Jaylen Brown (20 points), VJ Edgecombe (19 points) and Tyrese Maxey (17).

The Cavs got 23 points from Donovan Mitchell and 22 from Evan Mobley.

The Sixers' injured players included center Adem Bona (cervical spine sprain). Cleveland was down big man Jarrett Allen (right knee contusion). Sam Merrill sat out the second half with a right elbow injury.

With Friday's loss, the Sixers are 1-1 in Eastern Conference Group B of the NBA Cup. Their next Cup game is scheduled for Nov. 25 against the Heat.

The Sixers will conclude their three-road trip Sunday afternoon against the Bulls. Here are observations on their blowout loss to Cleveland:

After a missed Merrill three-pointer, the Sixers steamed ahead on the fast break and Edgecombe opened the scoring with a slam.

The Cavs replied with a 15-0 run kickstarted by six straight Mitchell points. Much like in the Sixers' Oct. 22 win over Cleveland, they were many levels below their best in the first quarter.

The Sixers began 0 for 4 from three-point range, including two LeBron James misses. The Cavs were also the better team in transition and limited the Sixers' chances to attack in the open floor by taking excellent care of the ball in the early going. Edgecombe was called for his second foul with 7:34 left in the first quarter.

Meanwhile, Joel Embiid expressed his frustration about a couple of early no-calls. Embiid's larger problem was that he couldn't hit any sort of shot besides free throws.

He went 0 for 9 from the floor in the game. The seven-time All-Star finished with six points and seven rebounds.

Embiid has had a subpar shooting start to the year, especially from three-point territory — he's now 3 for 28 (10.7 percent) — but Friday was the kind of extreme night that's bound to happen here and there over the course of a long season.

Of course, it's notable that Embiid's been playing through right foot plantar fasciitis and the Sixers have been keeping a close eye on his minutes. We'll see how the team manages his availability moving forward and whether Embiid is able to bounce back next time out.

James didn't play anywhere near his finest game either. He had eight points on 3-for-12 shooting, eight rebounds, three assists and six turnovers.

As a team, the Sixers were 36.5 percent from the field and 25 percent beyond the arc.

Jabari Walker rejoined the Sixers' rotation as the backup center with Bona sidelined. Anfernee Simons, former Cav Dean Wade and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope all remained rotation fixtures.

With Walker and Caldwell-Pope on the court next to three starters, the Sixers cut their deficit to single digits in the second quarter. Walker threw down a fast-break dunk that cut Cleveland's lead to 48-41. He gave the Sixers some good defensive possessions when switched on to James Harden and provided his usual physical, high-effort work on the glass.

Edgecombe was fantastic in the second, sinking three triples, racking up 15 points and nabbing three steals.

Many second-year players would have a tough time finding a rhythm after encountering early foul trouble, but Edgecombe was great as soon as he checked back in and delivered a ton of valuable buckets in the Sixers' comeback push.

The Sixers pulled to within 66-63 when Maxey picked a steal and threw a pretty one-handed bounce pass to Edgecombe for a dunk.

With Embiid and James offering little as scorers, Brown hit several shots that helped the Sixers stay in the game. After his 30-point performance last time out against the Pistons, Brown reached the 20-point mark for a third consecutive game.

Still, the Sixers' offense never got rolling. The Cavs maintained their lead and extended it late in the third quarter. By early in the fourth, the Sixers trailed by over 20 points.

Embiid didn't play the fourth quarter and logged 25 minutes. He's had zero made field goals on just one other occasion in his career, back in Nov. 2019 against the Raptors.

Even with their tremendous first nine games, the Sixers knew they'd hit speed bumps throughout the year. They'll try to get back on track Sunday in Chicago.

#2714. Jess McClain Has Her Sights Set on the 2028 Olympics After Her Stunning Second-Place Finish at the N.Y.C. Marathon (Exclusive)

Jess McClain finished second at the 2026 New York City Marathon, marking the first time an American woman has podiumed since 2018

McClain quit professional running back in 2020, but came back strong after learning how to "enjoy the process"

She's now setting her sights on becoming a first-time Olympian at the 2028 L.A. Games

Jess McClain is making history, one marathon at a time.

The professional runner, 34, placed second at the 2026 New York City Marathon, marking the first time an American woman has podiumed at the race since 2018 — and with a finish that has been on replay for all running fans. McClain's final time was 2:24:42, just six seconds behind winner Sheila Chepkirui, and one second ahead of third-place finisher Hellen Obiri, whom she narrowly beat out for silver in the final few strides of the race.

So what now? After celebrating her impressive performance in New York City with her friends and family, McClain — who, in addition to being a professional runner, works full-time as the executive director of two nonprofits — headed back home to Phoenix, Arizona, to resume her 9-to-5, begin training for her next race and catch up with PEOPLE.

"It was such a crazy whirlwind, honestly," McClain says of the hours after she crossed the finish line in second place. "I hung out with my husband and dad for a hot minute, and then celebrated with the New York Road Runners team and some college friends and fam over dinner. And then hung out with the Brooks family...It was the perfect combo of celebrations."

One of the most impressive parts of McClain's New York City performance came in the final stretch of the race. With under 80 meters to go, she caught up with Obiri, proceeding to pass her in the last 15 meters to clinch second place. When asked what was going through her mind during that final push, McClain said: "Honestly, I think when marathons are going well for me, I'm not doing a lot of thinking...When I overthink things, that's when things go a little awry."

"But I think it just reflects so much on the training I've been doing over the last year," she continues. "I did a lot of work to make those surges feel a little more comfortable, and a ton of practicing finishing super hard and running super fast at the end of 10 to 14 miles of running."

Coached by professional ultramarathoner David Roche, McClain's training schedule is no joke, with her hardest day of the week being Wednesday. McClain starts her day at 4:20 a.m., completing a 13-mile workout before she clocks in for her job as executive director at the Johnjay and Rich Love Up Foundation — where she does marketing, event planning and business development to help shelter dogs find their forever homes — and then gets in another 4-mile workout before going to bed around 8 to 9 p.m.

Jess McClain running the 2026 NYC MarathonCredit: Brooks Running

On race days, McClain's morning routine is never exactly the same. "It depends on the race," she explains. "With New York and Boston, they're pretty similar because we have that long trek out to the start line. So that kind of throws an interesting curveball in planning and digestion and all that stuff."

That said, she never strays too far from what she's used to.

"I usually try to wake up 45 minutes to an hour before we have to leave or report," she says. "In that time, I drink my water, have my pre-race nutrition supplement stuff. I try to get in carbs right away. I'll eat anything. I'll eat a muffin, a scone, a croissant, a bagel — I'm pretty chill on that front." Then she packs something extra to nibble on, grabs a bottle of liquid carbs like Gatorade to sip on, and heads to the start.

"I usually warm up with the other competitors and friends, and then just try to soak in the start line," she continues. "I think this year I really did that. Tracy Morgan was there giving us all high fives and he was crying. It was so crazy...The DJ was playing awesome music and everybody was dancing. It was just a really good vibe."

Jess McClain running the 2026 NYC MarathonCredit: Brooks Running

While McClain may be caught dancing before a race today, her path to finishing second at the 2026 New York City Marathon was far from typical. In fact, back in 2020, she stopped competing altogether.

"I was in a very weird mental funk for a long time," McClain says. "I just needed a full reset. Like, completely. Professionally, in terms of running, and personally."

She dropped her Brooks sponsorship, moved home into an apartment above her parents' garage, and put her life together "without running being the center of it."

"I think my lens was so small and I put so much weight on outcomes, results, performance and didn't know how to enjoy the process and the journey," she says. "It took a full eject to get to the point where I realized like, 'Hey, we can be high level. I can be running the Olympic trials, gaining on the lead pack after having had a total blast training and still living my life, you know, with balance in mind.' "

And McClain will be racing at the 2028 Olympic trials, in the hopes of securing one of the three spots on Team USA for the L.A. Games. Back in 2024, she was the first alternate for the U.S. team after finishing fourth at the trials, but with her recent performances, McClain is a favorite to make the team.

"The main goal is the marathon. So we'll compete in St. Louis at the trials in March 2028, and the goal's top three," she explains. "It seems far away, but it's not. But also, you know, I have big goals in between now and then. I'll probably run, like, two more marathons next year, get on the track, maybe run a fast half [marathon.]"

McClain also regularly competes in 10K races and also wouldn't be opposed to competing in that event in the Olympics if given the chance. "I want to run some fast 10Ks and if it ends up working out that I could compete in the trials in the 10, then I probably would."

Hellen Obiri, Jess McClain, and Sheila Chepkirui running the 2026 NYC MarathonCredit: Brooks Running

Looking even further ahead, beyond the 2028 Olympics, McClain isn't sure whether she'll want to continue training for another Olympic cycle in 2032 or shift her focus to more personal goals, like growing her family. Back in October 2025, she made the decision to freeze her eggs, posting about her thought process on social media. "Who knows how I'll feel over time, BUT I have found comfort in learning & taking action in some way," she wrote.

Never miss a story — sign up for PEOPLE's free daily newsletter to stay up-to-date on the best of what PEOPLE has to offer, from celebrity news to compelling human interest stories.

For now, she has Snoop Dogg and T-Pain tickets for February that she's very excited for, and she sees a fun family trip to Las Vegas coming up soon.

"I love going to concerts. I love checking out the latest, newest restaurant and having really good drinks and food," she says when asked what people may not know about her. "Obviously, I'm very dialed in when I need to be, but when I'm not, I indulge and I have fun."

#2710. Dortmund to end controversial partnership with arms maker Rheinmetall

Borussia Dortmund are ending their controversial partnership with arms manufacturer Rheinmetall, the Bundesliga club said in a statement on Friday.

The contract, which expires mid-2027, will not be extended after three years.

The decision was reached by mutual agreement and the decisive factor was the ongoing criticism from Dortmund fans regarding the partnership, the club acknowledged.

"We are aware of the criticism from our members and from some of the fans," Dortmund managing director Carsten Cramer said and explained that this was taken into account during the discussions with Rheinmetall.

Rheinmetall is Germany's largest arms company and has seen strong growth amid Russia's war in Ukraine and the general arms boom.

When the sponsorship deal was announced in 2024, there was heavy criticism from pacifists, human rights organizations and parts of the Dortmund fan base.

During a general assembly in that same year, club members voted against extending the contract. However, the decision was not binding for the Dortmund management.

Dortmund president Hans-Joachim Watzke recently told the Ausgerechnet podcast: "I underestimated how many Borussia Dortmund fans tell me: 'We're not against Rheinmetall. We just don't want Borussia Dortmund to promote a company that manufactures weapons.' That's a point of view I don't necessarily have to adopt, but I fully accept it."

#2709. Back in Philadelphia with Celtics, Paul George looks forward to ‘a regular game'

Back in Philadelphia with Celtics, Paul George looks forward to 'a regular game' originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Paul George's presence back in town was one of the many swirling morning storylines at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

For good reason, former Celtics teammates Jaylen Brown and Jayson Tatum will draw immense attention Tuesday night. After all, Brown has said there "might be a little lamb chops with some gravy" between the two, if not a full-blown beef.

But George's return to Philadelphia is more than a tiny subplot. Following two seasons in Philadelphia, he was the centerpiece of the Sixers' summer trade package to acquire Brown.

George told reporters before the Celtics' shootaround that it feels like "a regular game."

"Had I been here eight, nine, 10 years, different story," he said. "I was here two years. Obviously, we didn't have the best of luck or had a great, I think, partnership in terms of my ability to stay healthy and on the floor. So that kind of played into a lot of it.

"But obviously, it's a tremendous fan base, a great sports town to play in. So that was appreciated. There's no ill will for me. It'll be fun to just compete. And outside of that, it's a normal game."

The 36-year-old George indeed had trouble staying available for sustained stretches as a Sixer. He dealt with a variety of injuries and served a 25-game suspension last season for violating the NBA's anti-drug policy.

George did play well on both ends of the floor for much of the 2026 playoffs. He helped the Sixers come back to win a seven-game first-round series against the Celtics in historic fashion. The nine-time All-Star also brought a veteran steadiness to the Sixers' locker room and was glad to mentor younger players like VJ Edgecombe.

"Just his routine … even when he got hot, he didn't try to force it," Jabari Walker said Tuesday morning. "His game was smooth and I think that's how he is as a person, just not forcing anything and having a calm energy."

George has certainly enjoyed his early days as a Celtic.

Through nine games, he's averaged 20.4 points, 5.2 rebounds, 4.1 assists and 2.3 steals while shooting 42.5 percent from three-point range. Boston will enter Tuesday night's matchup second in the Eastern Conference standings at 8-2, the Sixers first at 9-2.

"I've been kind of blown away," George said. "I think it exceeded my expectations since being in Boston. You never know how much culture is involved and how much culture changes your outlook on things and the effect it has mentally, physically, just being in an environment … and the culture that Boston presents.

"So I've been thrilled. I've been playing some of my best basketball of late, and just been enjoying grinding it out with these guys out here. It's a fun style of play and I can't talk (enough) about just the thrill, the happiness and the excitement and joy that it has brought being here."

He was asked what sort of reception he expects from Sixers fans.

"Not sure," George said. "In some ways, I helped land them a future piece for them. So with that, not sure how the reception would be."

#2707. Thursday Night Football: Stefon Diggs' late TD gives Commanders 24-21 win

With 3:27 remaining in Thursday’s game, the Giants lined up with Jameis Winston under center on fourth-and-1 from their own 11. The team’s backup quarterback, who runs the team’s quarterback sneaks, yelled, “Hut One. Hut Two. Hut Three. Who let the dogs out? Who, who, who, who?”

The Giants took a delay of game and then punted.

The Commanders got the last laugh, winning 24-21 on Stefon Diggs’ 32-yard touchdown with 57 seconds left. The Commanders are 3-5-1 and the Giants 5-3-1.

In an entertaining second half, the teams traded the lead four times.

The Giants took a 21-17 lead with 8:13 left on Isaiah Likely’s 66-yard catch-and-run.

The Giants then had back-to-back interceptions of Jayden Daniels. Safety Jevon Holland, who is having an All-Pro season, took the ball away from Chig Okonkwo at the 2-yard line with the Commanders on the Giants 24 with 5:27 left, and Ar’Darius Washington stepped in front of Okonkwo on fourth-and-2 at the Washington 45 with 2:15 left.

The Giants, though, couldn’t run out the clock, and the Commanders made the most of it. They needed only three plays to go 71 yards thanks to a questionable 33-yard pass interference penalty on Deonte Banks, who was covering Treylon Burks. Three plays later, Diggs scored.

The Giants reached the Washington 48 on their final drive, but J.J. McCarthy’s deep throw to Malik Nabers was intercepted by Rasul Douglas with 25 seconds left to end it.

The Giants outgained the Commanders 399 to 340, but missed a field goal and had two turnovers.

Daniels was 23-of-33 for 249 yards with three touchdowns and two interceptions. Rachaad White ran for 47 yards on 11 carries, and Diggs caught six passes for 83 yards. Antonio Williams and Ben Sinnott each caught a touchdown pass.

McCarthy was 23-of-36 for 293 yards with a touchdown and an interception. Cam Skattebo had 18 carries for 78 yards and two touchdowns and caught three passes for 44 yards, and Likely had nine receptions for 127 yards and a touchdown.

#2706. John Harbaugh expresses confidence in K Dominic Zvada

Giants rookie kicker Dominic Zvada has missed six field goals in nine games. He missed another on Thursday night, a 33-yarder.

While it happened in the first quarter and not on the final play, it stands out in a game that was decided by three points.

After New York’s 24-21 loss to the Commanders, Giants coach John Harbaugh was asked about his level of confidence in Zvada.

“Yeah, we’re confident,” Harbaugh said. “You know, you can’t — as soon as a guy doesn’t make a play, I mean, start firing people left and right. Especially your kicker who’s a rookie. “But I’m not gonna panic, you know, halfway through the season when the guy who’s made a bunch of kicks, if that’s what you’re inferring we should be doing.  So, you know, I mean, we’re just not gonna knee-jerk it like that. He’s gonna make kicks. He’s gonna make a lot of kicks, I believe in him.  I think he’s really good, really talented. And we’re gonna give him an opportunity to do it. It’s up to him to do it.”

Basically, how much time will Zvada get before Harbaugh decides it’s not going to happen? That remains to be seen, if Zvada keeps missing kicks he should be making.

#2704. ‘Let's check the ball up': Jaylen Brown ready for first game against Celtics

'Let's check the ball up': Jaylen Brown ready for first game against Celtics originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

Jaylen Brown was asked Sunday whether he and Jayson Tatum had spoken since the former teammates addressed their relationship during the preseason.

Does he plan to approach Tatum before Tuesday night's game at Xfinity Mobile Arena?

"I mean, he's on his side, I'm on my side," Brown said. "We're playing basketball. Both of us are trying to win. So it's nothing to talk about. Let's check the ball up."

After months of public comments, documentaries and questions about how their partnership ended, the basketball will finally take over.

Brown will face Boston for the first time since the Celtics traded him to Philadelphia for Paul George and four future draft assets in July. He spent his first 10 NBA seasons in Boston, played nine alongside Tatum and helped the Celtics win the 2024 championship, earning Finals MVP honors.

Tuesday's 8 p.m. game on NBC will also bring together the top two teams in the Eastern Conference. The Sixers are 9-2. Boston, riding a three-game winning streak, is 8-2 and sits a half-game behind Philadelphia.

"Another good opportunity for our team to be able to show what we're made of," Brown said. "I'm looking forward to it. Big-time matchup, two heavyweights in the East. Let's get it."

Brown has not hidden his appreciation for Boston, even as more has emerged about the deterioration of his relationship with Tatum and the organization.

"I love Boston," he said Sunday. "Boston's a great city. A lot of people I developed relationships with, you know what I mean? But I'm just focused on what's in front of me right now. And that's the most important thing."

He also acknowledged everything that accompanies an abrupt end to a decade with one organization.

"Decisions were made," Brown said. "It's life. It's business. Move on. It's OK. … It's emotions. You've got to pack up and move your stuff. Your family's got to pack up and move. But it's life. It's happened to numerous amounts of people, myself included.

"So I just look forward to being able to build with my team over here, trying to make the best of my situation."

Brown faced the Celtics during the preseason, but Tuesday will be the first meeting that counts. He said he did not know whether that would introduce emotions that were absent during the exhibition schedule.

"We'll see how I feel when we get out there," Brown said. "As of now, I've got no emotion toward nothing. So I'm just ready to go."

Tatum was similarly restrained after Boston's 117-97 victory over Milwaukee on Sunday.

"It's another game on the schedule," Tatum said. "It's the Celtics versus the Sixers. In the words of Brad Stevens, they all count as one."

Tatum called the Sixers "an incredible group" with a "great coaching staff," but declined to add to the discussion surrounding his relationship with Brown.

"Drama gets clicks and views," he said. "That's not my thing." CBS Sports reported Tatum's full comments Sunday night.

Celtics head coach Joe Mazzulla was even more concise.

"It'll be fun," Mazzulla said. "It'll be a good atmosphere."

Brown is not the only centerpiece of the July deal who will face his former team.

George has settled quickly into Boston's lineup, averaging 20.4 points and supplying the high-volume outside shooting the Celtics have long prioritized. He scored 27 points and made five three-pointers Sunday as Boston beat Milwaukee for its third consecutive victory.

The Celtics have not needed George to duplicate everything Brown provided. He has fit alongside Tatum, Derrick White and Boston's returning core as another willing shooter and versatile defender.

Tatum is averaging 27.1 points, six rebounds and 7.8 assists. His playmaking has been especially important for a team that replaced Brown's downhill pressure with more shooting and ball movement.

Boston enters Tuesday ranked third in offensive rating and fourth in defensive rating. It is one of two NBA teams currently inside the top five on both ends of the floor.

The Celtics have also made 15.6 three-pointers per game, the second-highest average in the league. They set an NBA Cup record by hitting 24 against Charlotte on Friday, then made 18 more Sunday in Milwaukee.

That presents a clear challenge for a Sixers defense that has generally performed well but has occasionally surrendered clean perimeter looks after committing extra help toward the ball. Tatum, George, White, Payton Pritchard and Sam Hauser can all punish late rotations.

The Sixers have reached 9-2 without depending upon the same formula every night.

Tyrese Maxey leads them at 26.9 points per game. Brown is averaging 22.3 points, 6.7 rebounds and four assists while shooting 47.7 percent from the field and 39.2 percent from three. Joel Embiid and LeBron James have supplied scoring, passing and defensive flexibility around them.

Brown has repeatedly described the team as unfinished despite its record.

"From our perspective, it's been some growing pains for sure, even though we've been able to win," he said. "The result, we're not so much fixated on the result. It's more so about the process, and we've got to improve our process and our mentality to creating a winning environment."

Boston should provide the clearest early measure of that process.

The Celtics play considerably slower than the Sixers, but their half-court execution has been more efficient. Philadelphia will want to create turnovers and run before Boston can set its defense. The Celtics will attempt to control the pace, generate three-pointers and make the Sixers execute against a defense that has yet to allow an opposing player to score 30 points this season.

There is also the unavoidable Brown matchup. Boston could use Tatum, George and White against him at different points, giving the Celtics several defenders capable of absorbing his drives without immediately sending help.

Nick Nurse expects Brown to bring something extra, even if Brown has publicly downplayed the emotional component.

"It's going to be very different for him," Nurse said. "I think probably a little bit of emotion in there, too, but also I think he's going to be very motivated to play."

Boston's rotation is healthy entering the matchup. Two-way guard Devin Carter is out because of an illness.

Dominick Barlow and Ariel Hukporti remain out for the Sixers. Adem Bona could return after missing Sunday's contest.

The betting market views the matchup as essentially a toss-up. Monday afternoon listings had the spread moving between Boston minus-1.5 and Philadelphia minus-1.5, depending on the sportsbook, with the total at 215.5.

That fits the larger picture. Philadelphia owns the East's best record. Boston has the conference's strongest point differential and has outscored opponents by 10.7 points per game.

The surrounding conversation will center on Brown and Tatum until the opening tip. Brown does not intend to contribute any ceremonial small talk.

"He's on his side," Brown said. "I'm on my side."

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2698. Game Preview: San Antonio Spurs vs Golden State Warriors

Left for dead by plenty of pundits over the summer, the Golden State Warriors came storming out of the gates this season, led by the somehow still otherworldly play of Steph Curry and the surprising play of rookie small forward Yaxel Lendeborg. They were riding an 8-game win streak before losing both their match-up with the Houston Rockets on Wednesday night and Curry, who suffered an oblique abdominal tear just 6 minutes into that contest, never returning. Curry, who was averaging 30 points on ridiculous efficiency in the lead up to the Houston game, is out for at least the next 2 weeks, leaving the Warriors without the engine that drives their entire offense. Golden State to their credit hung with Houston most of the night thanks to Lendeborg's shotmaking, a focused team defensive effort, and offensive contributions from both vets and young guys alike.

Coming into this one on a 10 game winning streak, the San Antonio Spurs have been taking care of business. Facing Golden State without Curry makes them that much easier to guard, but head coach Steve Kerr's defensive game planning, Draymond Green's orchestration both on offense and defense, and Lendeborg's breakout is the sort of combination that could still make life rough on their opponents. San Antonio was able to sleepwalk their way into a big deficit before their huge comeback back win against the Chicago Bulls Wednesday night in Chicago, but against the well-coached Warriors that could be a recipe for disaster.

San Antonio Spurs (10-2) vs Golden State Warriors (8-4)November 13 2026 | 8:30 PM CTWatch: Amazon Prime | Listen: WOAI (1200 AM)Line: San Antonio -10.5

Spurs Injuries: Tobias Harris, calf (OUT), Devin Vassell, groin (day to day)

Golden State has been notoriously small for years, but they have just a single player on the roster this season that's taller than 6'8. That should mean open season for Victor Wembanyama, who has been on a historical tear to kick off his 4th season in the league and is coming off another huge performance in the win over Chicago. Draymond Green is still a versatile defender with an elite IQ on the defensive side of the ball, but at age 36 and in his 15th season, he is no longer the perennial DPOY-candidate he once was in his prime that could make life difficult on opposing bigs for significant stretches. Regardless though, expect him to draw a decent amount of the assignment on Wemby with help sprinkled in from Golden State's wings. Green and Wembanyama had a notable moment between them last season at the Frost Bank Center almost exactly a year to the day.

With Chef Curry out for the foreseeable future, the bulk of the offense could fall on the shoulders of rookie Yaxel Lendeborg. Lendeborg has been a revelation for Golden State, averaging 21.7 points, 7.4 rebounds, and 3.7 assists on 51% shooting from the field and 43% from 3 on solid volume. An older rookie at 24 years old, he's proven to be adept at attacking closeouts and getting into the teeth of the defense, using his big body (6'9" with a nearly 7'4" wingspan) to go at smaller defenders in the post, and seeking out contact and either finishing through it or finding his way to the charity stripe (6 attempts a game at the line). Opposing defenses have been preoccupied with Curry's offensive blitz to start the season and leaving Lendeborg as the #2 option, but that obviously changes with Steph out now. San Antonio has a variety of defenders they can and will send at him to see how he holds up as the focus of the defense. Should all else fail, they have the always lurking Wembanyama as the ultimate insurance policy.

Golden State has been among the league's most proficient 3 point shooting teams to begin this season, ranking 1st in both makes and percentage. That's largely (and obviously) been because of Curry's volume and consistency from distance, but it's not just about the numbers he puts up. It's also because of the sort of looks that his gravity is able to open up for others. Without him to warp help defenses and open up the easy catch and shoot opportunities for guys like Lendeborg and Brandin Podziemski, their offensive efficiency is likely about to take a hit. That doesn't mean that they still aren't going to launch them though, as they showed with their 17/51 showing in the loss to the Rockets.
