#2697. Luke McCaffrey knew the rules and made a heads-up play, causing a kickoff out of bounds

Commanders kickoff returner Luke McCaffrey made the smartest play of the game by not returning a kick in Thursday night’s win over the Giants.

With McCaffrey back to field a Giants kickoff, the ball landed near the sideline at the 5-yard line. The kick stayed in bounds, and some returners would have grabbed the ball and started running. But McCaffrey let the ball bounce, then stepped out of bounds, and then grabbed the ball with his feet down on the sideline.

By rule, the ball is out of bounds if it touches a player who is out of bounds, even if the ball actually stays in bounds. By touching the ball while his feet were out of bounds, McCaffrey forced a kickoff out of bounds penalty on the Giants, putting the ball on the 40-yard line for the Commanders.

“I thought Luke McCaffrey made a really smart play that won’t show up on the stat sheet,” Commanders head coach Dan Quinn said. “That’s a difficult play. Is it out of bounds? Is it not? I was nervous about it, that’s one of the ones where you hold your breath.”

Every kickoff returner needs to know that rule, but knowing the rule is easier than having the quick-thinking ability to do what McCaffrey did, in the fourth quarter with the game on the line. It was among the smartest football plays you’ll see.

#2696. Chiefs are preparing to face the NFL’s leading rusher: Bijan Robinson

The bulk of credit for the Kansas City Chiefs' 6-2 record goes to running back Kenneth Walker. His 872 rushing yards ranks second in the league as Kansas City's offense has retooled around the prized free agent signing.

For Kansas City to get a seventh win on Sunday in a road game against the Atlanta Falcons, the Chiefs will need a plan to slow down the running back who currently exceeds Walker's total by eight yards.

On Thursday, the architect of Kansas City's defense and the unit's longest-tenured player made it very clear that star running back Bijan Robinson is on their mind.

"We're trying to play fundamentally sound," said defensive tackle Chris Jones. "Reset the line of scrimmage with the D-line. He's a very patient runner — inside and outside. He can break a big one every time his hands are on the ball. For us, it's about playing fundamental football and playing disciplined."

Defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo has also noted Robinson's ability to run both inside and outside — and how quickly he switches between the two.

"Especially [against] this kind of offensive scheme," the coach explained, "It's all about first building a wall — it's interior to get it to go that way. Setting an edge, and I think the most important thing about this guy is tracking the hip. He's as good as anybody. It might be a designed outside run play, but he ends up and now it feels an inside run play. When you start chasing the outside and get turned, that's when he goes down hill. That's why we're preaching big this week about tracking the hips, so when he does decide to cut it back, we can eliminate some of those explosive runs. I think that's when he really is effective."

In their seven games, the Chiefs have allowed a single 100-yard rusher. They have held some of the league's best backs — including Jonathan Taylor of the Indianapolis Colts and Breece Hall of the New York Jets — under the mark.

Jones believes the guidance from the team's veteran coaching staff will serve them well again when they face Robinson.

"We've got really great coaches and great assistant coaches," Jones remarked. "Spags calls the defense and puts us in the right position to execute. We do a lot of film study and a lot of watching of the tendencies of a team and what they do best. We try to counterreact to that."

#2694. Vega Ioane credits Ravens veterans for helping him adjust at center

Adjusting to life in the NFL is difficult for any rookie, especially when the responsibilities keep changing. Fortunately for Baltimore's young offensive lineman, he's had a veteran group around him willing to help make that transition a little easier. The transition to center required more than simply learning a new position. It also demanded cooperation and communication from the entire offensive line, particularly as teammates adjusted to having a new player responsible for making calls before the snap.

Appearing on The Lounge Podcast with Ryan Mink and Garrett Downing, Ioane discussed how the veterans around him helped make the transition possible.

"It wasn't about me; it was about everyone else around me stepping up. In the offensive meeting room, we talked about how everyone needed to elevate their game for a new center."

He specifically credited John Simpson with helping him gain confidence while Simpson also managed his own responsibilities. That support was particularly meaningful considering the adjustment Ioane was making at the time.

"John Simpson helped build my confidence all week while worrying about his own job."

Playing center puts a rookie in the middle of more than the formation. He has to communicate with the quarterback, recognize what the defense is showing, and help keep the blocking assignments connected. The veterans around Ioane could make that adjustment easier by handling their own responsibilities and keeping the communication clear. His comments offer a useful reminder that developing a young lineman is a group effort, even when one player receives most of the attention.

Ioane also recognized former Ravens offensive guard Andrew Vorhees, Emery Jones, Ronnie Stanley, and the rest of the offensive line room and coaching staff for their support.

The rookie understands that his early development wouldn't have happened without the people around him. While his versatility has certainly attracted attention, he recognizes the importance of having experienced players willing to help him along the way.

His appreciation for the group was evident when discussing how much he continues to learn from the veterans.

"I've learned everything by watching and listening to the veterans around me. It all happens because of the guys in that room, not just me."

Ioane's willingness to acknowledge those contributions says plenty about his approach. The rookie may be establishing himself as a potential cornerstone for the future, but he understands the importance of the players helping him get there.

#2693. Bruce Arians says he wants to be a head coach in the NFL next season

Bruce Arians is thinking about coming out of retirement. Again.

Arians told Jordan Schultz that when he announced his retirement from the Buccaneers in March of 2022, it was because of health problems that have since been resolved, and he now wants to coach again.

“I had torn my Achilles early in that season, and I was wearing these prosthetic high heels, and it threw my back out, and I couldn’t stand on the sideline for four hours anymore without a lot of pain,” Arians said. “I was also monitoring an aneurysm on my heart, so I had some health issues. We did everything we thought we could do in Tampa after winning the Super Bowl, trying to get two, and then it was time to give it to Todd [Bowles]. Now that I’m all healthy again, I got the itch again. So, we’ll see.”

If Arians does come back next year, he’ll be the oldest head coach in NFL history. That distinction currently belongs to Pete Carroll, who was 74 when he coached the Raiders last season. Arians will turn 75 next season.

Arians’ first retirement announcement came from the Steelers after they did not renew his contract as their offensive coordinator following the 2011 season, but Arians later said he was forced out and didn’t want to retire. He then took a job as offensive coordinator of the Colts in 2012, and was their interim head coach for most of that season while Chuck Pagano battled leukemia. Arians coached so well that he was named the NFL’s Coach of the Year.

Once Pagano returned to the Colts, Arians became head coach of the Cardinals, and he won a second Coach of the Year award. He announced his retirement following the 2017 season, after five years as head coach of the Cardinals.

But in 2019 he came out of retirement to become head coach of the Buccaneers. He won a Super Bowl in Tampa Bay, then retired after three seasons. Arians thought that was it, but he said that his son is now coaching high school football, and in talking to his son about the job he realized how much he misses it himself.

“Another fire got lit,” Arians said. “I had no desire to go back, and I was still fighting some health issues, but now after the open heart surgery I’ve got so much more energy, it’s amazing.”

Arians may find, like Bill Belichick before him, that all the accomplishments in the world don’t guarantee an NFL head-coaching job. Or perhaps he’ll convince some owner to give the oldest coach ever a chance to do what he’s done three times before, and turn a franchise around.

#2689. Buccaneers have more rushing yards than passing yards, a rare feat in today's NFL

With the 2026 NFL season at the midway point, one of the bigger statistical oddities belongs to the Buccaneers, who are the only team in the league with more rushing yards than passing yards.

Through nine games, the Buccaneers have 1,475 rushing yards and 1,277 passing yards. Every other team has gained more yardage passing than running, and no other team is even close to having more rushing than passing yards.

The last time an NFL team finished a season with more rushing yards than passing yards was 2022, when the Bears finished with an NFL-high 3,014 rushing yards and an NFL-low 2,219 passing yards. That Bears team was led by Justin Fields, who rushed for 1,143 yards himself, but netted just 1,883 passing yards. With running back David Montgomery chipping in 801 rushing yards and Khalil Herbert gaining 731, the Bears were a team that could run effectively but couldn’t pass for anything.

The Buccaneers’ yardage totals come from some fairly unique circumstances. Baker Mayfield has played some of the worst football of his career when healthy, and he was also injured and missed three games, replaced by undrafted rookie Jalon Daniels. That has led the Bucs to rely more on their running game. And the weather contributed a huge portion of the Buccaneers’ run-pass yardage differential in Week 8, when the Bucs gained 322 yards rushing and minus-2 yards passing in a downpour against the Falcons.

Despite their one-dimensional offense, the Buccaneers are still playoff contenders, thanks to the NFC South’s status as the worst division in football. It won’t be surprising if there’s a playoff game in Tampa in January. If that happens, Bucs fans may be praying for another downpour.

#2686. Rockets Marcus Smart suspended three games by NBA

Marcus Smart of the Houston Rockets was suspended yesterday for three games without pay for throwing a punch at Charles Bassey in Wednesday night's victory over the the Golden State Warriors. The incident happened in the third quarter of the Rockets' win, and Smart was ejected and given a flagrant 2.

Smart and Bassey begun arguing after an Amen Thompson drive, and then a Smart right hand connected with Bassey. Houston's head coach Ime Udoka blamed Bassey for running his mouth, however, Bassey claims it was Smart who initiated the incident by "playing dirty the whole game."

"I remember the first half, I was trying to set a screen. He grabbed my knee. He was playing dirty. I think I was trying to get a rebound. He was grabbing my hand, and I was trying to run back on defense. Then, he got up on me and just swung. Obviously, that was weak. I just think that was, honestly, fake toughness.

"It didn't surprise me. I knew he was going to do something. I don't think he was trying to play. I think he was trying to get himself out of the game. I think he was trying to chill. He wasn't trying to hoop. That was fake toughness."

Smart will miss tonight's game against the Utah Jazz, Sunday's game against the Washington Wizards, and Monday's game against the Miami Heat. Reed Sheppard likely picks up extra minutes in Smart's place. He responded on Wednesday with the some clutch play down the stretch. Let's see if that continues.

Smart is averaging 8.3 points, 2.6 rebounds, 2 assists and 1 steal per game for the Rockets while shooting 43.9 percent from the field and 40 percent from deep. Houston is currently at 9-3 and in third place in the Western Conference.

The Rockets will miss Smart, who has somewhat taken on the old Dillon Brooks agitator role, but if any team has the depth to suck it up, it's the Rockets.

#2683. Rory McIlroy roars to lead with Tyrrell Hatton at DP World Tour Championship

Rory McIlroy stepped up his bid for a record-equalling eighth Race to Dubai title by moving into a share of the lead after the second round of the DP World Tour Championship.

A birdie on the 18th helped the Northern Irishman finish with a two-under-par round of 70, enough to tie at the top on five under alongside his Ryder Cup team-mate Tyrrell Hatton.

McIlroy will claim the Race to Dubai title on Sunday if he wins the tournament, or if he finishes second and Eugenio Chacarra, the current leader in the standings, does not win.

Chacarra fired a one-under-par 71 to stay in touch at one under for the tournament, while Jon Rahm, who could also win the Race to Dubai crown if he is victorious and McIlroy finishes no higher than third, is three shots off the pace.

Starting the day in joint-third place, McIlroy had looked in the mood to obliterate the field, with three birdies in the first 10 holes taking him to four under for the day.

Three birdies over the next six sapped his momentum, but a welcome birdie on the last left McIlroy in a strong position to match the Race's only eight-time winner, Colin Montgomerie.

McIlroy told Sky Sports: "I played very solidly for the first 11 holes then I felt like I put myself out of position, and once you do that on this golf course it starts to get very difficult.

Rory McIlroy has moved into a strong position in Dubai (Adam Davy/PA)

"If anything I started to get frustrated with the course. I've been coming to this course for 17 years and this is the toughest I think it's ever played. You just have to show a little bit of patience out there.

"It's easy to make bogeys but it's nice to birdie the last and feel like I salvaged the day a little bit."

Chacarra started the day in 23rd place and struggled for large parts before two consecutive birdies to finish earned him a one-under 71 and bumped him up to a share of 11th place overall.

Jon Rahm is not out of contention in Dubai (Adam Davy/PA)

First-round leader Joost Luiten fashioned a solitary birdie on the fifth as he struggled to maintain his earlier momentum and dropped to a share of third after a one-over 73.

Hatton's superb 69, despite bogeys on the 10th and 17th, lifted him level with McIlroy, while the round of the day was a 68 from South Africa's Jayden Schaper, an eagle on the second paving the way for him to move three shots off the lead.

Rahm, who would also need his compatriot Chacarra to finish no higher than ninth in order to win the Race, is lurking in joint-fifth place after a second-straight one-under round of 71.

#2681. Return to Germany an ‘unbelievable’ experience for Patriots practice squad tackle

Listed at 6-foot-9, 320 pounds, Lorenz Metz is the tallest player currently under contract with the New England Patriots. Despite his towering height, however, he is largely flying under the radar.

Not only is Metz is a member of the team's practice squad, but due to his international designation ineligible to play in any games this year. That will not change this week, despite the Patriots set to play the Detroit Lions just 50 miles from his hometown in the German province of Bavaria.

And yet, making the trip back home and getting to practice at the facilities of FC Bayern Munich is a special experience for the 29-year-old.

"I grew up about an hour from here," he said during a press conference on Thursday. "Bayern Munich was the team. Thomas Müller, [Manuel] Neuer — all of the Bayern players were my role models. And now standing out there on the field is unbelievable."

Born in Neuötting, a city of 9,000 people east of Munich, Metz's football journey started as a fan and somebody who couldn't escape the Patriots even back then.

"I think in 2012 they started showing regular season games in German free TV," he explained. "2012, 2014, 2016, the Patriots were pretty much on top with Tom Brady. That was the team everybody knew, with Tom Brady, who also everybody knew."

At the age of 18, Metz started his playing career with the Kirchdorf Wildcats, appearing in 12 games and registering 48 tackles and a sack in his lone season as a defensive lineman. Shortly thereafter, he moved to the United States to play college football at Cincinnati. He switched from defensive to offensive tackle upon arrival, and over the next five seasons saw action in 39 games with 26 starts.

Despite his success and being a one-time first-team All-AAC selection, Metz went unselected in the 2023 NFL Draft. He was initially picked up by the Bears as a free agent and also spent some time in Tampa before joining New England's practice squad for the playoff run in January.

Nine months later, he gets to experience the Patriots' trip to Germany — and embracing his role as a local. Not only did he get more than 30 tickets for friends and family for Sunday's game, he also treated his fellow offensive linemen and a handful of other teammates to dinner on Thursday night.

And despite his status for the game, he is looking forward to it as well. That is especially true with his brother having visited the first ever NFL game in Munich back in 2022.

"I was following it all," he said about that particular contest between the Seahawks and Buccaneers. "I already was in college in Cinicinnati, couldn't come to the game unfortunately, but did get two tickets for my brother. So, this is almost like a full-circle moment playing in that game and taking the field."

#2679. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2677. James Harden admits to being ‘James Harden’

Thirty-two points on 14 shots in a much-needed Cleveland Cavaliers win over the New York Knicks was a good reminder of who James Harden is. And in case there was still any confusion, the former MVP made sure to clear everything up afterward.

"My name is James Harden. I used to score a lot of points," Harden told reporters Wednesday evening.

That clarification was needed based on how Harden's first 11 outings had gone. He entered Wednesday's game in New York averaging an uncharacteristic 15.3 points per game, shooting a dreadful 36.4% from the field. Harden has been a step slow and unable to create space off the dribble.

There's a downstream effect to Harden not being able to score. The passing lanes dry up when defenders don't have to help cut off his drives. This has left him as an inefficient scorer and inept playmaker at the start of the season.

Wednesday, Harden showed that he still has the talent to be a dynamic scoring guard. He got the outside shot working in the second quarter, and then expanded his game from there. Defenders had to overplay him on the perimeter, which allowed him to attack inside. He used that to his advantage to score nine points in the fourth quarter, which included two finishes inside the paint.

In short, he was the Harden we've seen wreck defenses for over a decade and a half, not the one that we saw in the first 11 games this season.

Anything bought from the links helps support Fear the Sword. You can buy the comfortable Cavs hoodie HERE. You can also shop all of Homage's Cavs gear HERE.

The Cavs would be a championship contender if they could guarantee performances like this from Harden in the playoffs.

Being able to score and playmake at this level would mean teams couldn't load up to stop Donovan Mitchell, and it would create easy scoring opportunities for Jarrett Allen and Evan Mobley inside. But you can't ensure this version of Harden on a nightly basis, or even for big games he gets up for. Age catches up to every player, especially a 37-year-old like Harden who has played nearly 50,000 minutes in his 18-year career.

Instead of counting on Harden to play as he did in his prime, he's trying to find other ways to adapt his game to his current situation.

"I just focus on myself, things I need to do, and try to get in really good shape and learn my teammates and learn how to play a different brand of basketball, because I'm not the same fast person that I was like five or six years ago," Harden said.

Harden is still playing his way into shape, admitting that he wasn't as young as he used to be, so he "can't just be ready" at the start of the season. It takes a "bit of time to get adjusted to the speed, the pace, all of the above." But even when he does get back up to speed, the explosiveness isn't there for him to be the guy he was with the Houston Rockets.

Instead, Harden will need to find different ways to impact winning in this new reality he finds himself in. If someone can make that adjustment, it's a player as skilled and as smart as Harden. That adjustment won't happen overnight. There will undoubtedly be more lows like we saw in the embarrassing loss to the Charlotte Hornets earlier this week, but the Cavs are more than willing to endure those games if it means Harden can eventually find his way. Because in the end, the Cavaliers' hopes and dreams for this season and the next two depend on Harden putting the pieces together.

"Now I still score points, but I'm finding other ways to impact the game as well," Harden said. "And I think that's what people probably don't understand."

#2676. 3 keys to a Cincinnati Bengals victory vs. Pittsburgh Steelers

The 6-2 Cincinnati Bengals will host the 6-2 Pittsburgh Steelers on Sunday Night Football this week.

The Steelers defeated the Bengals 30-27 earlier this season in Pittsburgh. Can Cincinnati return the favor and take the lead in the AFC North standings?

If they are going to do so, here are three keys to victory.

Jaylen Warren has been playing really well for the Steelers this season. He was a huge reason they were able to get the victory earlier this season against the Bengals. He had almost 170 all-purpose yards during that game. He does damage where the Bengals often struggle against the run, and that is to the outside. He is also an effective pass catcher who can make huge chunk plays out of the backfield.

It will be a group effort to limit Jaylen Warren this week. That starts with the guys up front setting a good edge and forcing Warren to go back inside. Once that happens, they will need the linebackers and secondary players to make the tackle. Warren is elusive, shows good leg drive, and is critical for the success of the Pittsburgh offense. Slowing him down will be one of the biggest keys to earning a tough divisional victory on Sunday night.

Chase Brown ran for over six yards per carry on Sunday against the Falcons. While he has yet to top 100 yards rushing in a game this season, he is starting to be much more effective when his number is called. Last season, when the Bengals faced off against the Steelers at home, Chase Brown had just 11 carries. Even though he had just 11 carries, he was still able to top 100 yards rushing. You don't have to change your identity, but running effectively will be a big key on Sunday night.

Earlier this season against Pittsburgh, Brown ran for 61 yards on 13 carries. One thing that would certainly help the numbers in the running game would be to play with a lead. Getting an early lead and being able to effectively run the football will go a long way toward trying to get the victory and taking the lead in the division at 7-2.

When the Bengals played the Pittsburgh Steelers earlier this season, they had two crucial turnovers that cost them the game. The first turnover was a muffed punt by Ke'Shawn Williams. Not only did Williams muff the punt, but PJ Jules tried to pick the football up instead of just jumping on it.

That muffed punt came with the Bengals leading 27-24 early in the fourth quarter. The Steelers recovered the fumble and went on to add a field goal. That tied the game at the time at 27-27. After another Pittsburgh field goal put them up 30-27, the Cincinnati Bengals offense came back on the field with a chance to win the game.

The Bengals got the ball with 2:08 left on the clock. After 17-yard and 13-yard completions to Ja'Marr Chase, the Bengals were driving with an opportunity to win the game, or at least send it to overtime. They had the ball at midfield with a first down. This time, Dalton Risner got beat by Derrick Harmon, and Joe Burrow fumbled the ball while looking to get the ball out instead of taking the sack. The Steelers recovered the fumble and won the game 30-27.

If the Bengals can win the turnover battle, they should put themselves in a good position to win the football game. With a win, they will be sitting at the top of the division at 7-2. This is a massive matchup on Sunday Night Football in Cincinnati. There should be an electric atmosphere at Paycor Stadium this week.

The Chargers (0-8) will try to get their first win of the season on Monday night versus the Baltimore Ravens (4-5).

The Los Angeles Rams have reportedly placed All-Pro wide receiver Puka Nacua on injured reserve with a knee injury suffered last week, per ESPN's Adam Schefter.

That will have him out for the next four games, after Sean McVay previously noted Nacua would miss a "significant" period of time with the injury. It took some time to play out, however, as the team dealt with what McVay called "roster semantics."

Kirk Cousins' return to Minnesota will be marked with a familiar number: The team announced Thursday that their new quarterback will wear No. 8 going forward. That's the number Cousin wore with the Vikings when he played for them from 2018-2023.

Minnesota safety Jakobe Thomas, who was wearing No. 8 earlier this season, will switch to No. 6 to accommodate Cousins return.

Riley Patterson will kick for the Ravens this week in their Monday Night Football matchup with the Chargers, according to the NFL Network's Mike Garafolo. Patterson spent the past two seasons with the Dolphins, but was released last month.

The Patriots will be playing the Lions in Munich, Germany, on Sunday.

Running back TreVeyon Henderson did not practice on Wednesday, and with an upcoming flight across the pond, the team has already ruled him out.

Henderson was listed on the injury report as dealing with an illness. The running back revealed last Friday that he recently experienced "an unexpected and unusual medical emergency involving a series of unexplained neurological symptoms." Henderson was hospitalized, but has said that test results have been positive and reassuring.

Starting running back Rhamondre Stevenson also didn't practice on Wednesday due to a knee injury, but has not yet been ruled out, though he is expected to miss a few weeks.

Sean McVay delivered a mix bag of news Wednesday regarding injuries to the team's top two receivers.

Davante Adams could be back sooner than expected from a hamstring injury, potentially in Week 13 vs. the Chiefs. Puka Nacua, meanwhile, will remain sidelined for a "significant period of time" with knee and toe injuries.

Etienne has been out since Week 3 due to a hamstring injury and has since been on injured reserve.

His return to practice opens his 21-day window to return to action, meaning the Saints have three weeks to activate him to the 53-man roster or shut him down for the season.

Skattebo missed Sunday's win over the Eagles coming out of the team's bye week. The running back practiced this week, which sets him up for a return Thursday night against the Commanders.

McCarthy was sacked five times in the game and suffered a rib injury that briefly took him out of action. He would return and finished 12-for-19 for 127 yards passing.

"I feel really good," McCarthy said this week. "Obviously, Sunday, it's football, it's a physical game, but just credit to the athletic training staff, getting me back to feeling really good as quick as possible."

The 49ers acquired Keenan Allen ahead of Tuesday's trade deadline because of the various injuries the team has at the position.

San Francisco head coach Kyle Shanahan said on Wednesday that Mike Evans remains week-to-week due to an Achilles injury. At this point, he has not been added to IR, so Evans could suit up this week against the Cowboys, but he is starting the week by not practicing.

Shanahan added that currently there is no timeline for Evans' return.

The Rams are expected to be without star wide receiver Puka Nacua for more than a month after suffering two knee sprains in the team's most recent game.

Nacua, who would normally be added to IR to free up a roster spot, won't be, according to head coach Sean McVay. L.A. is still expecting Nacua to miss extended time, but NFL teams are only allowed eight player activations from IR per season.

If Nacua gets added, with the intention of activating him in December, he would take up an activation from another player that the Rams were planning on activating, which would rule them out for the year.

L.A. currently has WR Davante Adams, G Justin Dedich, DT Poona Ford and DE Kobie Turner on IR and the Rams likely want to be able to activate all of them later this year. Los Angeles has already used four activations with EDGE Myles Garrett, TE Terrance Ferguson, OT Keagan Trost and RB Ronnie Rivers.

The 49ers acquired Keenan Allen ahead of Tuesday's trade deadline to help bolster the banged-up wide receiver room.

The only problem is that Allen could still miss time this season. Kyle Shanahan acknowledged to reporters on Wednesday that the veteran wideout could still face league discipline this season stemming from his DUI in August.

According to the current CBA, a violation of the league's substance-abuse policy, which would include a DUI, comes with a minimum three-game suspension. Additionally, Allen's BAC was so high that the league can increase the suspension if it so chooses.

The league has reportedly been waiting for the DUI case against Allen to play out legally before issuing the suspension.

At 3-6, and with a rash of injuries — including one to their most recent QB1 — the Arizona Cardinals are turning to rookie Carson Beck.

Arizona benched and then traded Jacoby Brissett. His replacement, Gardner Minshew, suffered a UCL injury this past week in Seattle during a loss to the Seahawks.

In their absence, the No. 65 overall pick in this year's draft is getting the nod in the desert.

Beck will make his first career NFL start on Sunday when the Los Angeles Rams come to town, head coach Mike LaFleur said Wednesday. The former Georgia and Miami star will be tasked with moving the ball against a defense that features premier edge rusher Myles Garrett and stout defensive tackle Aaron Donald. Beck will have to do so with a thin receiving corps.

Pittsburgh head coach Mike McCarthy announced on Wednesday that the team is opening the 21-day practice window for defensive tackle Derrick Harmon.

The 23-year-old defender has been sidelined because of a sprained foot he suffered against the Bengals in Week 4. In limited action this season, he has 12 tackles, including 1.5 sacks and a forced fumble.

Pittsburgh is allowing the seventh-fewest yards per game and the third-fewest rush yards per game this season.

The Patriots will cross the pond this weekend to take on the Detroit Lions in Munich, Germany, on Sunday morning.

New England wide receiver A.J. Brown will travel with the team, head coach Mike Vrabel said. While this doesn't automatically mean he will play in Sunday's game, Vrabel noted it gives him the chance.

Brown has missed the Patriots' last two games due to a knee injury. The wide receiver has only played in three games for New England this season, as he missed the early part of the season because of a sprained ankle in Week 1.

The wide receiver has caught nine of his 20 targets for 101 yards. Brown has yet to score a touchdown this year.

#2669. Examining biggest Jets tendencies before Week 10’s game vs. Bills

The Jets are 2-7 entering Week 10's game in MetLife Stadium against the Buffalo Bills after Aaron Glenn's club lost 35-12 against the Chiefs a week ago.

But Gang Green is slightly better than their record indicates.

Let's dive into New York's tendencies before this AFC East clash on Sunday.

On Sunday, the Bills will face their fourth pure pocket passer of the 2026 campaign in Smith. The others being Jared Goff, Matthew Stafford, and Kirk Cousins.

Smith resides that lower-left quadrant, escaping the pocket on on a little over 10% of his dropbacks.

The Jets offense features five former first-round picks at marquee positions. Both of their tackles (Olu Fashanu and Armand Membo) were first-round picks. Two of their receivers (Garrett Wilson and Omar Cooper Jr.) — former selections in the first-round.

And the wild-card of them all, tight end Kenyon Sadiq — first-rounder in 2026.

While some of this talent hasn't fully acclimated to the NFL just yet, there's plenty of inherent talent within the Jets offensive unit.

As for Wilson, who missed last week's contest against the Chiefs, he has the seventh-best Average Separation Score, per Fantasy Points Data, among receivers who've run at least 99 routes entering Week 10. And it's Cooper Jr., not Wilson, who finds himself inside the Top 10 among all qualifying receivers in yards per route run currently at a hefty 2.73.

The Jets don't use a lot of window dressing in their offense. They're currently owners of the sixth-lowest motion rate at 56.0%. And Smith has used play-action on 25.1% of his dropbacks, the 20th-highest among qualifying quarterbacks.

More than most teams, what you see is what you get with the Jets offensively.

The Bills will get a reprieve from the blitzing extravaganza they experienced in Week 9's game against the Vikings, but they better stay prepare to deal with extra rushers.

Entering this game, the Jets are fourth in the NFL in blitz rate at 41.2%, per Fantasy Points Data. In most years, that's probably Top 2 or even the highest in the league. The blitz-happy way is foundational to Glenn's defenses.

Two other core elements of who the Jets are defensively — they don't move out of base often (so more linebackers, fewer defensive backs on the field), and they want to man-up in coverage.

New York has the 10th-highest base defense rate 33.3% — two spots lower than the Bills — and play man at the league's fourth-highest rate (31.7%).

The No. 2 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft has gotten out to an rather productive start to his NFL career.

My No. 1 overall player in the class, whom I gave a "Jared Verse Lite" comparison to, Bailey has 31 pressures through nine games, the 13th-most among all edge rushers in the NFL.

He hasn't regularly destroyed all left and right tackles in his path as much as the pressure total would indicate, but in Week 9 against the Chiefs, Bailey was genuinely tremendous. He displayed his whole pass-rush arsenal, highlighted by his patented outside speed rush and a speed-to-power based bull.

He's a big-time talent starting to come into his own getting after the quarterback — 20 of his 31 pressures have occurred in the past four games.

The Jets don't have the horses up front along the defensive line of a few years ago. But they're still a stingy run defense thanks to the likes of explosive linebacker Jamien Sherwood and thumping safety Dane Belton.

Discounting garbage time, New York's defense is currently ninth in the NFL in EPA per rush allowed.

The Jets also no longer boast Sauce Gardner out wide, D.J. Reed in the slot, and Jordan Whitehead at safety. And those truths have taken a toll on their pass defense.

The Jets are 30th in EPA per dropback surrendered and have allowed the fifth-highest passer rating at 103.5.

This matchup calls for the Bills to take to the air.

#2668. Brewers' Pat Murphy apologized to Yankees' Brian Cashman over viral comment about Jake Bauers free agency

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

In the aftermath of the World Series championship, Brewers manager Pat Murphy was caught on a hot mic talking to first baseman and NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, who heads into free agency this winter off a career year.

Murphy's message? "You're gonna be a rich f---er, but just remember when you were on that horseshit Yankees team and you guys were all playing for yourself, just remember, say, 'this is the way we used to do it.'"

The comment, predictably, drew backlash from those who assumed Murphy was taking a shot at the Yankees. Bauers was on the 2023 Yankees, when they went 82-80 and missed the playoffs.

"I called Brian Cashman right away when I heard it got out," Murphy said on the New York Post's "The Show with Joel Sherman and Jon Heyman released on Tuesday. "I picked up a phone and called Brian right away, and had a good conversation. And the best I could try to explain that I wasn't talking about the 2026 Yankees.

"After every celebration, I'd shake his hand. I'd say, 'You rich so-and-so, you're going to leave us,' " Murphy explained. "We're not going to be able to pay you. You're going to leave us and you're going to forget all about how we did things. … I would just give him this rhetoric every time.

"I was just referring to the teams that have a lot of high-paid, long-contract players," Murphy said. "That sometimes it's harder to get all those guys together to play together. And I used the Yankees because I knew Jake was with them before. … I regret saying it, but that was Jake and I's humor behind the scenes and I got caught."

First off, dudes talking to dudes when they don't realize anyone else is listening lends itself to a lot of comments they don't necessarily mean or, perhaps more importantly, don't include the context of a longstanding relationship between a manager and his player. There isn't anything really out of line here in terms of the Yankees shot. Any Yankees fan would tell you they agree with Murphy's assessment of that team.

Where I do believe there's a problem is the insinuation that a player getting a huge payday means that he'll just start playing only for himself instead of doing things as a team. The Dodgers' high individual salaries certainly didn't stop them from winning two straight World Series titles.

Further, Bauers made $2.7 million last season, double his previous high. MLB players have a finite shelf life and need the money they make to stretch, if they're lucky, for generations. He's set to make exponentially more in free agency in his one big payday to hopefully set up his family for decades. Some might think it insensitive of Murphy to mock that a player might need to look out for himself and his family.

Then again, take note of Murphy's quote when he says that's just their sense of humor. We don't know their personal relationship because it is just that: personal. Unless Bauers signs elsewhere and comes out guns blazing against Murphy, this whole thing is probably just much ado about nothing. It would be pretty shocking if Cashman took particular offense, either.

#2666. Former Yankees, Rangers All-Star Mark Teixeira wins U.S. House seat in Texas

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former Major League Baseball star Mark Teixeira is headed to Capitol Hill after winning the election for the United States House of Representatives seat in Texas' 21st district on Tuesday. Teixeira, the Republican candidate, beat Democrat Kristin Hook, a former federal scientist.

Teixeira will now take over the seat vacated by Republican Chip Roy, who didn't seek re-election.

"Together, we can build a better future for our families, our neighbors, and every community across Texas 21," Teixeira said in a statement. "I'm excited to get to work. I will be praying for all of you and for the future of this great nation. God bless Texas, and God bless America."

He was a rare win for the GOP in Texas on Tuesday, as Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the gubernatorial race and Democrat James Talarico flipped the Senate seat.

Teixeira, 46, was born and raised in Maryland before attending Georgia Tech as a big-time prospect. He was selected fifth overall in the first round of the 2001 Draft by the Rangers. He then came up through the Rangers' system and spent the first four and a half seasons of his career with the ballclub. He was traded to the Braves in 2007, then to the Angels in 2008 before signing a long-term free agent deal with the Yankees prior to the 2009 season. He finished his career with the Yankees.

In parts of 14 seasons, Teixeira hit .268/.360/.509 (126 OPS+) with 409 home runs, 1,298 RBI, five Gold Gloves, three All-Star Games, three Silver Sluggers and a World Series ring.

Teixeira is one of several familiar sports faces up for election on Tuesday. Former college football coach Tommy Tuberville won the Alabama gubernatorial race and former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya lost the Minnesota Senate race.

#2664. MLB rumors: The only Oriole not on the trading block, Rays' Drew Rasmussen plan and Astros add to manager hunt

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Brewers have now been World Series champions for just one week (minus a few hours) and they should still be basking in the glory for quite a while. As the offseason marches on, the next big date will be Nov. 17, when decisions on qualifying offers are due from the eight players who received one.

In the meantime, the rumor mill should be ever-so-slowly churning. We'll round it up here.

The Houston Astros moved on from general manager Dana Brown in August and fired manager Joe Espada after the 2026 season. Newly hired general manager Randy Flores is now tasked with landing a new dugout boss, and a three-time MVP and future Hall of Famer is in the mix. The Astros will interview Albert Pujols for the manager job this week, per The Athletic.

Pujols has long made it known that he desires to be an MLB manager. He recently interviewed for vacancies with the Padres and Angels (both last offseason) and he also managed the Dominican Republic in the World Baseball Classic this past spring. It should be further noted that Pujols is in the fourth year of a 10-year, $100 personal services contract with the Angels that was part of the mega-deal he signed with them as a player prior to the 2012 season as a player.

Other known candidates for the Astros manager job are Rangers bench coach Luis Urueta and Yankees bench coach (not to mention former Tigers and Angels manager) Brad Ausmus. Former Astros third baseman Morgan Ensberg, the manager of the Triple-A Rays affiliate Durham Bulls, will also interview this week, according to MLB.com.

The Orioles are willing to listen to trade offers on any player other than Pete Alonso as they seek both rotation and outfield help, according to The Baltimore Banner. The  Orioles reportedly aren't "actively shopping" any players, but they are looking for upgrades at starting pitcher and outfielder and realize one of the ways that could happen is via a trade.

Surely they wouldn't sell low on Gunnar Henderson, given his immense upside, so we can probably take him off the table unless some team makes it worth their while. There is a glut of infielders, though. With Alonso at first base and Henderson at short, they have Jackson Holliday, Christian Encarnacion-Strand, Jordan Westburg and Coby Mayo for two spots. Even using one of the four at designated hitter, it's easy to see where a deal could happen.

Westburg and Encarnacion-Strand are under team control through 2029 while Holliday is controlled through 2030 and Mayo through 2031.

The American League champion Rays recently picked up the $20 million club option on All-Star starting pitcher Drew Rasmussen. That would be a franchise-record salary for one player in a single season. It might seem odd to exercise an option and then deal a player to an outsider, but locking Rasmussen in for a one-year deal makes him an attractive trade candidate instead of just letting him walk in free agency, and this is how the Rays generally operate. We've seen it so many times: they get ahead of losing guys to free agency, sometimes even dealing them a year or two earlier. They've done it with Randy Arozarena, Isaac Paredes, Tyler Glasnow and even going back to franchise legends like David Price, Evan Longoria and Ben Zobrist.

The Rays right now are saying they intend to keep Rasmussen for 2027.

"Not a declarative this, that, whatever, but I can sit here very confidently and say that every intention right now is thinking about Ras anchoring our rotation and how to make this team better going into next year," club president Erik Neander said on Tuesday, via the Tampa Bay Times.

If they want to contend again next year, it sure seems like they need Rasmussen, with Nick Martinez and Freddy Peralta off to free agency. That leaves Rasmussen atop the rotation, followed by Shane McClanahan, Griffin Jax, Ryan Pepiot and a bunch of question marks. There are questions attached to McClanahan, Jax and Pepiot too.

Harry Kane will present the Ballon d'Or to the England fans at Wembley Stadium tomorrow ahead of the game against Croatia.

The Bayern Munich star will also break the record for all-time England appearances which he currently shares with Peter Shilton.

“It's definitely up there [with the biggest achievements of my career],” said Kane, speaking in an interview with GOAL.com.

This is an article version of the CBS Sports HQ AM Newsletter, the ultimate guide to every day in sports. You can sign up to get it in your inbox every weekday morning here.

One of the biggest benefits of the NIL era is that college basketball has more elite talent than ever, now that players are returning for bigger paychecks instead of bolting for NBA money at the first opportunity.

That made selecting our 2026-27 CBS Sports Preseason All-America teams especially difficult, but our experts nailed it. Each of the three teams features players who will be performing at the next level very soon, but the best of those might be Florida superstar Thomas Haugh.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2661. Biggest MLB offseason questions: How long will lockout last? Will we see a free agency frenzy?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Not so long ago, the Milwaukee Brewers were crowned World Series champions, and at the moment of the last out, the 2026-27 Major League offseason began. So let's talk about that.

The winter ahead is one shot through with uncertainty, as labor strife figures to roil the sport and perhaps even compromise the 2027 season. Those matters, vital as they are, won't be the only story, and we'll still have the familiar presences of free agency and trade talk to sustain us.

To set the scene for all that's ahead in advance of the 2027 campaign – good, ill, or somewhere in the middle – we're here to take a look at the five questions that will inform an offseason that's going to be quite unusual and – for good, ill, or somewhere in the middle – probably unforgettable. Let's explore those five queries right now …

The current collective bargaining agreement – or CBA, the accord that governs the working relationship between clubs/owners and players – is set to expire at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1 of this year. At that time, MLB owners are all but certain to lock out the players. That's a labor stoppage, and that means the offseason will be brought to a sudden halt. The lockout, the purpose of which is to preempt a players' strike, will last until a new CBA is agreed to. Agreeing to a new CBA will be no simple matter, and owners and their hireling, commissioner Rob Manfred, are pushing for a cap on team payrolls. The players, as represented by their union, the MLBPA, have never shown any willingness to agree to a cap-and-floor system. There are a lot of other issues to iron out, as the CBA is an all-encompassing document, but the fight over a cap will be what drags out the lockout.

The heart of the matter is whether the lockout will last long enough to push back, abbreviate, or – perish the thought – cancel entirely the 2027 season. The latter is the worst-case scenario and is highly unlikely, but it's a possibility, however remote. More of a threat is a 2027 season that doesn't span the usual 162 games.

We have a recent precedent to guide us. The last time the CBA was up for negotiation during the offseason of 2021-22, owners locked out the players for 99 days. That meant a shortened spring training by about two and a half weeks and forced the regular season calendar to be compressed, albeit while still preserving the 162-game docket. As such, we can say that if the lockout lasts beyond the middle of March 2027, then we'll likely lose regular-season games.

For further context, here's a brief history of modern labor stoppages in the sport:

Just two, the 1981 and 1994-95 player strikes, significantly compromised seasons. The 1994-95 stoppage cost us the 1994 World Series, and it took years for the sport to recover from the resulting fan disaffection.

As for the 2027 season, the worst-case scenario may not be the loss of the entire season but rather the loss of 60 games off the regular-season slate. Here's the explanation from our recent Lockout 101 piece:

"… [I]f the lockout extends into late May or so and costs at least 60 games, then most of the league's national broadcast and streaming contracts would be extended for another year, through 2029. That matters because Manfred and the league hope to bundle and centralize team streaming rights and share those revenues equally, and the current timeline would theoretically allow that to happen at the same time the national contracts are up for renegotiation in 2028. Tacking on another year to those national contracts would push back the significant windfall that owners and the league are expecting from that new media rights structure. This amounts to a major incentive, at least on the league side, to agree to a new CBA before June arrives."

Obviously, the hope is that the lockout doesn't even affect the spring training calendar, let alone cost us a major chunk of the regular season.

As noted, the big fight is over whether or not MLB will have a cap-and-floor structure moving forward, as is the case in the NFL, NBA, and NHL. Owners have tied every single proposal wrinkle to date to the players' acceptance of a cap. However, it remains highly unlikely, at least until further notice, that the union would ever agree to such a thing.

The other major issue is a likely restructuring of the revenue-sharing system. Specifically, the next CBA is highly likely to revise the system so that local broadcast revenues are shared much more evenly. Fortunately, there's already some common ground on this issue, and a reordering of that system would directly address the revenue disparities within MLB that are such a reliable source of consternation – and misinformation – without the grievous labor war that a continued cap push would force upon us.

Otherwise, some other key wrinkles and changes may come out of the wash. That list potentially includes:

This doesn't get into evergreen matters like an increase in the minimum salary, draft bonus pools, the qualifying offer system, active roster sizes, and so forth. There's a lot to sort out, to say the least. The expectation is that the next CBA is going to lead to sweeping changes to the sport starting in 2027 and, perhaps by design, growing over time. Even if there's no cap and floor, the economic structure of MLB is almost certain to look very different after this winter.

Overall, this is one of the weakest free agent classes in living memory, but there is elite superstar value to be found at the tip-top with back-to-back (for the moment) American League Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal.

Skubal, who turns 30 on Nov. 20, remains foremost in the discussion for best pitcher in baseball, and he's going to be paid like it. The expectation is that he'll wind up signing the largest pitcher contract in MLB history and perhaps also fetch the highest-ever annual salary for a pitcher. It's not out of the question that Skubal's next contract could approach or even surpass $400 million in total value. At those rates, the incumbent Los Angeles Dodgers and the free-spending New York Mets are the consensus favorites. The Chicago Cubs are also reportedly heavily interested in Skubal, and surprise bidders are always possible. Other notable free agent names include Freddy Peralta, Michael King, Jazz Chisholm Jr., Trevor Rogers, Adrian Morejon, and Teruaki Sato. Our ranking of the top 50 2026-27 free agents has you covered.

The "when" of all this is more complicated thanks to the upcoming lockout detailed above. Will premium free agents and their representatives rush to find some stability in advance of the stoppage, during which no major-league transactions will be permitted, or will they decide that the long game will be better for their markets? It's possible that the biggest spenders on the team side will look to make moves early, as the barrel of the next CBA figures to be leveled directly at them and their abundant revenues. Or maybe the unknown will have a chilling effect on spending before we arrive at the lockout.

The past is not always prelude, but let's note that we saw a flurry of spending leading up to the lockout of 2021-22. Indeed, in November 2021, MLB teams committed more than $1.7 billion to free agents prior to the lockout. The Texas Rangers alone guaranteed $500 million to a new middle infield – Corey Seager and Marcus Semien – before the lockout put an end to such things. In all, teams put ink to paper on five nine-figure contracts prior to the 2021-22 lockout.

The comparisons may not entirely hold since this upcoming CBA should bring about a much more drastic re-ordering of the sport than the current expiring CBA did. As such, teams may proceed cautiously given all the uncertainties. Or, as just mentioned, they may seek to get business done before the ways of doing business change entirely. We'll see soon enough. If we do see the dollars start flying before the lockout, then the upcoming Nov. 10-12 general managers meetings in Las Vegas may occasion the groundwork for all those deals.

Will a lackluster free agent class mean more headline-grabbing trades? That may indeed be answered in the affirmative this winter. Yes, the CBA uncertainty will have a bearing on trades, especially those that involve the assumption of major salary obligations, but big trades still figure to be a prominent part of this offseason.

It's of course impossible to know who's going to be dealt ahead of time, but some big names perhaps on the move this winter include Francisco Lindor, Mason Miller, Spencer Strider, Hunter Greene, Otto Lopez, Jeremy Peña, Ketel Marte, Jacob deGrom, and of course others. Paul Skenes? Almost certainly not, but you'll just as certainly hear his name bandied about.

Turning back to last lockout, it was mostly minor trades before the sport shut down. Yes, we'll see big ones this time around, but they may not happen until we have a new CBA in place and the lockout is over.

Let's make time for the losers, shall we? The teams that didn't make the postseason in 2026 and otherwise qualify will take part in the draft lottery, which is presently scheduled for Dec. 8. That lottery will determine which teams get the top six picks in the 2027 MLB Draft.

This year, 16 of the 18 non-playoff teams will be in the lottery. Non-playoff teams can be barred from the lottery if they've had lottery picks in two consecutive seasons. If a team is a revenue-sharing payor, then it can't be in the lottery in consecutive years. Those wrinkles this year mean that the San Francisco Giants and Pittsburgh Pirates will not be in the lottery and can't pick higher than 10th in the 2027 Draft.

Here's how the preliminary lottery odds look for those 16 teams in the mix, based on how they finished the 2026 season:

It's too soon to know which players will be in the mix for that top pick since the amateur seasons haven't begun yet. However, two early favorites to go No. 1 are University of Florida shortstop Brendan Lawson and Mississippi State left-hander Tomas Valinicius.

#2660. NFL trade deadline: Jonathan Taylor leads candidates for offseason moves after staying put

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The deals that got across the finish line at the 2026 NFL trade deadline included a couple of blockbusters that shook up the balance of power at the front of the Super Bowl race. But just as meaningful were the moves that never materialized. For instance, the Cincinnati Bengals and Philadelphia Eagles called off an agreed-upon transaction that would have bolstered the former's defense. Even more significant than the nixed Arnold Ebiketie deal were the offers for Jonathan Taylor and other stars that never resulted in trades, either.

Taylor was supposed to be the belle of the ball at the deadline, but the Indianapolis Colts turned down interest from other teams when they did not receive the first-round pick they sought in a return package. Stars like George Pickens and other players like Will McDonald IV who would have been plug-and-play starters on other teams remained in place on their present rosters.

The players teams made and entertained calls on but did not switch at the deadline immediately became names to monitor ahead of the next trade window, which opens in the spring at the start of the 2027 league year.

Here are the 10 biggest names that did not change teams at the trade deadline but who could be on the move in the offseason.

The Indianapolis Colts were the most aggressive sellers at the trade deadline, but Jonathan Taylor was not among the four players they shipped out of town. The three-time Pro Bowler is a gargantuan asset because he is an elite-tier running back with no guaranteed money on his contract in 2027 or 2028, so he can remain an affordable and prolific foundational piece of the Colts' rebuild. Those same factors make him tremendously valuable on the trade market, though, and for a team that is going nowhere fast, it would behoove the Colts to take the right deal if it came to them in the offseason. They reportedly turned down offers that included second-round picks and more, so it will probably take at least a first-rounder to pry him away next spring or summer.

Unless the Dallas Cowboys re-sign George Pickens, they may regret not trading him. They likely could have garnered a sizable return package for their No. 2 wide receiver -- who would be a No. 1 on most teams -- and that would have arguably been the more prudent move than keeping him on a squad that is on the outside looking in on the playoff picture. Jerry Jones declined to sign Pickens to a long-term extension last offseason and could again use the franchise tag on the standout pass-catcher, but Pickens is worthy of a lucrative multi-year deal and may seek one elsewhere if Jones is hesitant again.

Will McDonald IV requested a trade from the New York Jets on the eve of the trade deadline, citing frustration with his playing time. He played 50% or more of the team's defensive snaps just three times over the first nine weeks and most recently saw only 24 snaps of work in Week 9. Darren Mougey did not heed his request, though, and retained him despite reported interest from other teams, including the Jacksonville Jaguars. New York has myriad options at edge rusher and will feature David Bailey most prominently in the years to come, so a clear path to a larger role may not manifest for McDonald. In that case, he could amplify his search for a trade in the offseason.

A reunion between Khalil Mack and the Chicago Bears would have made all the sense in the world, but the Los Angeles Chargers showed no interest in moving him, and the Bears used their draft capital on Jeffery Simmons instead. That the Chargers held onto all but one player despite their putrid 0-8 record was a major surprise. There were draft picks to be had for Mack, Ladd McConkey and even Justin Herbert, but the Chargers elected to keep their core intact even as it looks unsalvageable in a miserable campaign. Mack is a prime candidate to walk in free agency since he is in the latter stages of his career and would thus be more likely to seek a home on a contending squad rather than a bottom-dweller like Los Angeles.

Teams inquired about Tony Pollard, but none constructed a trade package strong enough for the Tennessee Titans to move on from him. The 29-year-old's value has never been higher on the heels of back-to-back 100-yard performances in which he totaled five touchdowns, and that could have played a role in the Titans driving a hard bargain. Retaining him is a short-term play that will allow Tennessee to continue to evaluate second-year quarterback Cam Ward but may not be much more than that since Pollard can leave in free agency if he pleases. At 29, he is not on the same career timeline as the rest of the team's offensive building blocks, anyway.

It makes ample sense for the Jacksonville Jaguars to hold onto anyone and everyone as they prepare for a potential Super Bowl run. If it ain't broke, don't fix it. But Brian Thomas Jr. is only a marginal part of their stellar passing attack and lost ground to Parker Washington and Jakobi Meyers in the pecking order for targets. His Pro Bowl-caliber rookie season looks more and more like a flash in the pan. Unless the Jaguars truly believe they can maximize the former first-round pick's talent in the final year of his contract, his situation will be one to revisit in the next trade window that opens in March. This is not dissimilar to the situation that led to Marvin Harrison Jr. being traded to the Houston Texans for a second-round pick and sixth-rounder, but the Jaguars are a contender and would reasonably prefer not to toy with their lineup until after the season.

Budda Baker is an Arizona Cardinals legend. If the 2026 trade deadline—when the Cardinals are projected as potential sellers amid on-field struggles —was not the time to move him, they may just let him play out his career in the desert. As the Cardinals' roster continues to shift in a younger direction, though, a split could make sense. Baker will be 31 when the 2027 league year begins, and the Cardinals are poised to take a quarterback in the first round of the draft, restarting the clock on their contention timeline. As an eight-time Pro Bowler still in his prime, Baker would garner the kind of return that would help Arizona load up on draft picks and build around that incoming quarterback.

As with the other trade candidates on expiring deals, Riq Woolen's potential exit in free agency could net the Philadelphia Eagles a valuable compensatory draft pick. That is probably the justification for keeping him, because Howie Roseman was willing to move on from some foundational pieces in the weeks leading up to the deadline, and Woolen seemed as tradeable as any of them. Woolen has been solid for the Eagles in pass defense but regressed from the standout level he performed at with the Seattle Seahawks -- his 103.3 passer rating allowed is by far a career-worst -- so Philadelphia may not aim to retain him on a multi-year deal regardless.

There have been rumblings of a possible Josh Sweat trade since the spring. Nothing came to fruition in the offseason, and the Arizona Cardinals stood pat at the trade deadline, too. But as the team remains mired in the early stages of a deep rebuild, any tensions between Sweat and the front office may grow louder in advance of his next opportunity to seek a way out. Sweat reportedly requested a trade last spring amid frustration with his contract, but both he and the team worked to quell that narrative over the last handful of months. It is clear that moving him is not a top priority for the Cardinals, but the standout pass rusher will be one to keep monitoring at the start of the new league year in 2027 in case that changes.

The Tennessee Titans have phased Calvin Ridley out of their receiving corps, with Carnell Tate, Wan'Dale Robinson, Elic Ayomanor, and Chimere Dike outproducing him in catches. Two tight ends and two running backs also have more targets than him this season. If he is no longer part of their plans, it makes little sense to retain him for the final year of his $92 million contract. His dead cap hit shrinks from $22.5 million to $7.5 million this spring, so if the idea behind keeping him on the roster is to maximize future financial flexibility, that decrease in liability should free things up on the books enough to move on from him at the start of the next league year.

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is a week old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. We've ranked the top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and built you a calendar of the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Thursday's hot stove happenings.

The Phillies will seek a left-handed setup man this offseason, reports The Athletic. Philadelphia has Tanner Banks and Tim Mayza, though both are middle-innings lefties more than high-leverage relievers. Manager Don Mattingly's late-inning unit is all righties at the moment: Jonathan Bowlan, Caleb Kilian, Jhoan Duran, and Alex McFarlane.

We ranked four lefty relievers among our top 50 free agents: Adrian Morejon (No. 2), JoJo Romero (No. 31), Alex Vesia (No. 35), and Kris Bubic (No. 45). Morejon and Bubic may get opportunities to start next season. Other free agent lefties include Tim Hill, A.J. MInter, Sean Newcomb, Steven Okert, AJ Puk, and former Phillie Gregory Soto.

The Yankees need almost an entirely new bullpen this offseason, and they have interest in re-signing setup man Paul Blackburn, according to the New York Daily News. New York tendered closer David Bednar the $23.15 million qualifying offer and seems likely to get him back, either on the QO or on a multi-year deal, but they will need to improve the setup crew regardless.

We ranked Blackburn as the No. 33 free agent this offseason. He had a terrific season with the Yankees in 2026, his first year as a full-time reliever. The Yankees have shown the ability to drum up quality relievers almost out of nowhere. They tend to let those guys leave as free agents, then build up someone else to replace them. This happened when Blackburn replaced Luke Weaver.

Among their list of wants this offseason, the Marlins will look to add to their rotation and bullpen, as well as a corner bat, reports the Miami Herald. That corner bat could be at first base, third base, left or right fields. Sandy Alcantara and Eury Pérez are the only locks for Miami's rotation, though Max Meyer should be ready to go next season following this year's neck injury.

Gold Glove finalist Javier Sanoja filled in at third base capably this year, though he fits best as a super utility man who plays all over. Owen Caissie, Griffin Conine, and Heriberto Hernández are Miami's corner outfield options, and Kyle Stowers moved from the outfield to first base in 2026. There are opportunities to improve aplenty for the Marlins.
